subtopic: Standard form with mass and counting
statement: A grain of sand has mass $6.4\times10^{-4}$ g. A sandbag contains $8\times10^{7}$ grains of sand. (a) Find the total mass of sand in the bag, in grams. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2] (b) Write your answer to part (a) in kilograms, in the form $a\times10^{k}$. [1] (c) A different bag holds $2.56\times10^{3}$ g of sand. Find the number of grains in this bag, giving your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$. [3]
tips: Multiply or divide the decimal parts and the powers of ten separately. Always finish by checking that the decimal part lies in $[1,10)$.

subtopic: Upper bounds and percentage error of a tank volume
statement: The length, width and height of a rectangular tank are measured as $2.4$ m, $1.8$ m and $1.5$ m, each correct to one decimal place. (a) Calculate the volume of the tank using these measured values. [1] (b) Find the greatest possible volume of the tank, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Suppose the true volume is the greatest possible volume. Find the percentage error in the volume calculated in part (a). Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the least possible volume of the tank, correct to three significant figures. [1]
tips: A measurement given to one decimal place can be up to $0.05$ away from the true value, so use $\pm0.05$ on each dimension. Percentage error is measured relative to the true value.

subtopic: Solving exponential equations and simplifying powers
statement: (a) Solve $4^{x+1}=8^{2x-3}$. [3] (b) Simplify $\left(27a^{6}b^{-3}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\div\left(ab^{-2}\right)$, giving your answer in the form $ka^{m}$, where $k,m\in\mathbb{Z}$. [3] (c) Show that $\sqrt{12}+\sqrt{27}=5\sqrt{3}$. [2]
tips: Write both sides of an exponential equation with the same base before equating the exponents. For fractional powers, apply the power to each factor separately.

subtopic: Laws of logarithms and logarithmic equations
statement: (a) Let $\log_2 x=a$ and $\log_2 y=b$. Express $\log_2\!\left(\dfrac{x^{3}\sqrt{y}}{8}\right)$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Solve $\log_3 x+\log_3(x-6)=3$. [4] (c) Solve $5^{2x-1}=7$, giving your answer in exact form in terms of natural logarithms. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\log_2 x^{3}+\log_2\sqrt{y}-\log_2 8$ [M1] $3a+\tfrac12 b$ [A1] $-3$, so $3a+\tfrac12 b-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\log_3\big(x(x-6)\big)=3$ [M1] $x^{2}-6x-27=0$ [A1] $x=9$ or $x=-3$ [A1] reject $x=-3$ because $\log_3(-3)$ is undefined, so $x=9$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $2x-1=\dfrac{\ln7}{\ln5}$ [M1] $x=\dfrac12\left(1+\dfrac{\ln7}{\ln5}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: After combining logarithms, always check each solution against the domain of the original equation. To solve $a^{u}=b$ take logarithms of both sides.

subtopic: Compound interest and effective annual rate
statement: Kavya invests \$15\,000 in an account that pays a nominal annual interest rate of $3.6\%$, compounded monthly. (a) Find the value of the investment after 8 years. Give your answer to the nearest cent. [2] (b) Find the number of complete months after which the value of the investment first exceeds \$25\,000. [3] (c) Find the effective annual interest rate, as a percentage correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: With a TVM solver use $I\%=3.6$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ and $N=96$. For part (b) the answer must be a whole number of months, so round up.

subtopic: Mortgage repayments and outstanding balance
statement: Marek takes out a loan of \$240\,000 to buy a flat. The loan has a nominal annual interest rate of $4.2\%$, compounded monthly. He makes equal repayments at the end of each month for 25 years. (a) Find the monthly repayment, correct to the nearest cent. [2] (b) Find the total interest paid over the 25 years, using the unrounded repayment. Give your answer to the nearest dollar. [2] (c) Find the outstanding balance after 10 years (120 repayments), to the nearest dollar. [2] (d) After 10 years Marek increases his monthly repayment to \$1500. Find the number of further repayments needed to clear the loan. The final repayment may be smaller than \$1500. [3]
tips: Enter the loan as a positive PV and the repayment as a negative PMT in your GDC finance solver. In part (d) a fractional answer for N means one more, smaller, repayment is needed, so round up.

subtopic: Depreciation rate from two values
statement: A machine is bought for \$48\,000. Each year its value falls by the same percentage $r\%$ of its value at the start of that year. After 3 years its value is \$30\,000. (a) Find the value of $r$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Using the unrounded value of $r$, find the value of the machine after 7 years, to the nearest dollar. [2] (c) Using the unrounded value of $r$, find the least number of complete years after which the value of the machine is below \$10\,000. [2]
tips: Use the unrounded growth factor $(0.625)^{1/3}$ from your calculator memory in parts (b) and (c). Check $n=10$ and $n=11$ directly, as the value after 10 years is just above \$10\,000.

subtopic: Two linear equations from ticket prices
statement: At a school concert, 3 adult tickets and 2 child tickets cost \$47 in total. 2 adult tickets and 5 child tickets cost \$68 in total. Let an adult ticket cost \$$a$ and a child ticket cost \$$c$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the equations to find $a$ and $c$. [3] (c) Find the cost of 4 adult tickets and 3 child tickets. [1]
tips: Multiply the equations so that one variable has equal coefficients, then subtract. Check your answers by substituting into the second original equation.

subtopic: Three-variable system with a parameter
statement: Consider the system of equations $x+2y+z=8$, $2x+y-z=1$, $3x+3y+kz=c$, where $k,c\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the system has a unique solution only if $k\neq0$. [3] (b) For $k=2$ and $c=15$, find the solution of the system. [2] (c) Let $k=0$. (i) Find the value of $c$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and write down the general solution in terms of a parameter. [4] (ii) State what can be said about the solutions when $k=0$ and $c$ takes any other value. [1]
markscheme: (a) the determinant of the coefficient matrix is computed (GDC): $\det=-3k$ [M1][A1] a unique solution exists if and only if $\det\neq0$, so $k\neq0$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) enter the augmented matrix or use a matrix solver [M1] $x=1,\ y=2,\ z=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c)(i) adding the first two equations gives $3x+3y=9$, so $x+y=3$ [M1] the third equation ($k=0$) is $3x+3y=c$, consistent only if $c=9$ [A1] with $x=t$: $y=3-t$ [A1] $z=2+t$ [A1] [4 marks] (ii) the equations are inconsistent, so there is no solution [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A zero determinant means no unique solution: you must then decide between no solutions and infinitely many by checking consistency. Verify your parametric solution in all three equations.

subtopic: Arithmetic with Cartesian complex numbers
statement: Let $z=3+4i$ and $w=1-2i$. (a) Find $zw$, giving your answer in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{z}{w}$, giving your answer in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Find the real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $(a+bi)(2-i)=5+5i$. [3]
tips: To divide complex numbers multiply by the conjugate of the denominator. To find unknown real and imaginary parts, expand and equate real and imaginary parts.

subtopic: Polar form products and powers
statement: Let $z=1+i\sqrt3$ and $w=-1+i$. (a) Write $z$ and $w$ in the form $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [4] (b) Hence find $zw$ in the form $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, where $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3] (c) Find $z^{6}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|z|=2$ [A1] $\arg z=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] $|w|=\sqrt2$ [A1] $\arg w=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) moduli multiply, arguments add: $2\sqrt2$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=\dfrac{13\pi}{12}$ [M1][A1] adjust to the required range: $2\sqrt2\left(\cos\!\left(-\dfrac{11\pi}{12}\right)+i\sin\!\left(-\dfrac{11\pi}{12}\right)\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z^{6}=2^{6}\left(\cos2\pi+i\sin2\pi\right)$ [M1] $=64$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch the point to choose the correct quadrant for the argument. After adding arguments, subtract $2\pi$ if the result is outside the stated range.

subtopic: Conjugate root theorem for a cubic
statement: The cubic equation $z^{3}+az^{2}+bz+20=0$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, has a root $1+2i$. (a) Write down a second root of the equation. [1] (b) Find the third root. [2] (c) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [3]
tips: Complex roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs. The product of the roots of $z^3+az^2+bz+d$ is $-d$, which gives the real root quickly.

subtopic: Phasor addition of alternating currents
statement: Two alternating currents in a circuit, in amperes, are modeled at time $t$ seconds by $I_1=6\cos(\omega t)$ and $I_2=4\cos\!\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, where $\omega=120\pi$. Each current is the real part of $z\,e^{i\omega t}$ for a complex number $z$. (a) Write down the complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$ for $I_1$ and $I_2$, giving $z_2$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) The total current $I_1+I_2$ is the real part of $(z_1+z_2)e^{i\omega t}$. Find the modulus and the argument of $z_1+z_2$, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Hence find the maximum value of the total current and the smallest positive value of $t$ at which it occurs. Give $t$ to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z_1=6$ [A1] $z_2=4e^{-i\pi/3}=2-2\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z_1+z_2=8-2\sqrt3\,i$ [M1] modulus $=\sqrt{76}=8.72$ [A1] argument $=-0.409$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $I_1+I_2=8.72\cos(\omega t-0.409)$, so the maximum current is $8.72$ A [A1] maximum when $120\pi t-0.4086=0$ [M1] $t=0.00108$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Writing each current as the real part of $z e^{i\omega t}$ turns the sum of two sinusoids into addition of complex numbers. Set the phase equal to $0$ to find where the cosine is maximal.

subtopic: Inverse matrix and solving matrix equations
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det A$. [1] (b) Find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) Hence solve $A\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (d) The matrix $B$ satisfies $AB=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. Find $B$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4(2)-3(2)=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $A^{-1}=\dfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $x=1,\ y=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $B=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ (multiplying on the left) [M1] $=\dfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: from $AB=C$ you get $B=A^{-1}C$, not $CA^{-1}$. Check by multiplying $A$ by your answer.

subtopic: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and powers of a matrix
statement: Let $M=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the eigenvalues of $M$ are $2$ and $5$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [2] (c) Write down matrices $P$ and $D$, with $D$ diagonal, such that $M=PDP^{-1}$. [2] (d) Hence find $M^{6}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(M-\lambda I)=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2$ [M1] $\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+10=0$ [A1] $\lambda=2$ or $5$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda=5$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=2$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [2 marks] (c) $P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $D=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $M^{6}=PD^{6}P^{-1}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 10438 & 5187 \\ 10374 & 5251 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The columns of $P$ must be listed in the same order as the eigenvalues in $D$. Check your final matrix by confirming that its trace equals $5^{6}+2^{6}=15689$.

subtopic: Three-state Markov chain for bike-share stations
statement: A city has three bike-share stations $A$, $B$ and $C$. Each night every bike is returned to a station, and the stations of bikes after one day are described by the transition matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.6 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$, where the columns give the probabilities of moving from $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. At the start of Monday there are 500 bikes at $A$, 300 at $B$ and 200 at $C$. (a) Interpret the entry $0.3$ in $T$. [1] (b) Find the expected number of bikes at each station after two days. [3] (c) Find the expected long-term number of bikes at each station, giving answers to one decimal place. [3] (d) Find the smallest number of days after which the expected number of bikes at $A$ is below $360$. [3] (e) State one reason why the model may not be realistic. [1]
markscheme: (a) the probability that a bike at $C$ is at $B$ after one day is $0.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $T^{2}\begin{pmatrix} 500 \\ 300 \\ 200 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix} 392 \\ 359 \\ 249 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] (A: 392, B: 359, C: 249) [3 marks] (c) solve $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $s_A+s_B+s_C=1000$, or compute a high power of $T$ [M1] proportions $\dfrac{10}{29},\dfrac{11}{29},\dfrac{8}{29}$ [A1] $344.8,\ 379.3,\ 275.9$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) number at $A$ after $n$ days: $371.1$ ($n=3$), $359.51$ ($n=4$) [M1][A1] smallest $n=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) for example: bike movements may depend on the day of the week; or bikes are removed for repair; the probabilities are unlikely to be constant [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Check that every column of $T$ sums to $1$ before multiplying, and apply $T$ to a column vector on the right. For the long-term distribution use the eigenvalue $1$ eigenvector, scaled to the total of $1000$ bikes.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain with exact steady state
statement: A streaming service has Basic and Premium subscribers. Each month, $20\%$ of Basic subscribers upgrade to Premium and $30\%$ of Premium subscribers downgrade to Basic. Everyone else stays on the same plan. Let $T$ be the transition matrix, with the state vector written as (Basic, Premium). (a) Write down $T$. [2] (b) Initially there are 1000 subscribers, all on Basic. Find the number of subscribers on each plan after two months. [3] (c) Find the eigenvalues of $T$. [3] (d) Find the long-term number of Basic subscribers. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each correct column) [2 marks] (b) after one month $\begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] after two months $T\begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 700 \\ 300 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] 700 Basic and 300 Premium [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(0.8-\lambda)(0.7-\lambda)-0.06=0$ [M1] $\lambda^{2}-1.5\lambda+0.5=0$ [A1] $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=0.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) eigenvector for $\lambda=1$: $-0.2x+0.3y=0$, so $y=\dfrac23x$ [M1] $x+y=1$ gives $x=0.6$ [A1] long-term Basic $=600$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The columns of a transition matrix sum to $1$, so $1$ is always an eigenvalue. The steady state is the eigenvector for $\lambda=1$ scaled so its entries sum to the total population.

subtopic: Currency exchange with commission
statement: Anika exchanges 850 British pounds (GBP) for Japanese yen (JPY) at a rate of $1$ GBP $=187.35$ JPY. The bank charges a commission of $1.5\%$ on the yen received. (a) Find the number of yen Anika receives, to the nearest yen. [2] (b) During her trip she spends 124\,000 JPY. She exchanges the rest back into GBP at a rate of $1$ GBP $=190.20$ JPY. The bank charges a commission of $1.5\%$ on the pounds received. Find the amount she receives, to the nearest penny. [3] (c) Find the net cost in GBP of Anika's trip money, that is the amount she paid minus the amount she got back. [1]
tips: Apply the commission once, to the amount received, and keep track of which currency each figure is in. Divide by the rate when converting yen back to pounds.

subtopic: Rounding, estimation and percentage error
statement: Consider the expression $E=\dfrac{48.7\times2.04}{0.0097}$. (a) Write down $0.0047963$ correct to three significant figures. [1] (b) Estimate the value of $E$ by rounding each number to one significant figure. [2] (c) Use your GDC to calculate $E$. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, with $a$ correct to three significant figures. [1] (d) Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (b), using the value from part (c) as the exact value. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit, so $0.00480$ keeps the trailing zero. For percentage error use the unrounded GDC value, not the three significant figure answer.

subtopic: Logarithmic scale for earthquake energy
statement: The energy $E$ joules released by an earthquake of magnitude $M$ satisfies $\log_{10}E=4.8+1.5M$. (a) Find the energy released by an earthquake of magnitude $6.3$. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2] (b) Show that an earthquake of magnitude $7.1$ releases about $15.8$ times as much energy as one of magnitude $6.3$. [3] (c) An earthquake releases $1000$ times as much energy as one of magnitude $6.3$. Find its magnitude. [2]
tips: Subtracting two logarithms gives the logarithm of a ratio, so a change in the exponent corresponds to a multiplication of the energy. Multiplying energy by $10^{3}$ adds $3$ to $\log_{10}E$.

subtopic: Cube roots of a negative real number
statement: (a) Solve the equation $z^{3}=-8$, giving the three roots in the form $a+bi$. [5] (b) Write down the sum of the three roots. [1] (c) In the complex plane, the three roots are the vertices of a triangle. Find the exact area of this triangle. [3]
markscheme: (a) $-8=8(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi)$ [M1] $z=2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}\right)$ [M1] $z=1+\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] $z=-2$ [A1] $z=1-\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $0$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) base between $1\pm\sqrt3 i$ has length $2\sqrt3$ [A1] perpendicular height from $-2$ to the line $x=1$ is $3$ [A1] area $=\dfrac12(2\sqrt3)(3)=3\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the right-hand side in polar form and add multiples of $2\pi$ to the argument before dividing by $3$. The $n$ roots of $z^{n}=w$ are equally spaced on a circle, which makes areas and symmetry easy to see.

subtopic: Regular deposits into a savings annuity
statement: Rhea deposits \$400 at the end of every month into an account that pays a nominal annual interest rate of $3.9\%$, compounded monthly. (a) Find the value of the account immediately after the last deposit at the end of 12 years. Give your answer to the nearest cent. [2] (b) Find the least number of monthly deposits needed for the account to exceed \$100\,000. [3] (c) After 12 years find (i) the total amount Rhea has deposited; (ii) the interest earned, to the nearest dollar. [2]
tips: Use a TVM solver with $PV=0$ and a negative PMT for deposits. When solving for $N$ always round up to the next whole deposit.

subtopic: Retirement fund with start-of-year withdrawals
statement: A retirement fund of \$350\,000 earns interest at $4.5\%$ per year, compounded annually. Withdrawals of \$30\,000 are made at the start of each year, the first withdrawal being made immediately. (a) Show that the balance at the end of the first year, after the first withdrawal and the interest, is \$334\,400. [2] (b) Find the number of complete withdrawals of \$30\,000 that can be made. [3] (c) Find the largest equal annual withdrawal, to the nearest dollar, that allows exactly 20 withdrawals to be made, with the balance zero after the last. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(350000-30000)\times1.045$ [M1] $=334\,400$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) balance after $n$ withdrawals and a year's interest: $334400,\ 318098,\ \ldots$ (use a sequence or TVM in begin mode) [M1] after the 14th withdrawal the balance is $\$54\,659\ge30000$ [A1] after the 15th withdrawal the balance is $\$25\,769<30000$, so 15 complete withdrawals [A1] [3 marks] (c) TVM in BEGIN mode: $N=20$, $I\%=4.5$, $PV=-350000$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=C/Y=1$ [M1][M1] $PMT=\$25\,748$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Withdrawals at the start of a year are an annuity due: set your GDC payment mode to BEGIN. Check part (b) by listing balances year by year.

subtopic: Three-feed mixture using a matrix solver
statement: A gardener mixes three feeds $A$, $B$ and $C$. Each kilogram of feed $A$ contains 2 units of nitrogen, 1 unit of phosphorus and 3 units of potassium. Feed $B$ contains 3, 2 and 1 units per kilogram and feed $C$ contains 1, 4 and 2 units per kilogram, in the same order. The mixture must contain exactly 22 units of nitrogen, 30 units of phosphorus and 25 units of potassium. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the masses in kilograms of feeds $A$, $B$ and $C$. (a) Write down three equations in $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (b) Find the values of $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (c) Feeds $A$, $B$ and $C$ cost \$1.20, \$0.80 and \$1.50 per kilogram respectively. Find the cost of the mixture. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2x+3y+z=22$ [A1] $x+2y+4z=30$ and $3x+y+2z=25$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) enter the coefficient matrix and use the inverse or system solver [M1] $x=4,\ y=3,\ z=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1.20(4)+0.80(3)+1.50(5)$ [M1] $=\$14.70$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each row of the system corresponds to one nutrient. Check the solution by substituting into all three equations.

subtopic: Successive percentage changes and reverse percentages
statement: In a sale, the price of a jacket is reduced by $20\%$, and then the sale price is reduced by a further $15\%$. The final price is \$68. (a) Find the original price of the jacket. [3] (b) Find the overall percentage reduction from the original price to the final price. [2] (c) The shop wants to raise the final price back to the original price. Find the percentage increase needed, giving your answer as an exact fraction. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.8\times0.85\times P=68$ [M1] $0.68P=68$ [A1] $P=\$100$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) final price is $68\%$ of the original [M1] reduction $=32\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{100-68}{68}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{8}{17}$, that is $\dfrac{800}{17}\%$ ($\approx47.1\%$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Successive percentage changes multiply, they do not add. A percentage increase is always measured from the starting price of that step, here the \$68.

subtopic: Eigenvalue condition with an unknown matrix entry
statement: The matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix} k & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ has an eigenvalue $4$. (a) Show that $k=2$. [3] (b) Find the other eigenvalue of $M$. [2] (c) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(M-4I)=(k-4)(3-4)-2=0$ [M1] $4-k-2=0$ [A1] $k=2$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) trace $=k+3=5$, so the eigenvalues sum to $5$ [M1] other eigenvalue $=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\lambda=4$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [2 marks]
tips: If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue then $\det(M-\lambda I)=0$. The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace, which saves solving a quadratic.

subtopic: Complex conjugate equation and modulus-argument
statement: The complex number $z=a+bi$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, satisfies $2z+3z^{*}=10-3i$, where $z^{*}$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. (a) Find $z$. [3] (b) Find the modulus and the argument of $z$, giving each to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find $z^{2}$ in the form $c+di$. [1]
tips: Substitute $z=a+bi$ and $z^{*}=a-bi$, then equate real and imaginary parts. Give the argument in radians unless told otherwise.

subtopic: Distance in light-years and percentage error in light speed
statement: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. Take the speed of light as $3.00\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and a year as $365.25$ days. (a) Show that one light-year is approximately $9.47\times10^{12}$ km. [2] (b) A star is $4.24$ light-years from Earth. Find its distance in kilometers, giving your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, with $a$ correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) A probe travels towards the star at a constant speed of $1.50\times10^{4}$ km s$^{-1}$. Using the unrounded distance from part (b), find the time taken in years, to three significant figures. [3] (d) The exact speed of light is $299\,792\,458$ m s$^{-1}$. Find the percentage error in using $3.00\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Convert units carefully: $1$ m s$^{-1}$ is $10^{-3}$ km s$^{-1}$, and a year is $365.25\times24\times3600$ seconds. For percentage error, divide by the exact value.

subtopic: Sigma notation and arithmetic series
statement: (a) Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{12}(3k+4)$. [3] (b) Given that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}(3k+4)=140$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$, show that $3n^{2}+11n-280=0$ and hence find $n$. [4]
tips: Identify the first term and common difference from the first two values of $k$, then use $S_n=\frac{n}{2}(2u_1+(n-1)d)$. Reject any root that is not a positive integer.

subtopic: Recurring decimals as geometric series
statement: (a) Write $0.272727\ldots$ as the sum of an infinite geometric series and hence express it as a fraction in its simplest form. [3] (b) Show that $0.4363636\ldots=\dfrac{24}{55}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $0.27+0.0027+0.000027+\cdots$ with $u_1=0.27$ and $r=0.01$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{0.27}{1-0.01}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{27}{99}=\dfrac{3}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $0.4+0.036+0.00036+\cdots$ where the recurring part is geometric with $u_1=0.036$ and $r=0.01$ [M1] recurring part $=\dfrac{0.036}{0.99}=\dfrac{2}{55}$ [A1] $\dfrac25+\dfrac{2}{55}=\dfrac{22}{55}+\dfrac{2}{55}=\dfrac{24}{55}$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: Split the decimal into the non-recurring part and a geometric series whose ratio is a power of $\tfrac{1}{10}$ matching the repeating block length. Then add the fractions over a common denominator.

subtopic: Sum to infinity and convergence condition
statement: A geometric series has first term $8$ and sum to infinity $20$. (a) Find the common ratio. [2] (b) Find the third term. [1] A second geometric series has first term $5$ and common ratio $\dfrac{x-1}{3}$. (c) Find the set of values of $x$ for which the second series converges. [3] (d) The sum to infinity of the second series is $3$. Find the value of $x$. [2]
tips: The sum to infinity exists only when $|r|<1$. In part (d) check that your answer lies inside the interval found in part (c).

subtopic: Arithmetic training plan distances
statement: A runner follows a training plan. In week 1 she runs 12 km. In each following week she runs 1.5 km more than in the previous week. (a) Find the distance she runs in week 13. [2] (b) Find the total distance she runs in the first 16 weeks. [2] (c) Find the first week in which she runs more than 35 km. [2] (d) Find the first week by which her total distance since week 1 first reaches at least 500 km. [2]
tips: Use the arithmetic formulas with $u_1=12$ and $d=1.5$. For part (d) solve with a table of values on your GDC and check the weeks either side of the boundary.

subtopic: Drug accumulation modeled by a geometric series
statement: A patient takes a 200 mg dose of a drug at the start of each day. During each 24 hours, $35\%$ of the drug present in the body is eliminated. Let $A_n$ be the amount of the drug, in mg, in the body immediately after the $n$th dose. (a) Show that $A_2=330$ and find $A_3$. [2] (b) Show that $A_n=\dfrac{200\left(1-0.65^{n}\right)}{0.35}$. [3] (c) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $A_n>500$. [2] (d) Find the value that $A_n$ approaches in the long term. Hence state whether a dose-limit of $600$ mg is ever exceeded. [2]
tips: Write $A_n$ as the sum of the doses still present, each scaled by $0.65$ for every day it has spent in the body. For the long-term value, let $0.65^{n}\to0$.

subtopic: Comparing geometric and arithmetic savings deposits
statement: Two savings plans do not earn interest; the question is about the deposits. Under Plan A, Dev deposits \$2000 in year 1 and each year deposits $5\%$ more than in the previous year. Under Plan B, Dev deposits \$2500 in year 1 and each year deposits \$80 more than in the previous year. (a) Find the deposit in year 10 under each plan, to the nearest cent. [2] (b) Find the total deposited in the first 10 years under each plan, to the nearest cent. [3] (c) Find the smallest number of years for which the total deposited under Plan A exceeds the total deposited under Plan B. [3] (d) Explain why Plan A exceeds Plan B for all larger numbers of years. [1]
markscheme: (a) A: $2000(1.05)^{9}=\$3102.66$ [A1] B: $2500+9(80)=\$3220.00$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) A: $\dfrac{2000(1.05^{10}-1)}{0.05}$ [M1] $=\$25\,155.79$ [A1] B: $\dfrac{10}{2}\left(5000+9(80)\right)=\$28\,600.00$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{2000(1.05^{n}-1)}{0.05}>\dfrac{n}{2}\left(5000+80(n-1)\right)$ [M1] GDC graph or table: $n=19$ gives $61\,078<61\,180$ [M1] $n=20$ gives $66\,132>65\,200$, so $n=20$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) From year 12 onward the yearly deposit under Plan A exceeds that under Plan B (for example $3421>3380$) and the difference keeps growing, so after the totals cross at $n=20$ the gap keeps widening [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Plan A is geometric with $r=1.05$ and Plan B is arithmetic with $d=80$. For the crossing point use a table on your GDC and check the year just before the first time the inequality holds.

subtopic: Declining oil output as a geometric sequence
statement: An oil field produces 4.2 million barrels in its first year. Each year the output is $94\%$ of the output in the previous year. (a) Find the output in year 6, in millions of barrels, to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the total output in the first 10 years, in millions of barrels, to three significant figures. [2] (c) The field is closed in the first year in which the output is below 2.5 million barrels. Find the year in which the field is closed. [2] (d) Find the total output the field would produce if it could operate indefinitely. [2]
markscheme: (a) $4.2(0.94)^{5}$ [M1] $=3.08$ million barrels [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{4.2\left(1-0.94^{10}\right)}{1-0.94}$ [M1] $=32.3$ million barrels [A1] [2 marks] (c) $4.2(0.94)^{n-1}<2.5$ [M1] year 9 gives $2.56$ and year 10 gives $2.41$, so year $10$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{4.2}{1-0.94}$ [M1] $=70$ million barrels [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The output in year $n$ is $u_n=u_1r^{n-1}$, so year 6 uses the power $5$. Check the years either side of the boundary in part (c) to avoid an off-by-one error.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence whose terms form a geometric sequence
statement: An arithmetic sequence has first term $5$ and common difference $d$, where $d\neq0$. The second, fifth and fourteenth terms of the arithmetic sequence are the first three terms of a geometric sequence. (a) Show that $d=10$. [4] (b) Write down the common ratio of the geometric sequence. [1] (c) Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the arithmetic sequence. [2] (d) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which the sum of the first $n$ terms of the geometric sequence exceeds $10^{6}$. [3]
tips: Three terms $a,b,c$ are geometric when $b^{2}=ac$. Remember to use the condition $d\neq0$ to discard the root $d=0$ that appears when you factorize.

subtopic: Stacked logs and partial sums of an arithmetic series
statement: Logs are stacked in rows. The bottom row has 28 logs and each row above has one log fewer than the row below it. The top row has 1 log. (a) Show that row $n$, counting from the bottom, has $29-n$ logs. [1] (b) Find the total number of logs in the complete stack. [2] (c) Only 300 logs are available. Find the number of complete rows that can be built starting from the bottom. [3] (d) Find the number of logs left over. [1]
markscheme: (a) arithmetic with $u_1=28$ and $d=-1$, so $u_n=28-(n-1)=29-n$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $28$ rows: $S_{28}=\dfrac{28}{2}(28+1)$ [M1] $=406$ logs [A1] [2 marks] (c) $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(28+(29-n)\right)=\dfrac{n(57-n)}{2}\le300$ [M1] $n=13$ gives $286$ and $n=14$ gives $301>300$ [M1] $13$ complete rows [A1] [3 marks] (d) $300-286=14$ logs [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When the total is capped, test consecutive values of $n$ rather than rounding the root of the equation. A row may only be built if there are enough logs left to complete it.

subtopic: Annuities and perpetuities with geometric series
statement: This question investigates savings plans and endowment funds using geometric series. In all parts, interest is compounded annually at an annual rate $r$ and payments are made at the end of each year. (a) A saver deposits \$$P$ at the end of each year, starting at the end of year 1. Show that the value of the account immediately after the $n$th deposit is $\dfrac{P\left((1+r)^{n}-1\right)}{r}$. [3] (b) Anya deposits \$1200 at the end of each year at $r=0.035$. (i) Find the value of her account immediately after the 15th deposit, to the nearest dollar. [1] (ii) Find the least number of deposits needed for the account to exceed \$30\,000. [3] (c) A scholarship fund pays \$$X$ at the end of each year, forever. The present value of the payment made at the end of year $k$ is $\dfrac{X}{(1+r)^{k}}$. (i) Show that the total present value of all the payments is $\dfrac{X}{r}$. [4] (ii) Find the amount needed to fund a scholarship of \$6000 per year when $r=0.04$. [1] (d) A donor gives only \$120\,000 to a fund with $r=0.04$, which pays \$6000 at the end of each year. Let $B_n$ be the balance of the fund immediately after the $n$th payment. (i) Show that $B_n=150\,000-30\,000(1.04)^{n}$. [4] (ii) Find the number of full payments of \$6000 that the fund can make, and the balance immediately after the last full payment, to the nearest dollar. [4] (e) The scholarship now rises by $2\%$ each year, so the payment at the end of year $k$ is $6000(1.02)^{k-1}$. With $r=0.04$, show that the total present value of all the payments is \$300\,000. [3] (f) A fund of \$200\,000 pays the rising scholarship from part (e), and the balance after the $n$th payment is $B_n=300\,000(1.02)^{n}-100\,000(1.04)^{n}$. Find the number of full payments the fund can make. [3] (g) State two assumptions made in this model that may not hold in practice. [2]
markscheme: (a) value $=P(1+r)^{n-1}+P(1+r)^{n-2}+\cdots+P$ [M1] geometric series with first term $P$ and common ratio $(1+r)$, $n$ terms [A1] $S_n=\dfrac{P\left((1+r)^{n}-1\right)}{(1+r)-1}=\dfrac{P\left((1+r)^{n}-1\right)}{r}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b)(i) $\dfrac{1200\left(1.035^{15}-1\right)}{0.035}=\$23\,155$ [A1] (ii) $\dfrac{1200\left(1.035^{n}-1\right)}{0.035}>30000$ [M1] $n>18.27$ (logarithms or GDC) [A1] $n=19$ [A1] [4 marks] (c)(i) first term $\dfrac{X}{1+r}$ and common ratio $\dfrac{1}{1+r}$ [A1] $\left|\dfrac{1}{1+r}\right|<1$ so the series converges [R1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{X/(1+r)}{1-\frac{1}{1+r}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{X}{r}$ [AG] (ii) $\dfrac{6000}{0.04}=\$150\,000$ [A1] [5 marks] (d)(i) $B_n=120000(1.04)^{n}-\dfrac{6000\left((1.04)^{n}-1\right)}{0.04}$ [M1][A1] $=120000(1.04)^{n}-150000(1.04)^{n}+150000$ [M1] $=150000-30000(1.04)^{n}$ [AG] (ii) payment $n$ can be made if $B_n\ge0$: $(1.04)^{n}\le5$ [M1] $n\le\dfrac{\ln5}{\ln1.04}=41.03$ [A1] 41 full payments [A1] $B_{41}=\$208$ [A1] [8 marks] (e) first term $\dfrac{6000}{1.04}$ and common ratio $\dfrac{1.02}{1.04}$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{6000/1.04}{1-\frac{1.02}{1.04}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6000}{0.02}=\$300\,000$ [AG] [3 marks] (f) $B_n\ge0$ gives $3(1.02)^{n}\ge(1.04)^{n}$ [M1] $n\ln\dfrac{1.04}{1.02}\le\ln3$, so $n\le56.58$ [M1] $56$ full payments [A1] [3 marks] (g) for example: the interest rate stays constant for decades [A1] the scholarship grows at exactly $2\%$ per year (inflation is constant) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Parts (a) and (c) are geometric series results: identify the first term, the common ratio and the number of terms before using the formula. In part (d)(ii) a payment can only be made if the balance after it is not negative, so test $B_n\ge0$.

subtopic: Quotient rule and stationary points of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}+1}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{2-2x^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{2}}$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the origin. [2]
tips: Write down $u$, $v$, $u'$ and $v'$ before applying the quotient rule. A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero, so you can ignore the denominator when finding stationary points.

subtopic: Tangent and normal to a trigonometric curve
statement: Let $f(x)=3\cos(2x)+4x$, for $0\le x\le\pi$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, giving your answer in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Find the $x$-intercept of this tangent. [1] (d) Find the equation of the normal to the graph of $f$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=-6\sin(2x)+4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=3\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\pi=\pi$ [A1] $f'\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=-6+4=-2$ and $y-\pi=-2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [M1] $y=-2x+\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) normal gradient $=\dfrac12$ [M1] $y-\pi=\dfrac12\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use radians throughout. The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.

subtopic: Second derivative and points of inflection with a Gaussian factor
statement: Let $f(x)=xe^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\left(1-x^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$. [3] (b) Show that $f''(x)=\left(x^{3}-3x\right)e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$. [3] (c) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection of the graph of $f$, justifying that the concavity changes. [3] (d) Find the coordinates of the local maximum point. [2]
markscheme: (a) product rule with $u=x$ and $v=e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [M1] $f'(x)=e^{-x^{2}/2}+x\left(-x\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [A1] $=\left(1-x^{2}\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $f''(x)=-2xe^{-x^{2}/2}+\left(1-x^{2}\right)\left(-x\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [M1][A1] $=\left(x^{3}-3x\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $f''(x)=0$ gives $x\left(x^{2}-3\right)=0$ [M1] $x=0,\ \pm\sqrt3$ [A1] each root is simple so the sign of $f''$ changes at each [R1] [3 marks] (d) $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=\pm1$ and $f''(1)=-2e^{-1/2}<0$ [M1] local maximum at $\left(1,e^{-1/2}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The exponential factor is never zero, so factorize it out and solve the polynomial factor. A zero of $f''$ is a point of inflection only if $f''$ changes sign there.

subtopic: Maximizing the volume of an open box
statement: An open box is made from a rectangular metal sheet of length 48 cm and width 30 cm by cutting a square of side $x$ cm from each corner and folding up the sides. (a) Show that the volume of the box is $V=4x^{3}-156x^{2}+1440x$. [2] (b) State the possible values of $x$. [1] (c) Use calculus to find the value of $x$ that gives the maximum volume, justifying that it is a maximum. [4] (d) Find the maximum volume. [1]
tips: State the domain from the geometry: each cut must leave positive length and width. Reject any stationary point outside the domain and justify the maximum with $V''$.

subtopic: Minimizing trip cost with a speed limit
statement: A delivery truck makes a 400 km trip at a constant speed of $v$ km h$^{-1}$. The driver is paid \$45 per hour. The fuel cost for the whole trip is \$$0.018v^{2}$. Let \$$C$ be the total cost of the trip. (a) Show that $C(v)=\dfrac{18\,000}{v}+0.018v^{2}$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dC}{dv}$. [2] (c) Find the speed that minimizes the cost, and the minimum cost, to three significant figures. [3] (d) The speed limit on the route is $70$ km h$^{-1}$. Find the minimum possible cost of the trip, to the nearest cent, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) time $=\dfrac{400}{v}$ hours [M1] wages $=45\times\dfrac{400}{v}=\dfrac{18000}{v}$, so $C=\dfrac{18000}{v}+0.018v^{2}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=-\dfrac{18000}{v^{2}}+0.036v$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) solve $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$ [M1] $v=79.4$ km h$^{-1}$ [A1] $C=\$340$ ($340.18$) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $C'(v)<0$ for $0<v<79.4$, so $C$ decreases up to the limit and the least cost is at $v=70$ [R1] $C(70)=\$345.34$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A constrained optimization problem may have its minimum at the boundary rather than at the stationary point. Check the sign of $C'$ on the allowed interval.

subtopic: Particle kinematics with a cubic displacement
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its displacement from a fixed point $O$ is $s=2t^{3}-15t^{2}+36t$ meters, for $0\le t\le5$, where $t$ is in seconds. (a) Find expressions for the velocity $v$ and the acceleration $a$ at time $t$. [2] (b) Find the times when the particle is momentarily at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the first 5 seconds. [3] (d) Find the minimum velocity of the particle during the first 5 seconds. [2]
tips: Distance is not the same as displacement: split the journey at each time when $v=0$ and add the absolute changes. A minimum of $v$ occurs where $a=0$ with $a'>0$.

subtopic: Drug concentration, maximum and fastest decrease
statement: The concentration of a drug in a patient's blood, in mg per liter, is modeled by $C(t)=20te^{-0.5t}$, where $t\ge0$ is the time in hours after the drug is taken. (a) Find $C'(t)$. [3] (b) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs. [3] (c) Find the rate of change of the concentration when $t=1$, to three significant figures. [1] (d) Find the time at which the concentration is decreasing at its greatest rate. [2]
markscheme: (a) product rule [M1] $C'(t)=20e^{-0.5t}+20t\left(-0.5\right)e^{-0.5t}$ [A1] $=20e^{-0.5t}(1-0.5t)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $C'(t)=0$ gives $t=2$ [M1][A1] $C(2)=40e^{-1}=14.7$ mg/L [A1] [3 marks] (c) $C'(1)=10e^{-0.5}=6.07$ mg L$^{-1}$ h$^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) the rate of decrease is greatest where $C'$ is a minimum, so find the minimum of $C'(t)$ with the GDC (or solve $C''(t)=0$) [M1] $t=4$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The fastest decrease of $C$ corresponds to the minimum of $C'$, which is a point of inflection of $C$. Use your GDC to find the minimum of the derivative graph.

subtopic: Tangent, normal and gradient conditions for a logarithmic curve
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln\left(x^{2}+3\right)$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at $x=1$, in the form $y=mx+c$ with $m$ and $c$ correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) The normal to the graph at $x=1$ meets the $x$-axis at the point $P$. Find the $x$-coordinate of $P$, to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the values of $x$ for which the gradient of the graph is $0.3$. [2]
tips: The derivative of $\ln u$ is $u'/u$. In part (d) rearrange into a quadratic equation, or use your GDC to find the intersections of $y=f'(x)$ with $y=0.3$.

subtopic: Closest point on a logarithmic curve to a given point
statement: The point $P$ has coordinates $(5,0)$. The point $Q(x,\ln x)$ lies on the curve $y=\ln x$, for $x>0$. Let $D$ be the distance $PQ$. (a) Show that $D^{2}=(x-5)^{2}+(\ln x)^{2}$. [1] (b) Find the value of $x$ for which $PQ$ is a minimum, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the minimum value of $PQ$, to three significant figures. [2] (d) Show that, at this minimum, the line $PQ$ is perpendicular to the tangent to the curve at $Q$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $D^{2}=(x-5)^{2}+(\ln x-0)^{2}$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) minimizing $D^{2}$ is equivalent to minimizing $D$ [M1] solve $\dfrac{d\left(D^{2}\right)}{dx}=2(x-5)+\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}=0$ with the GDC (or find the minimum of the graph) [M1] $x=4.67$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $D^{2}=2.484\ldots$ [M1] $PQ=1.58$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) gradient of the tangent $=\dfrac1x=0.2141\ldots$ [A1] gradient of $PQ=\dfrac{\ln x}{x-5}=-4.670\ldots$ [A1] product $=-1$, so perpendicular [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Minimizing $D^{2}$ gives the same $x$ as minimizing $D$ and avoids a square root. Use the unrounded value of $x$ from your GDC when checking perpendicularity in part (d).

subtopic: Investigating the family x e^(-kx) as a drug concentration model
statement: This question investigates the family of functions $f(x)=xe^{-kx}$, for $x\ge0$ and $k>0$, which can model the concentration of a drug in the bloodstream. (a) Show that $f'(x)=(1-kx)e^{-kx}$. [2] (b) Find, in terms of $k$, the coordinates of the local maximum point of the graph of $f$, and justify that it is a maximum. [4] (c) Show that $f''(x)=k(kx-2)e^{-kx}$, and hence show that the graph of $f$ has exactly one point of inflection. Find its coordinates in terms of $k$. [5] (d) The concentration of a drug, in mg per liter, $t$ hours after it is taken is $C(t)=40te^{-0.5t}$. (i) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs. [2] (ii) Find the length of time for which the concentration exceeds 20 mg per liter, to three significant figures. [3] (e) Show that the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point of inflection meets the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{4}{k}$. [4] (f) For the drug in part (d), use the result of part (e) to estimate when the drug is cleared from the blood. Find the actual concentration at that time, and comment on the estimate. [3] (g) A different drug has concentration $C(t)=Ate^{-kt}$. Its concentration is greatest at $t=3$ hours, where it equals 30 mg per liter. Find $k$ and $A$. [4]
markscheme: (a) product rule with $u=x$ and $v=e^{-kx}$ [M1] $f'(x)=e^{-kx}-kxe^{-kx}=(1-kx)e^{-kx}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=0$ and $e^{-kx}>0$ so $1-kx=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac1k$ [A1] $f\!\left(\dfrac1k\right)=\dfrac{1}{ek}$, so $\left(\dfrac1k,\dfrac{1}{ek}\right)$ [A1] $f'>0$ for $x<\dfrac1k$ and $f'<0$ for $x>\dfrac1k$, so a maximum [R1] [4 marks] (c) $f''(x)=-ke^{-kx}+(1-kx)(-k)e^{-kx}$ [M1] $=k(kx-2)e^{-kx}$ [AG] $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=\dfrac2k$ [A1] $f''$ changes from negative to positive at $x=\dfrac2k$, so exactly one point of inflection [R1] $\left(\dfrac2k,\dfrac{2}{ke^{2}}\right)$ [A1] [5 marks] (d)(i) $C=40f$ with $k=0.5$: maximum at $t=2$ hours [A1] $C(2)=29.4$ mg/L [A1] (ii) solve $40te^{-0.5t}=20$ with the GDC [M1] $t=0.715$ and $t=4.31$ [A1] duration $=3.59$ hours [A1] [5 marks] (e) $f'\!\left(\dfrac2k\right)=(1-2)e^{-2}=-e^{-2}$ [A1] tangent: $y-\dfrac{2}{k}e^{-2}=-e^{-2}\left(x-\dfrac2k\right)$ [M1][A1] $y=0$ gives $x-\dfrac2k=\dfrac2k$, so $x=\dfrac4k$ [AG] [4 marks] (f) with $k=0.5$ the estimate is $t=8$ hours [A1] $C(8)=40(8)e^{-4}=5.86$ mg/L [A1] this is about $20\%$ of the maximum concentration, so the drug is not fully cleared and the estimate is too early [R1] [3 marks] (g) maximum at $t=\dfrac1k=3$, so $k=\dfrac13$ [M1][A1] $C(3)=3Ae^{-1}=30$ [M1] $A=10e=27.2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Part (b) of this question is the key result: for the family $xe^{-kx}$ the maximum is at $x=1/k$. Reuse the results for general $k$ in parts (d), (f) and (g) rather than recomputing from scratch.

subtopic: Modulus, argument and Euler form of a second-quadrant number
statement: Let $z=-1+\sqrt3\,i$. (a) Find $|z|$. [1] (b) Find $\arg z$, in radians, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. [2] (c) Write $z$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [1] (d) Hence find $z^3$ in Cartesian form. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|z|=\sqrt{1+3}=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $z$ lies in the second quadrant, reference angle $\arctan\sqrt3=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $\arg z=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $z=2e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $z^3=2^3e^{2\pi i}$ [M1] $=8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch the point first: the quadrant tells you whether to add or subtract the reference angle from $\pi$. In Euler form, powers multiply the argument by the exponent and cube the modulus.

subtopic: Conjugates and dividing by a complex number
statement: Let $z=4-3i$. (a) Write down $z^*$, the complex conjugate of $z$. [1] (b) Find $zz^*$. [2] (c) Find real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $(a+bi)(1+2i)=z$. [3]
tips: Multiplying a complex number by its conjugate always gives a real number, the squared modulus. Use the same trick to remove $i$ from a denominator.

subtopic: Using conjugate roots to factorize a cubic
statement: The polynomial $p(z)=z^3-5z^2+9z-5$ has real coefficients and $z=2+i$ is a root of $p(z)=0$. (a) Write down a second non-real root. [1] (b) Hence find a quadratic factor of $p(z)$ with real coefficients. [2] (c) Find all three roots of $p(z)=0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2-i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\left(z-(2+i)\right)\left(z-(2-i)\right)=(z-2)^2-i^2$ [M1] $=z^2-4z+5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Divide (or compare coefficients): $p(z)=(z^2-4z+5)(z-1)$ [M1] [A1] Roots: $z=1$, $z=2+i$, $z=2-i$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Non-real roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs, so a quadratic factor with real coefficients is $z^2-(\text{sum})z+(\text{product})$.

subtopic: Powers of 1+i using de Moivre
statement: Let $z=1+i$. (a) Write $z$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$, where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [2] (b) Find $z^{10}$ in Cartesian form. [2] (c) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $z^n$ is real and positive. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=\sqrt2$ [A1] $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $z=\sqrt2\,e^{\frac{\pi}{4}i}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z^{10}=(\sqrt2)^{10}e^{\frac{10\pi}{4}i}=32e^{\frac{5\pi}{2}i}$ [M1] $=32e^{\frac{\pi}{2}i}=32i$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $z^n$ has argument $\dfrac{n\pi}{4}$, which must be a multiple of $2\pi$ [M1] smallest positive $n$ is $8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For powers, convert to Euler form first. A number is real and positive exactly when its argument is a multiple of $2\pi$.

subtopic: Cube roots of an imaginary number
statement: (a) Write $8i$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$, with $r>0$. [1] (b) Solve $z^3=8i$, giving the three solutions in the form $re^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [4] (c) Write the three solutions in Cartesian form. [2] (d) Show that the sum of the three solutions is zero. [1]
markscheme: (a) $8i=8e^{\frac{\pi}{2}i}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $z^3=8e^{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi\right)i}$, so $z=2e^{\left(\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2k\pi}{3}\right)i}$ [M1] $z=2e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}$ [A1] $z=2e^{\frac{5\pi}{6}i}$ [A1] $z=2e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}i}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\sqrt3+i$ and $-\sqrt3+i$ [A1] $-2i$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $(\sqrt3+i)+(-\sqrt3+i)+(-2i)=0$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The solutions of $z^n=w$ have equal modulus $|w|^{1/n}$ and arguments spaced by $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$. Bring the arguments back into the stated interval at the end.

subtopic: Square root of a complex number by equating parts
statement: Let $(x+yi)^2=5+12i$, where $x$ and $y$ are real. (a) Show that $x^2-y^2=5$ and $xy=6$. [2] (b) Hence find the two square roots of $5+12i$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(x+yi)^2=x^2-y^2+2xyi$ [M1] equating real and imaginary parts: $x^2-y^2=5$ and $2xy=12$, so $xy=6$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $y=\dfrac6x$ so $x^2-\dfrac{36}{x^2}=5$, giving $x^4-5x^2-36=0$ [M1] $(x^2-9)(x^2+4)=0$ [A1] $x^2=9$ since $x$ is real [R1] $x=3,\ y=2$ or $x=-3,\ y=-2$, so the roots are $\pm(3+2i)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Whenever two complex numbers are equal, both their real parts and their imaginary parts must match. Substitute one equation into the other to get a quadratic in $x^2$.

subtopic: Solving a conjugate equation for z
statement: (a) Find the complex number $z$ that satisfies $z+2z^*=9-4i$. [3] (b) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$, giving $\arg z$ in an exact form. [2] (c) Find $z^2$ in the form $a+bi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Let $z=a+bi$. Then $z+2z^*=a+bi+2a-2bi=3a-bi$ [M1] $3a=9$ and $-b=-4$ [M1] $z=3+4i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $|z|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$ [A1] $\arg z=\arctan\dfrac43$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $z^2=9+24i+16i^2$ [M1] $=-7+24i$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Put $z=a+bi$ and collect real and imaginary parts separately; the conjugate flips only the sign of the imaginary part.

subtopic: Quotient of two complex numbers and its powers
statement: Let $z_1=\sqrt3+i$ and $z_2=1-i$. (a) Write $z_1$ and $z_2$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [3] (b) Hence write $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [2] (c) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)^n$ is purely imaginary, and find the value of $\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)^n$ for this $n$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $z_1=2e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}$ [A1] $|z_2|=\sqrt2$ [A1] $z_2=\sqrt2\,e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}i}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Divide moduli, subtract arguments [M1] $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=\sqrt2\,e^{\frac{5\pi}{12}i}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)^n=2^{n/2}e^{\frac{5n\pi}{12}i}$, purely imaginary when $\dfrac{5n\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+k\pi$ [M1] $5n=6+12k$ [A1] $n$ must be an integer, so test $k=0,1,2$: $\dfrac65,\ \dfrac{18}{5},\ 6$ [M1] $n=6$ [A1] value $=2^3e^{\frac{5\pi}{2}i}=8i$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: A number is purely imaginary when its argument is $\frac{\pi}{2}$ plus a multiple of $\pi$. Turn that into an equation for $n$ and look for the first integer solution.

subtopic: Conjugate pair roots of a real quadratic
statement: The quadratic equation $z^2+bz+c=0$, where $b,c\in\mathbb{R}$, has one root $3-2i$. (a) Write down the other root. [1] (b) Find the value of $b$ and the value of $c$. [3] (c) Find $(3-2i)^2$ in the form $x+yi$. [2]
tips: For a real quadratic with a non-real root, the other root is its conjugate. Use sum $=-b$ and product $=c$ for $z^2+bz+c$.

subtopic: Adding two voltages with phasors
statement: Two alternating voltages in a circuit, in volts, are $V_1=4\cos(\omega t)$ and $V_2=4\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$. A voltage $R\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ is represented by the complex number $Re^{i\varphi}$. (a) Write down the complex numbers representing $V_1$ and $V_2$. [1] (b) Find the complex number representing $V_1+V_2$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (c) Hence write $V_1+V_2$ in the form $R\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ with $R>0$ and $0<\varphi<\pi$. [3] (d) State the maximum value of $V_1+V_2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $4$ and $4e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $4+4\left(-\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)$ [M1] $=2+2\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $R=\sqrt{4+12}=4$ [A1] $\varphi=\arctan\sqrt3=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] $V_1+V_2=4\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $4$ volts [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Waves of the same frequency add by adding their phasors, which are complex numbers. Convert the sum back to modulus-argument form to read off amplitude and phase.

subtopic: Robotic arm tip modeled by repeated complex multiplication
statement: The tip of a robotic arm is at the point representing the complex number $P_0=5+2i$, where lengths are in cm. At each step the tip's position is multiplied by $w=0.9\left(\cos25^\circ+i\sin25^\circ\right)$, so that $P_{n+1}=wP_n$. (a) Find $P_1$ in the form $a+bi$, giving $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the smallest $n$ for which the tip is within $2$ cm of the origin. [3] (c) The tip first lies in the third quadrant at step $n=k$. Find $k$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P_1=(5+2i)\times0.9\left(\cos25^\circ+i\sin25^\circ\right)$ [M1] $=3.32+3.53i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|P_n|=0.9^n\sqrt{29}$ [M1] $0.9^n\sqrt{29}<2$ [M1] $n=10$ (since $n=9$ gives $2.09$ and $n=10$ gives $1.88$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\arg P_n=\arctan\dfrac25+25n=21.8^\circ+25n^\circ$ [M1] third quadrant needs $180^\circ<\arg P_n<270^\circ$; $n=6$ gives $171.8^\circ$ and $n=7$ gives $196.8^\circ$, so $k=7$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each multiplication by $w$ shrinks the modulus by $0.9$ and rotates by $25^\circ$, so work with modulus and argument separately. Check consecutive values of $n$ against the boundaries.

subtopic: Complex roots of a quadratic with modulus and argument
statement: Consider the equation $z^2-5z+9=0$. (a) Solve the equation, giving the solutions in the form $a+bi$ with exact values of $a$ and $b$. [2] (b) Show that both solutions have modulus $3$. [2] (c) Let $\alpha$ be the solution with positive imaginary part. Find $\arg\alpha$, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) Find $\alpha^5$ in the form $x+yi$, giving $x$ and $y$ to 4 significant figures. [3]
tips: A negative discriminant gives a conjugate pair, which automatically share the same modulus. For powers, use $\alpha=re^{i\theta}$ and keep the unrounded argument in your calculator.

subtopic: Sixth roots of 64 forming a regular hexagon
statement: The solutions of $z^6=64$ are represented in the complex plane as the vertices of a polygon. (a) Find the six solutions in the form $re^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3] (b) Find the area of the polygon, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the distance between two adjacent vertices is $2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z=64^{1/6}e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{6}}$ [M1] modulus $2$ [A1] $z=2e^{0i},\ 2e^{\pm\frac{\pi}{3}i},\ 2e^{\pm\frac{2\pi}{3}i},\ 2e^{\pi i}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The polygon is made of six identical triangles with two sides $2$ and included angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] area of each $=\dfrac12(2)(2)\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\sqrt3$ [A1] total $=6\sqrt3=10.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Cosine rule: $d^2=2^2+2^2-2(2)(2)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=8-4=4$ [A1] $d=2$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: The $n$th roots of a number lie on a circle and are equally spaced by $\frac{2\pi}{n}$. A regular polygon splits into $n$ congruent triangles meeting at the centre.

subtopic: Impedance of a series RLC circuit
statement: In a series circuit a resistor has resistance $R=30\ \Omega$, an inductor has reactance $X_L=40\ \Omega$ and a capacitor has reactance $X_C=16\ \Omega$. The impedance is the complex number $Z=R+i(X_L-X_C)$. The supply voltage has amplitude $V_0=120$ V. (a) Write $Z$ in the form $a+bi$. [1] (b) Find the modulus $|Z|$ and the argument $\arg Z$ in radians, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) The current amplitude is $I_0=\dfrac{V_0}{|Z|}$. Find $I_0$ in amperes. [2] (d) The current lags the voltage by the angle $\arg Z$. State this angle in radians. [1] (e) The capacitor is replaced by one with a different reactance $X_C$ so that the current amplitude is as large as possible. Find this value of $X_C$ and the maximum current amplitude. [2]
markscheme: (a) $Z=30+24i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $|Z|=\sqrt{30^2+24^2}$ [M1] $=38.4\ \Omega$ [A1] $\arg Z=\arctan\dfrac{24}{30}=0.675$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $I_0=\dfrac{120}{38.42}$ [M1] $=3.12$ A [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.675$ rad [A1] [1 mark] (e) $|Z|$ is smallest when the imaginary part is zero, so $X_C=40\ \Omega$ [A1] $I_0=\dfrac{120}{30}=4$ A [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Impedance combines resistance (real part) and net reactance (imaginary part), so its modulus is smallest when the imaginary part vanishes. Keep extra digits in $|Z|$ before dividing.

subtopic: Combining two sinusoidal voltages into one using complex numbers
statement: Two voltages, in volts, are $V_1=12\cos(50t)$ and $V_2=9\cos\left(50t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, where $t$ is time in seconds. A voltage $R\cos(50t+\varphi)$ is represented by $Re^{i\varphi}$. (a) Write down the complex numbers representing $V_1$ and $V_2$. [1] (b) Find the complex number representing $V_1+V_2$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Hence express $V_1+V_2$ in the form $R\cos(50t+\varphi)$, with $R$ and $\varphi$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the smallest positive value of $t$ for which $V_1+V_2=0$. [2]
tips: Express each wave as a phasor, add the phasors, then read amplitude and phase from the modulus and argument. Use radians throughout since the phase is given in radians.

subtopic: Multiplying and dividing complex numbers in Euler form
statement: Let $z_1=6e^{0.9i}$ and $z_2=2e^{-1.4i}$. (a) Find $z_1z_2$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$, with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$, with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [2] (c) Write $z_1$ in the form $a+bi$, giving $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Multiply moduli, add arguments [M1] $z_1z_2=12e^{-0.5i}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Divide moduli, subtract arguments [M1] $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=3e^{2.3i}$ [A1] ($2.3<\pi$ so it is in the required interval) [2 marks] (c) $6\cos0.9=3.73$ [A1] $6\sin0.9=4.70$ [A1] so $z_1=3.73+4.70i$ [2 marks]
tips: Make sure your calculator is in radian mode for part (c). After combining arguments, check the result lies in $(-\pi,\pi]$.

subtopic: Cubic with a real root and a conjugate pair
statement: Let $p(z)=z^3-9z^2+33z-65$. (a) Show that $z=5$ is a root of $p(z)=0$. [1] (b) Find the other two roots of $p(z)=0$. [3] (c) The three roots are represented in the complex plane. Find the area of the triangle whose vertices are the three roots. [2] (d) Verify that the sum and product of the three roots agree with the coefficients of $p(z)$. [2]
tips: The conjugate pair is symmetric about the real axis, so the triangle has a vertical side. For a cubic $z^3+bz^2+cz+d$, the roots sum to $-b$ and multiply to $-d$.

subtopic: Impedance of two components in parallel
statement: Two components in an AC circuit have impedances $Z_1=6+8i$ ohms and $Z_2=12-5i$ ohms. When they are connected in parallel, the combined impedance $Z$ satisfies $\dfrac1Z=\dfrac1{Z_1}+\dfrac1{Z_2}$. (a) Show that $Z=\dfrac{Z_1Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}$. [2] (b) Find $Z$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find $|Z|$ and $\arg Z$, each to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) The supply voltage has amplitude $100$ V. Find the amplitude of the total current, given that current amplitude equals voltage amplitude divided by $|Z|$. [2]
tips: For parallel components add reciprocals, which leads to product over sum. Use the conjugate of the denominator to divide complex numbers, or the complex-number mode of your GDC.

subtopic: Spiral path generated by a rotation and contraction
statement: A point $P_n$ in the complex plane has position $P_0=10$ and $P_{n+1}=wP_n$ for $n\ge0$, where $w=0.8e^{\frac{\pi}{5}i}$. Distances are in cm. (a) Find $P_1$ and $P_2$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Show that $|P_{n+1}-P_n|=10(0.8)^n|w-1|$. [2] (c) The point moves along the straight segments $P_0P_1$, $P_1P_2$, $P_2P_3,\dots$ and continues indefinitely. Find the total length of this path, to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the smallest $n$ for which $|P_n|<0.5$. [2]
tips: Lengths of successive segments scale by the modulus of $w$, giving a geometric series. Work out $|w-1|$ with unrounded values to avoid accuracy loss.

subtopic: Damped oscillator with complex characteristic roots
statement: The motion of a mass on a damped spring satisfies the characteristic equation $2s^2+cs+50=0$, where $c>0$ is the damping constant. The motion oscillates only if the equation has non-real roots. (a) Find the range of values of $c$ for which the motion oscillates. [3] (b) For $c=8$, solve the equation, giving the roots in the form $a+bi$ with exact values. [2] (c) For $c=8$, the displacement is proportional to $e^{-2t}\cos(bt)$ where $b$ is the imaginary part found in part (b). Find the period of the oscillation, in seconds, to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the factor by which the amplitude is multiplied during one period, to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: The sign of the discriminant decides whether roots are real. For $e^{at}\cos(bt)$ the period is $\frac{2\pi}{b}$ and the amplitude changes by $e^{a\times\text{period}}$ each cycle.

subtopic: Echoes modeled as a complex geometric series
statement: A sound produces a signal represented by the complex number $1$. Each successive echo has its amplitude multiplied by $0.9$ and its phase advanced by $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ relative to the previous one, so the echoes are represented by $1,w,w^2,\dots$ where $w=0.9e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}$. The total signal after $n$ terms is $S_n=1+w+\dots+w^{n-1}$. (a) Write $w$ and $w^2$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Explain why the series converges, and find $S_\infty$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Find $|S_\infty|$ to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) Show that $\left|S_\infty-S_n\right|=\dfrac{0.9^n}{|1-w|}$ and hence find the smallest $n$ for which $\left|S_\infty-S_n\right|<0.01$. [4]
tips: A complex geometric series converges when $|w|<1$ and its sum is $\frac{1}{1-w}$, exactly as in the real case. The remainder after $n$ terms is $\frac{w^n}{1-w}$; use moduli to compare it with the tolerance.

subtopic: Fifth roots of unity and an exact cosine sum
statement: Let $\omega=e^{\frac{2\pi}{5}i}$. (a) Solve $z^5=1$, giving all five solutions as powers of $\omega$. [2] (b) Show that the sum of the five solutions is zero. [2] (c) Hence show that $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}=-\dfrac12$. [3] (d) Use your GDC to verify the result in part (c) numerically. [1] (e) The five solutions are the vertices of a regular pentagon. Find the length of one side of this pentagon, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z=e^{\frac{2k\pi}{5}i}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$ [M1] so the solutions are $1,\ \omega,\ \omega^2,\ \omega^3,\ \omega^4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z^5-1=0$ has no $z^4$ term, so the sum of the roots is $0$ [M1] [A1] (alternatively $1+\omega+\dots+\omega^4=\dfrac{1-\omega^5}{1-\omega}=0$) [2 marks] (c) $\omega+\omega^4=2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ and $\omega^2+\omega^3=2\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}$ since these are conjugate pairs [A1] taking real parts of $1+\omega+\omega^2+\omega^3+\omega^4=0$ [M1] $1+2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+2\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}=0$, so the sum is $-\dfrac12$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) $0.309-0.809=-0.500$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) Side $=|\omega-1|$ [M1] $=2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5}=1.18$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Roots of unity sum to zero, and conjugate pairs add to twice their real part, which is how exact trigonometric values often arise. The distance between two points on the unit circle separated by angle $\theta$ is $2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$.

subtopic: Drone flight path using complex numbers
statement: A drone leaves a launch point at the origin of a complex plane, where the real axis points east and the imaginary axis points north, with distances in km. It flies $5$ km in the direction making an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ with the positive real axis. It then turns $90^\circ$ anticlockwise and flies a further $3$ km. (a) Write the first displacement as a complex number in the form $a+bi$, to 3 significant figures. [1] (b) Find the second displacement as a complex number in the form $a+bi$, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the drone's final position as a complex number, to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) Find the final distance of the drone from the launch point, to 3 significant figures. [2] (e) Find the bearing of the drone from the launch point, to the nearest degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) $5e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}=4.33+2.50i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) New direction is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1] $3e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}=-1.50+2.60i$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2.83+5.10i$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\sqrt{2.830^2+5.098^2}$ [M1] $=5.83$ km [A1] [2 marks] (e) Angle from east $=\arctan\dfrac{5.098}{2.830}=61.0^\circ$ [M1] bearing $=90^\circ-61.0^\circ=29^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A turn through an angle corresponds to multiplying by $e^{i\theta}$, equivalently adding $\theta$ to the argument. Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so subtract the angle from the east axis from $90^\circ$.

subtopic: Quartic with two conjugate pairs of roots
statement: The polynomial $p(z)=z^4-6z^3+15z^2-18z+10$ has real coefficients and $z=1+i$ is a root of $p(z)=0$. (a) Write down a second root. [1] (b) Find a quadratic factor of $p(z)$ with real coefficients. [2] (c) Hence find the other two roots of $p(z)=0$. [4] (d) Find the sum of the squares of the moduli of the four roots. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\left(z-1-i\right)\left(z-1+i\right)=(z-1)^2+1$ [M1] $=z^2-2z+2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $p(z)=(z^2-2z+2)(z^2+az+5)$ with constant term $10$ [M1] compare $z^3$ coefficients: $a-2=-6$, so $a=-4$ [A1] $z^2-4z+5=0$ [M1] $z=2\pm i$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $|1\pm i|^2=2$ each and $|2\pm i|^2=5$ each [M1] total $=2+2+5+5=14$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide out the known real quadratic factor, either by long division or by comparing coefficients. For $|z|^2$ with $z=a+bi$ use $a^2+b^2$.

subtopic: Gain and phase shift of an electronic filter
statement: An electronic filter multiplies the complex amplitude of an input signal by the complex number $H=1.2-0.9i$. The gain of the filter is $|H|$ and its phase shift is $\arg H$. (a) Find the gain and the phase shift, in radians, to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) An input signal has complex amplitude $8e^{0.4i}$. Find the output signal in the form $re^{i\theta}$, with $r$ and $\theta$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Identical filters are connected one after another, with the input signal of part (b). Find the smallest number of filters for which the output amplitude exceeds $100$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|H|=\sqrt{1.2^2+0.9^2}$ [M1] gain $=1.5$ [A1] phase shift $=\arctan\left(\dfrac{-0.9}{1.2}\right)=-0.644$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Multiply moduli, add arguments [M1] $12e^{-0.244i}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $8(1.5)^n>100$ [M1] $n=7$ (since $8(1.5)^6=91.1$ and $8(1.5)^7=137$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $H$ scales the amplitude by $|H|$ and shifts the phase by $\arg H$. Several filters in series multiply gains, giving a power of $|H|$.

subtopic: Three-phase and six-phase supplies using roots of unity
statement: This question investigates how alternating voltages combine, using complex numbers. A voltage $A\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ is represented by the complex number $Ae^{i\varphi}$ (a phasor), and voltages of the same frequency add by adding their phasors. Let $\zeta=e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}$. A three-phase supply has three voltages $V_A=A\cos(\omega t)$, $V_B=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ and $V_C=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)$, where $A>0$. (a) Write $\zeta$ in the form $a+bi$ and show that $\zeta^3=1$. [2] (b) (i) Show that $1+\zeta+\zeta^2=0$. [2] (ii) Hence show that $V_A+V_B+V_C=0$ for all $t$. [3] (c) The line voltage is $V_A-V_B$. Show that $V_A-V_B=\sqrt3A\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$. [4] (d) For $A=325$ V, find the amplitude of the line voltage to 3 significant figures. [1] (e) Phase $C$ fails, so only $V_A+V_B$ remains. Show that $V_A+V_B=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, and show that this equals $-V_C$. [3] A six-phase supply uses the voltages $A\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{k\pi}{3}\right)$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4,5$, with phasors $z^k$ where $z=e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}$. Let $S_m=1+z+\dots+z^{m-1}$. (f) (i) Write down an expression for $S_4$ as a quotient, using the formula for the sum of a geometric series. [1] (ii) Show that $S_4=\sqrt3\,i$. [4] (g) Hence show that $\cos\theta+\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)+\cos(\theta+\pi)=-\sqrt3\sin\theta$. [3] (h) (i) Show that $\left|1-z^m\right|=2\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ for $m=1,2,\dots,5$. [3] (ii) The first $m$ phase voltages of the six-phase supply with $A=10$ V are added together. Find all values of $m$, with $1\le m\le5$, for which the amplitude of the sum exceeds $15$ V. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\zeta=-\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [A1] $\zeta^3=e^{2\pi i}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b)(i) $\zeta^2=e^{\frac{4\pi}{3}i}=-\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [A1] $1+\zeta+\zeta^2=1-\dfrac12-\dfrac12+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)i=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (ii) Phasors of $V_A,V_B,V_C$ are $A,\ A\zeta^{-1}=A\zeta^2,\ A\zeta^{-2}=A\zeta$ [M1] their sum is $A(1+\zeta+\zeta^2)=0$ [A1] so the sum of the voltages, the real part of $e^{i\omega t}$ times the sum of phasors, is $0$ for all $t$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) Phasor of $V_A-V_B$ is $A(1-\zeta^2)$ [M1] $=A\left(\dfrac32+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)$ [A1] modulus $A\sqrt{\dfrac94+\dfrac34}=\sqrt3A$ and argument $\arctan\dfrac{\sqrt3/2}{3/2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ [A1] so $V_A-V_B=\sqrt3A\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ [AG] [4 marks] (d) $325\sqrt3=563$ V [A1] [1 mark] (e) Phasor of $V_A+V_B$ is $A(1+\zeta^2)=A\left(\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)$ [M1] $=Ae^{-\frac{\pi}{3}i}$, so $V_A+V_B=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [A1] From (b), $V_A+V_B=-V_C=-A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+\pi\right)=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [R1] [3 marks] (f)(i) $S_4=\dfrac{1-z^4}{1-z}$ [A1] [1 mark] (ii) $z^4=e^{\frac{4\pi}{3}i}=-\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$, so $1-z^4=\dfrac32+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [M1] [A1] $1-z=\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$, which has modulus $1$; multiply numerator and denominator by $\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [M1] $S_4=\left(\dfrac32+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)\left(\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)=\dfrac34-\dfrac34+\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)i=\sqrt3\,i$ [AG] [4 marks] (g) The sum equals $\mathrm{Re}\left(e^{i\theta}S_4\right)$ [M1] $=\mathrm{Re}\left(\sqrt3\,i(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\right)$ [A1] $=-\sqrt3\sin\theta$ [A1] [3 marks] (h)(i) $\left|1-z^m\right|$ is the distance between the points $1$ and $z^m=e^{i m\pi/3}$ on the unit circle; with the origin they form an isosceles triangle with equal sides $1$ and apex angle $\dfrac{m\pi}{3}$ [M1] splitting it into two right-angled triangles gives base $=2\times1\times\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ [A1] and $\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}>0$ for $m=1,\dots,5$, so $\left|1-z^m\right|=2\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ [R1] [3 marks] (ii) $|1-z|=2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=1$, so $|S_m|=2\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ and the amplitude is $20\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ [M1] require $\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}>0.75$ [A1] $m=2$ ($17.3$ V), $m=3$ ($20$ V), $m=4$ ($17.3$ V) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Part (b) is the key idea: the three phasors are the cube roots of unity scaled by $A$, so they cancel exactly. In (f) and (h) a geometric series of phasors gives a closed form whose modulus can be found with $|1-e^{i\varphi}|=2\sin\frac{\varphi}{2}$.

subtopic: Matrix product, determinant and inverse of 2x2 matrices
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{AB}$. [2] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{A}$. [1] (c) Find $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2-1 & 0+2 \\ 3-4 & 0+8 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{A}=8-3=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a $2\times2$ matrix swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries and divide by the determinant. Remember that $\mathbf{AB}\neq\mathbf{BA}$ in general.

subtopic: Solving a pair of linear equations with an inverse matrix
statement: Consider the system $2x+y=7$ and $3x+2y=12$. (a) Write the system in the form $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{c}$. [1] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. [3] (c) Hence solve the system. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\det\mathbf{M}=4-3=1$ [M1] $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $x=2,\ y=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiply by the inverse on the left of both sides: $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{c}$. Check the answer by substituting into the original equations.

subtopic: Finding a parameter from a given eigenvector
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Given that $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}$, (a) find the value of $k$ and the corresponding eigenvalue. [3] (b) Find the other eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$. [2] (c) Find an eigenvector corresponding to the other eigenvalue. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2k+2 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}=\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\lambda=7$ [A1] $2k+2=14$, so $k=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace: $6+1=7$ [M1] other eigenvalue $=7-7=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(\mathbf{A}-0\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives $6x+2y=0$ [M1] $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$ (or any multiple) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ directly, since the second component immediately gives $\lambda$. The eigenvalues of a $2\times2$ matrix add to the trace and multiply to the determinant.

subtopic: Powers of a triangular matrix by diagonalization
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write down the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [1] (b) Find a corresponding eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Hence find an expression for $\mathbf{A}^n$ in terms of $n$. [3] (d) Write down the top-right entry of $\mathbf{A}^5$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $3$ and $2$ (the diagonal entries of a triangular matrix) [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\lambda=3$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=2$: $(\mathbf{A}-2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives $x+y=0$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\begin{pmatrix} 3^n & 0 \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 3^n & 3^n-2^n \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $3^5-2^5=211$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$, raising only the diagonal entries to the power $n$. Test your formula with $n=1$, which must return $\mathbf{A}$.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain steady state and eigenvalues
statement: In a two-party election system, each year $10\%$ of supporters of party $A$ switch to party $B$, and $20\%$ of supporters of party $B$ switch to party $A$. The proportions supporting $A$ and $B$ are modeled by $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x}_n$, where $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$. Initially the proportions are $\mathbf{x}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{x}_1$. [2] (b) Find the steady state proportions. [3] (c) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{x}_1=\begin{pmatrix} 0.9(0.5)+0.2(0.5) \\ 0.1(0.5)+0.8(0.5) \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.55 \\ 0.45 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ gives $0.9x+0.2y=x$, so $x=2y$ [M1] with $x+y=1$ [M1] $x=\dfrac23,\ y=\dfrac13$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\lambda^2-1.7\lambda+0.7=0$ [M1] $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-0.7)=0$, so $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=0.7$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A steady state satisfies $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ and its entries add to $1$. The eigenvalue $1$ always appears for a transition matrix whose columns sum to $1$.

subtopic: Singular matrix condition and inverse with a parameter
statement: Let $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} k & 2 \\ 3 & k+1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the values of $k$ for which $\mathbf{M}$ has no inverse. [3] (b) For $k=1$, find $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. [3] (c) For $k=1$, solve $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=k(k+1)-6=0$ [M1] $k^2+k-6=0$ [A1] $(k+3)(k-2)=0$, so $k=2$ or $k=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\det\mathbf{M}=-4$ [M1] $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=-\dfrac14\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix} -\frac12 & \frac12 \\ \frac34 & -\frac14 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{M}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $x=1,\ y=\dfrac32$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A square matrix has no inverse exactly when its determinant is zero. Verify part (c) by multiplying $\mathbf{M}$ by your answer.

subtopic: Three equations in three unknowns with a parameter
