[1] (d) Find an expression for the velocity $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}$, and hence find the maximum speed of the diaphragm, correct to three significant figures. [3] (e) Find the first time after $t=0$ at which the displacement equals $0.3$ mm, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $=0.4$ mm [A1] period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{660\pi}=\dfrac{1}{330}$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) Frequency $=330$ Hz [A1] [1 mark] (c) $x(0.001)=0.4\sin(0.66\pi)=0.351\ \text{mm}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $v=0.4\times660\pi\cos(660\pi t)$ [M1] $=264\pi\cos(660\pi t)$ [A1] maximum speed $=264\pi=829\ \text{mm/s}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.4\sin(660\pi t)=0.3$ so $\sin(660\pi t)=0.75$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\sin^{-1}0.75}{660\pi}=4.09\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The period of $\sin(kt)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$, and the frequency is the reciprocal of the period. The maximum speed is the amplitude of the velocity function, which is the displacement amplitude multiplied by $k$.

subtopic: Combining two sinusoidal signals into a single cosine
statement: Two alternating signals arriving at a sensor have voltages $4\sin(3t)$ and $3\cos(3t)$ volts, where $t$ is the time in seconds. The combined voltage is $V(t)=4\sin(3t)+3\cos(3t)$. (a) Use your GDC to find the maximum value of $V(t)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, and the first time $t>0$ at which it occurs, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) The combined voltage can be written in the form $V(t)=A\cos\left(3(t-p)\right)$, where $A>0$ and $0<p<\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. Write down the value of $A$ and the value of $p$. [2] (c) Solve $V(t)=2.5$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, giving all solutions correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Graph $V(t)$ and find the maximum point [M1] maximum $=5.00$ V [A1] first at $t=0.309\ \text{s}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $A=5$ (the maximum value) [A1] the maximum of $A\cos(3(t-p))$ first occurs when $t=p$, so $p=0.309$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $5\cos(3(t-0.3091))=2.5$ or solve $V(t)=2.5$ on the GDC [M1] $t=0.658,\ 2.05,\ 2.75$ [A1] and $t=4.15,\ 4.85,\ 6.24$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A sum of a sine and cosine with the same frequency is a single sinusoid, so its graph has constant amplitude and the same period. When counting solutions on $0\le t\le2\pi$, remember the period here is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so the pattern repeats three times.

subtopic: Intersections of a sine curve and a straight line
statement: The upper edge of a roller-coaster track is modeled by $f(x)=3\sin(2x)+1$ for $0\le x\le6$, where $x$ is the horizontal distance in tens of metres and $f(x)$ is the height in metres above a platform. A straight support cable is modeled by $g(x)=0.5x+0.5$. (a) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (b) Use your GDC to find the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=g(x)$, correct to three significant figures. [4] (c) Hence find the values of $x$ in $0\le x\le6$ for which the track is above the cable, that is $f(x)>g(x)$. [2]
tips: Check the whole domain for intersections: set the GDC window so that all of $0\le x\le6$ is visible and look at the graph before deciding how many solutions exist. For an inequality, test a point in each interval, including the end of the domain.

subtopic: Area of an isosceles triangular flowerbed
statement: A triangular flowerbed has two sides of length $10$ m, with an angle of $\theta$ radians between them, where $0<\theta<\pi$. (a) Show that the area of the flowerbed is $50\sin\theta\ \text{m}^2$. [1] (b) The area of the flowerbed is $30\ \text{m}^2$. Find the two possible values of $\theta$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the maximum possible area of the flowerbed, and the value of $\theta$ at which it occurs. [2] (d) Find the perimeter of the flowerbed when its area is a maximum, correct to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) Area $=\tfrac12(10)(10)\sin\theta=50\sin\theta$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $50\sin\theta=30$ so $\sin\theta=0.6$ [M1] $\theta=0.644$ [A1] $\theta=\pi-0.6435=2.50$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Maximum area $=50\ \text{m}^2$ [A1] when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Third side $=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt2$ so perimeter $=20+10\sqrt2=34.1$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When $\sin\theta$ is known, there are two angles in $0<\theta<\pi$: the acute one and its supplement $\pi-\theta$. The largest value of $\sin\theta$ is $1$, which occurs at a right angle between the two equal sides.

subtopic: Rate of growth of a cyclical fox population
statement: The number of foxes $P$ in a nature reserve, $t$ years after the start of a study, is modeled by $P(t)=800+300\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)$, for $0\le t\le10$. (a) Find the maximum and minimum populations predicted by the model. [2] (b) Find an expression for $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$. [2] (c) Find the maximum rate of increase of the population, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Use your GDC to find the values of $t$ in $0\le t\le10$ for which the population is increasing at a rate of at least $100$ foxes per year, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $=800+300=1100$ [A1] minimum $=800-300=500$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=300\times\dfrac{\pi}{5}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)$ [M1] $=60\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The maximum of $\cos$ is $1$ [M1] so the maximum rate is $60\pi=188$ foxes per year [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $60\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)\ge100$ [M1] $0\le t\le1.61$ [A1] and $8.39\le t\le10$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The derivative of $a\sin(bt)+d$ is $ab\cos(bt)$, so the largest rate of change is $ab$. For part (d) sketch the derivative and find where it is above the line $y=100$, remembering the whole domain, including both ends.

subtopic: Energy demand over a day from a sinusoidal model
statement: The electricity demand $D$ megawatts (MW) in a town, $t$ hours after midnight, is modeled by $D(t)=420+130\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-9)\right)$, for $0\le t\le24$. (a) Find the maximum demand, and the time of day at which it occurs. [3] (b) The total energy used between $t=6$ and $t=18$, in megawatt-hours (MWh), is given by $\displaystyle\int_6^{18}D(t)\,dt$. Find this energy, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Without integrating, explain why the mean demand over $0\le t\le24$ is $420$ MW, and hence write down the total energy used in the whole day. [2] (d) Use your GDC to find, correct to the nearest minute, the length of time in the day for which the demand exceeds $500$ MW. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximum demand $=420+130=550$ MW [A1] $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-9)\right)=1$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-9)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $t=15$, that is $15{:}00$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_6^{18}D(t)\,dt$ [M1] $=5740$ MWh [A1] [2 marks] (c) $24$ hours is exactly one period, so the sine term averages to zero over the day [R1] total energy $=420\times24=10\,080$ MWh [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $D(t)=500$: $t=11.53$ and $t=18.47$ [M1] Time $=6.936$ hours $\approx6$ h $56$ min [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integration of a sinusoid over a whole number of periods leaves only the contribution of the midline, which is a quick check on a GDC answer. Convert decimal hours to minutes at the end only.

subtopic: Quadratic in cosine from a sin squared equation
statement: Consider the equation $5\cos x=3\sin^2x+1$, for $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$. (a) Show that the equation can be written as $3\cos^2x+5\cos x-4=0$. [2] (b) Hence find the values of $\cos x$ that satisfy the equation, and state which value cannot give a solution. [2] (c) Find all solutions of the equation, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$ so $5\cos x=3(1-\cos^2x)+1$ [M1] $3\cos^2x+5\cos x-4=0$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\cos x=\dfrac{-5\pm\sqrt{73}}{6}$ so $\cos x=0.591$ or $\cos x=-2.26$ [A1] The second value is less than $-1$ so it gives no solution [R1] [2 marks] (c) $x=\cos^{-1}(0.5907)=53.8^\circ$ [M1] [A1] and $x=360^\circ-53.8^\circ=306.2^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$ to get a quadratic in $\cos x$, then reject any root outside $-1\le\cos x\le1$. Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants, so there are two solutions in one full turn.

subtopic: Water level and the passing times of a canal boat
statement: The water level $L$ metres at a canal bridge, $t$ hours after midnight, is modeled by $L(t)=3.2+1.4\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{12.4}\right)$, for $0\le t\le24$. A canal boat can pass under the bridge only when the water level is at most $2.4$ m. (a) Write down the maximum and minimum water levels. [2] (b) Write down the time between two consecutive high tides. [1] (c) Use your GDC to find the times during the $24$ hours when the water level equals $2.4$ m, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the total time during the $24$ hours for which the boat can pass under the bridge, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $=3.2+1.4=4.6$ m [A1] minimum $=3.2-1.4=1.8$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) The period is $12.4$ hours [A1] [1 mark] (c) Solve $3.2+1.4\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{12.4}\right)=2.4$ [M1] $t=4.30$ and $t=8.10$ [A1] $t=16.7$ and $t=20.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The boat can pass when $4.30\le t\le8.10$ and $16.7\le t\le20.5$ [M1] total time $=2\times(3.799)=7.60$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The model has period $12.4$ hours, so in $24$ hours there are almost two complete cycles; make sure your graph window shows both. A boat can pass when the water is low, so you need the intervals where the graph is below the line $L=2.4$.

subtopic: Tangent model for a lighthouse beam on a shore
statement: A lighthouse is $400$ m from a long straight shoreline, at the nearest point $N$ on the shore. Its beam rotates at a constant rate and the angle between the beam and the line from the lighthouse to $N$ is $\dfrac{\pi t}{60}$ radians, where $t$ is the time in seconds after the beam points at $N$. The beam lights up the point on the shore at a distance $x$ metres from $N$, where $x(t)=400\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{60}\right)$, for $0\le t<30$. (a) Find the position of the illuminated point when $t=10$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the time at which the illuminated point is $800$ m from $N$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) State what happens to the model as $t$ approaches $30$ seconds, and explain why. [2] (d) Using $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}$, find the speed of the illuminated point along the shore when $t=10$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x(10)=400\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=231$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $400\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{60}\right)=800$ so $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{60}\right)=2$ [M1] $t=21.1$ s [A1] [2 marks] (c) As $t\to30$, $\dfrac{\pi t}{60}\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x\to\infty$ (vertical asymptote) [A1] the beam becomes parallel to the shoreline and never meets it [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=400\times\dfrac{\pi}{60}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi t}{60}\right)}$ [M1] [A1] at $t=10$: $\dfrac{20.94}{\cos^2(\pi/6)}=27.9$ m/s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The tangent function has vertical asymptotes where its input is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ plus a multiple of $\pi$, which corresponds here to the beam being parallel to the shore. Do not forget the chain rule factor $\dfrac{\pi}{60}$ when you differentiate.

subtopic: Finding sine model parameters from period and a point
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=a\sin(bx)+4$, where $a>0$ and $b>0$. The period of $f$ is $\pi$ and the graph of $f$ passes through the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},7\right)$. (a) Find the value of $b$ and the value of $a$, correct to three significant figures. [4] (b) Write down the range of $f$, giving the end values correct to three significant figures. [1] (c) Use your GDC to solve $f(x)=6$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: The period of $\sin(bx)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$, so fix $b$ first and then use the given point to find $a$. Within $0\le x\le\pi$ the graph of $\sin(2x)$ completes a whole cycle, so a value between the extremes occurs twice.

subtopic: Pressure variation of a pure musical tone
statement: The pressure variation $p$ pascals of a pure musical tone at a microphone, $t$ seconds after a reference time, is modeled by $p(t)=0.6\sin(880\pi t)$. (a) Write down the amplitude of the pressure variation. [1] (b) Find the exact period of the tone. [2] (c) Find the number of complete cycles in $0.05$ seconds. [1] (d) Find the first time $t>0$ at which $p(t)=0.3$, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.6$ Pa [A1] [1 mark] (b) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{880\pi}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1}{440}$ s [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.05\times440=22$ complete cycles [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\sin(880\pi t)=0.5$ [M1] $880\pi t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ so $t=\dfrac{1}{5280}=1.89\times10^{-4}$ s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The period of $\sin(kt)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$. For the first positive solution of $\sin u=0.5$ take $u=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, the smallest positive angle.

subtopic: Seasonal ice cream sales modeled with a sine function
statement: The monthly sales $S$ of an ice cream shop, in hundreds of dollars, are modeled by $S(m)=420+260\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(m-4)\right)$, where $m$ is the month with $m=1$ for January, $m=2$ for February, and so on, for $1\le m\le12$. (a) Find the maximum and minimum monthly sales predicted by the model, and the months in which they occur. [2] (b) Find the predicted sales in October. [1] (c) Use your GDC to find the months in which the model predicts sales above $500$ hundred dollars. [3] (d) The shop owner uses the model, with $m=13,14,\ldots$, to predict sales in the following year. Give two reasons why this may not be reliable. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $=420+260=680$ in July ($m=7$) [A1] minimum $=420-260=160$ in January ($m=1$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) $S(10)=420+260\sin\pi=420$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Solve $S(m)=500$: $m=4.60$ and $m=9.40$ [M1] [A1] Sales exceed $500$ from May to September [A1] [3 marks] (d) Any two valid reasons, for example: the model repeats exactly the same pattern every year and ignores any growth or decline in the business [R1] it ignores variation due to weather, price changes or special events [R1] [2 marks]
tips: State the months as whole numbers when the question asks for months, using the interval found with your GDC. For validity comments, give specific reasons related to the context, such as ignored trends or the use of the model beyond the original data.

subtopic: Height of a swinging pendulum bob
statement: A pendulum of length $1.5$ m swings back and forth. The angle $\theta$ radians that the string makes with the vertical, $t$ seconds after the pendulum is released from rest, is modeled by $\theta(t)=0.4\cos(2.5t)$. The height of the bob above its lowest possible position is $h(t)=1.5\left(1-\cos\theta(t)\right)$ metres. (a) Find the period of the motion, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the maximum height of the bob, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the height of the bob when $t=0.8$ s, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Use your GDC to find the first time at which the bob is $0.05$ m above its lowest position, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Calculate the angle first, in radians, and then the height, so keep the GDC in radian mode. Since cosine is even, the height is the same when the angle is positive or negative, so the first time may occur before the string reaches the vertical.

subtopic: Intersection and enclosed area of a sine curve and its translation
statement: Let $f(x)=2\sin x+1$ and let $g(x)=f\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$. (a) Describe the transformation that maps the graph of $f$ onto the graph of $g$. [1] (b) Use your GDC to find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graphs of $f$ and $g$ intersect, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Show that the exact $x$-coordinates of these points are $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ by considering the symmetry of the sine curve, or by substituting into the equation $f(x)=g(x)$. [2] (d) Find the area of the region enclosed between the graphs of $f$ and $g$ for $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\le x\le\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) A horizontal translation of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the right [A1] [1 mark] (b) Graph $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ [M1] $x=2.09$ and $x=5.24$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) At $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$: $f=2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+1=\sqrt3+1$ and $g=2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}+1=\sqrt3+1$ [M1] At $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$: $f=-\sqrt3+1$ and $g=2\sin\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)+1=-\sqrt3+1$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Area $=\displaystyle\int_{2\pi/3}^{5\pi/3}\left|f(x)-g(x)\right|dx$ [M1] where $g>f$ on this interval [R1] Area $=4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Two sine curves of equal amplitude cross where they have the same value, which happens at points symmetric about the maximum of the shifted function, so check the exact values to confirm your GDC answers. For the area, use the numerical integration function and enter the absolute difference of the two functions.

subtopic: Modeling daylight hours and solar panel energy over a year
statement: This question uses a sinusoidal model for the number of hours of daylight in a city to investigate the yearly energy produced by a solar panel. The number of hours of daylight $D$ on day $t$ of the year is modeled by $D(t)=a\sin\left(b(t-c)\right)+d$, for $0\le t\le365$, where $a>0$, $b>0$ and $t$ is measured in days. The longest day has $16.8$ hours of daylight and the shortest day has $7.2$ hours of daylight. (a) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $d$. [2] (b) The model has a period of $365$ days and the longest day occurs when $t=172$. Find the exact value of $b$, and find the value of $c$. [3] (c) Use your GDC to find the number of days in the year with more than $14$ hours of daylight, correct to the nearest day. [3] (d) Find $\dfrac{dD}{dt}$, and hence find the greatest rate at which the number of hours of daylight increases, in minutes per day, correct to three significant figures. State the value of $t$ at which this occurs. [3] A solar panel produces $0.45$ kWh of energy for every hour of daylight. (e) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{365}D(t)\,dt$ and hence find the total energy produced in the year if there were no clouds. Give your answers in hours and kWh respectively. [4] (f) The number of hours of daylight was measured on four days of the year. The data are: day $t$: 30, 100, 200, 300; observed $D$: 8.6, 13.4, 15.9, 9.4. Find the value predicted by the model for each of these days, correct to two decimal places, and find the sum of the squares of the differences between the observed and predicted values. Comment on how well the model fits the data. [4] (g) Cloud cover reduces the energy produced. The energy produced on day $t$ is modeled by $E(t)=0.45\,D(t)\,C(t)$ kWh, where $C(t)=0.65+0.15\cos\left(b(t-172)\right)$ is the proportion of daylight energy that is captured. (i) Find the total energy produced in the year according to this model, correct to three significant figures. [3] (ii) Find the percentage by which this energy is less than the cloud-free total from part (e), correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{16.8-7.2}{2}=4.8$ [A1] $d=\dfrac{16.8+7.2}{2}=12$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{365}$ [A1] the maximum occurs when $b(172-c)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $172-c=91.25$ so $c=80.75$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $4.8\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t-80.75)\right)+12=14$ [M1] $t=106$ and $t=238$ [A1] Number of days $=132.6\approx133$ days [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dD}{dt}=4.8b\cos\left(b(t-c)\right)$ [M1] [A1] The greatest rate is $4.8b=0.0826$ hours per day, which is $4.96$ minutes per day, when $t=80.75$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\displaystyle\int_0^{365}D(t)\,dt=4380$ hours (equal to $12\times365$ because the sine term has zero mean over one period) [M1] [A1] Energy $=0.45\times4380=1971$ kWh [A1] [A1] [4 marks] (f) Predicted values: $D(30)=8.32$, $D(100)=13.56$, $D(200)=16.25$, $D(300)=9.16$ [A1] Differences (observed $-$ predicted) $=0.28,\ -0.16,\ -0.35,\ 0.24$ [M1] Sum of squares $=0.286$ [A1] The sum is small and the differences are all less than $0.4$ hours, so the model is a good fit [R1] [4 marks] (g) (i) $\displaystyle\int_0^{365}0.45\left(4.8\sin\left(b(t-c)\right)+12\right)\left(0.65+0.15\cos\left(b(t-172)\right)\right)dt$ [M1] [A1] $=1340$ kWh [A1] (ii) $\dfrac{1971-1340.3}{1971}\times100$ [M1] $=32.0\%$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Use the information about the longest day to fix $c$: the maximum of a sine function occurs when its bracket equals $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. For the energy parts, use numerical integration on your GDC with the unrounded values, and compare with the cloud-free total to interpret the result in context.

subtopic: Longest rod in a cuboid cabinet and its angle with the base
statement: A storage cabinet is a cuboid with a rectangular base measuring $30$ cm by $40$ cm and an interior height of $120$ cm. A thin metal rod is to be placed inside the cabinet with one end at a bottom corner and the other end at the opposite top corner. (a) Find the length of a diagonal of the base. [2] (b) Find the length of the longest rod that fits in the cabinet. [2] (c) The rod makes an angle $\theta$ with the base of the cabinet. Find the exact value of $\tan\theta$, and hence write down the value of $\sin\theta$. [3]
tips: Break a 3D problem into two right-angled triangles: first the base diagonal, then the space diagonal. For the angle, draw the right-angled triangle formed by the rod, the base diagonal and the vertical edge.

subtopic: Exact volume and surface area of a cylindrical tin
statement: A cylindrical tin of olive oil has radius $5$ cm and height $12$ cm. (a) Find the volume of the tin. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$. [2] (b) Find the total outer surface area of the tin, including both circular ends. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$. [2] (c) The tin is filled with oil to $\dfrac34$ of its height. Find the volume of oil, in terms of $\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\times5^2\times12$ [M1] $=300\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2\pi(5)^2+2\pi(5)(12)$ [M1] $=50\pi+120\pi=170\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac34\times300\pi$ [M1] $=225\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Keep the answer in terms of $\pi$ when asked; do not use your calculator on a Paper 1 question like this. A cylinder has two circular ends and one curved face.

subtopic: Cone party hat and the sector formed by its curved surface
statement: A party hat is made in the shape of a cone with base radius $6$ cm and vertical height $8$ cm. The hat has no base. (a) Find the slant height of the cone. [2] (b) Find the volume of the cone, in terms of $\pi$. [2] (c) Find the area of the curved surface of the hat, in terms of $\pi$. [2] (d) The curved surface is cut along a slant edge and laid flat to form a sector of a circle of radius $10$ cm. Find the angle of the sector, in radians, in terms of $\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ [M1] $=10$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac13\pi(6)^2(8)$ [M1] $=96\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\pi\times6\times10$ [M1] $=60\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Arc length of sector $=$ circumference of base $=2\pi(6)=12\pi$ [M1] $10\theta=12\pi$ [M1] $\theta=\dfrac{6\pi}{5}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The slant height, not the vertical height, is used in the curved surface area formula. When the cone is unrolled, the arc length of the sector equals the circumference of the base.

subtopic: Melting a large sphere into small spheres
statement: A jeweler melts a solid gold sphere of radius $3$ cm and uses all of the gold to make identical small spherical beads, each of radius $1$ cm. Assume no gold is lost. (a) Find the volume of the large sphere, in terms of $\pi$. [2] (b) Find the volume of one bead, in terms of $\pi$. [1] (c) Hence find the number of beads that can be made. [2] (d) Find the total surface area of the $27$ beads as a multiple of the surface area of the large sphere. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac43\pi(3)^3$ [M1] $=36\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac43\pi$ $\mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $36\pi\div\dfrac43\pi$ [M1] $=27$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Surface area of one bead $=4\pi(1)^2=4\pi$, so total $=108\pi$ [M1] Surface area of the large sphere $=4\pi(3)^2=36\pi$ [A1] Ratio $=\dfrac{108\pi}{36\pi}=3$, so three times as large [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Compare volumes, not radii, when one shape is recast into another. The surface area scales with the square of the radius while the volume scales with the cube.

subtopic: Right square pyramid: slant height, surface area, angles
statement: A solid right pyramid has a square base of side $10$ cm. Its apex is vertically above the centre of the base at a height of $12$ cm. (a) Find the volume of the pyramid. [2] (b) Show that the slant height of a triangular face, measured from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge, is $13$ cm. [2] (c) Find the total surface area of the pyramid, including its base. [3] (d) Write down an expression for the tangent of the angle between a triangular face and the base. [1] (e) Find the exact length of a sloping edge of the pyramid. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac13\times10^2\times12$ [M1] $=400\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Horizontal distance from centre of base to midpoint of an edge $=5$ [M1] $\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Area of one triangular face $=\dfrac12(10)(13)=65$ [M1] Four faces $=260$ [A1] Total $=100+260=360\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) Half of the base diagonal $=\dfrac{10\sqrt2}{2}=5\sqrt2$ [M1] Edge $=\sqrt{12^2+(5\sqrt2)^2}=\sqrt{194}$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two different right-angled triangles are needed: one using the half-side for the slant height of a face, and one using the half-diagonal for a sloping edge. Check that you use the correct horizontal distance in each.

subtopic: Grain silo: cylinder with a hemispherical roof
statement: A grain silo is modeled as a cylinder of radius $3$ m and height $10$ m, topped by a hemisphere of radius $3$ m. The base of the cylinder sits flat on the ground. (a) Find the total volume of the silo, in terms of $\pi$. [3] (b) The curved outside surface of the silo (cylinder wall and hemisphere roof) is to be painted. Find the area to be painted, in terms of $\pi$. [3] (c) A second silo is a plain cylinder with the same radius and the same volume as the first. Find its height. [2]
markscheme: (a) Cylinder $=\pi(3)^2(10)=90\pi$ [A1] Hemisphere $=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac43\pi(3)^3=18\pi$ [A1] Total $=108\pi\ \mathrm{m}^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Cylinder wall $=2\pi(3)(10)=60\pi$ [A1] Hemisphere $=2\pi(3)^2=18\pi$ [A1] Total $=78\pi\ \mathrm{m}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\pi(3)^2h=108\pi$ [M1] $h=12$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Treat each piece separately and add. Remember that the curved surface of a hemisphere is half of $4\pi r^2$, and that the circular base is not painted here.

subtopic: Right triangular prism: diagonal and angle with the base
statement: A solid right prism has a horizontal triangular base $ABC$ with a right angle at $B$, $AB=6$ cm and $BC=8$ cm. The vertical edges $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ each have length $5$ cm, so that $DEF$ is the top face directly above $ABC$. (a) Find the length of $AC$. [2] (b) Find the volume of the prism. [2] (c) Find the exact length of the diagonal $DC$. [3] (d) Find the exact value of $\tan\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $DC$ and the base $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ [M1] $=10$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) Area of base $=\dfrac12(6)(8)=24$ [M1] Volume $=24\times5=120\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Triangle $DAC$ has a right angle at $A$ [R1] $DC=\sqrt{10^2+5^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{125}=5\sqrt5$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (d) The angle is $\angle DCA$ [M1] $\tan\theta=\dfrac{AD}{AC}=\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Identify the right-angled triangle that contains the line in question; the angle between a line and a plane is measured from the line to its projection on the plane. Here the projection of $DC$ on the base is $AC$.

subtopic: Sphere inscribed in a cylinder: volume and surface ratios
statement: A solid sphere of radius $r$ fits exactly inside a closed cylinder, so that the sphere touches the curved wall and both circular ends of the cylinder. (a) Write down the height of the cylinder in terms of $r$, and show that the volume of the cylinder is $2\pi r^3$. [2] (b) Show that the volume of the sphere is $\dfrac23$ of the volume of the cylinder. [2] (c) Show that the area of the curved surface of the cylinder equals the surface area of the sphere. [2] (d) The volume of the sphere is $288\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$. Find the radius and the volume of the cylinder. [2]
markscheme: (a) Height $=2r$ [A1] $V=\pi r^2(2r)=2\pi r^3$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\frac43\pi r^3}{2\pi r^3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac23$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Curved area of cylinder $=2\pi r(2r)=4\pi r^2$ [M1] which equals the surface area of the sphere $4\pi r^2$ [AG] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac43\pi r^3=288\pi\Rightarrow r^3=216$, so $r=6$ cm [A1] Cylinder volume $=2\pi(6)^3=432\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For "show that" questions, write each algebraic step; do not substitute numbers. Use the fact that the sphere's diameter equals both the cylinder's height and its base diameter.

subtopic: Capacity of a rectangular fish tank in liters
statement: A fish tank is a cuboid with interior base $50$ cm by $40$ cm and interior height $30$ cm. Note that $1000\ \mathrm{cm}^3=1$ liter. (a) Find the capacity of the tank in liters. [2] (b) The tank is filled with water to $\dfrac34$ of its height. Find the volume of water in liters. [2] (c) A solid ornament of volume $3$ liters is placed on the bottom of the tank and is completely covered by the water. Find the rise in the water level, in cm. [2]
markscheme: (a) $50\times40\times30=60000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [M1] $=60$ liters [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac34\times60$ [M1] $=45$ liters [A1] [2 marks] (c) Volume of ornament $=3000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$, base area $=2000\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [M1] Rise $=\dfrac{3000}{2000}=1.5$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Convert units at the start: $1000\ \mathrm{cm}^3=1$ liter. A submerged object raises the water level by its volume divided by the base area of the tank.

subtopic: Scale model of a water tower: lengths, volumes and areas
statement: A water tower has a cylindrical tank of radius $4.5$ m and height $10$ m. A museum builds a scale model of the tank, which is also a cylinder, with radius $18$ cm and height $40$ cm. (a) Find the volume of the real tank in cubic meters, and give the capacity in liters, to three significant figures. Note that $1\ \mathrm{m}^3=1000$ liters. [3] (b) Find the volume of the model in $\mathrm{cm}^3$. [2] (c) Show that the model is built to a scale of $1:25$, and show that the ratio of the volume of the real tank to the volume of the model is $25^3$. [3] (d) The curved surface of the model required $0.15$ liters of paint. Assuming the same coverage, find the amount of paint needed for the curved surface of the real tank. [2]
markscheme: (a) Volume $=\pi(4.5)^2(10)$ [M1] $=636\ \mathrm{m}^3$ [A1] Capacity $=636000$ liters [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\pi(18)^2(40)$ [M1] $=40700\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $450\div18=25$ and $1000\div40=25$, so both dimensions have scale factor $25$ [R1] Real volume in $\mathrm{cm}^3=636000000$ [M1] $\dfrac{636000000}{40700}=15625=25^3$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) Area scale factor $=25^2=625$ [M1] $0.15\times625=93.75\approx93.8$ liters [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Lengths scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$. Convert to the same units before comparing the volumes.

subtopic: Cylindrical water tank: capacity, drawdown and painting
statement: A water tank is a closed cylinder with internal radius $1.2$ m and internal height $2.5$ m. It stands upright on a flat base. (a) Find the volume of the tank in $\mathrm{m}^3$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Write down the capacity of the tank in liters, correct to three significant figures. Note that $1\ \mathrm{m}^3=1000$ liters. [1] (c) The tank is full. Then $3000$ liters of water are pumped out. Find the distance, in meters, that the water level falls. [3] (d) The curved outer wall of the tank is to be painted. Find the area to be painted, in $\mathrm{m}^2$, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Write the unit conversion explicitly: $1000$ liters is $1\ \mathrm{m}^3$. Removing water lowers the level by the volume removed divided by the base area.

subtopic: Conical sand pile with a given angle of repose
statement: Sand is poured onto flat ground and forms a cone with base radius $2.4$ m. The sloping surface of the pile makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with the ground. (a) Find the height of the pile, in meters, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of sand in the pile, in $\mathrm{m}^3$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) The sand has a density of $1600\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Find the mass of the pile, in tonnes. Note that $1$ tonne $=1000$ kg. [2] (d) A tarpaulin is used to cover the whole sloping surface of the pile. Find the least area of tarpaulin needed, in $\mathrm{m}^2$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Draw the right-angled triangle formed by the height, radius and slant height of the cone. Use unrounded values from your calculator in later parts to avoid accumulated rounding error.

subtopic: Percentage error in the volume of a ball bearing
statement: A steel ball bearing is measured to have a diameter of $2.4$ cm. Its true diameter is $2.5$ cm. (a) Calculate the volume of the ball bearing using the measured diameter, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Calculate the true volume of the ball bearing, correct to three significant figures. [1] (c) Find the percentage error in the volume caused by using the measured diameter, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The steel has density $7.85\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Find the mass, in kilograms, of $500$ ball bearings of the true size, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Measured radius $=1.2$ cm [A1] $V=\dfrac43\pi(1.2)^3=7.24\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac43\pi(1.25)^3=8.18\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\left|\dfrac{7.24-8.18}{8.18}\right|\times100$ [M1] $=11.5\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $500\times8.18\times7.85=32100$ g [M1] $=32.1$ kg [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Percentage error is the absolute difference between the approximate and exact values divided by the exact value. Small errors in a length are magnified in a volume because the radius is cubed.

subtopic: Glass pyramid entrance: slant height, angles and cost
statement: The entrance hall of a museum is a glass pyramid. Its base is a horizontal square of side $35$ m and its apex is vertically above the centre of the base at a height of $21$ m. The four triangular faces are made entirely of glass. (a) Find the slant height of a triangular face, measured from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the angle between a triangular face and the base, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [2] (c) Find the length of a sloping edge of the pyramid, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the total area of glass, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) Glass costs \$185 per square meter, including fitting. Find the cost of the glass, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{21^2+17.5^2}$ [M1] $=27.3$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{21}{17.5}$ [M1] $\theta=50.2^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Half the base diagonal $=\dfrac{35\sqrt2}{2}=24.7$ [M1] Edge $=\sqrt{21^2+24.7^2}$ [M1] $=32.5$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $4\times\dfrac12\times35\times27.3$ [M1] $=1910\ \mathrm{m}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $1910\times185$ [M1] $=\$354000$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Be clear which right-angled triangle you use: the half-side gives the face, the half-diagonal gives the edge. Round only the final answer.

subtopic: Diagonals and angles inside a rectangular room
statement: A room is a cuboid $ABCDEFGH$. The floor $ABCD$ is a horizontal rectangle with $AB=8$ m and $BC=6$ m. The vertical edges $AE$, $BF$, $CG$ and $DH$ each have length $3.5$ m, so that $EFGH$ is the ceiling directly above the floor. A cable runs in a straight line from corner $A$ on the floor to corner $G$ on the ceiling. (a) Find the length of $AC$. [2] (b) Find the length of the cable $AG$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the angle between the cable $AG$ and the floor, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [2] (d) Find the angle between the cable $AG$ and the edge $AB$, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{8^2+6^2}$ [M1] $=10$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sqrt{10^2+3.5^2}$ [M1] $=10.6$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{3.5}{10}$ [M1] $\theta=19.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $AB$ is perpendicular to the plane $BCGF$, so angle $ABG=90^\circ$ [R1] $\cos\phi=\dfrac{8}{10.6}$ [M1] $\phi=41.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane uses the projection of the line on the plane. For the angle with an edge, find a triangle with a right angle at the end of that edge.

subtopic: Triangular prism tent: cross-section, volume and canvas
statement: A tent has the shape of a triangular prism lying on one of its rectangular faces. Its two ends are isosceles triangles with equal sides $1.8$ m and an angle of $80^\circ$ between the equal sides. The tent is $3.2$ m long. (a) Find the area of one triangular end of the tent, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of air inside the tent, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the width of the ground sheet, that is, the side opposite the $80^\circ$ angle, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) The tent is made from two sloping rectangular sides, two triangular ends and a rectangular ground sheet. Find the total area of material, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: The area of a triangle with two sides and the included angle is $\frac12ab\sin C$. The cosine rule gives the third side of the end triangle.

subtopic: Ice cream cone topped with a hemisphere of ice cream
statement: An ice cream cone is a hollow cone with a circular opening of radius $3.2$ cm and slant height $11.5$ cm. The cone is filled to the brim with ice cream, and a hemisphere of ice cream of the same radius sits on top. (a) Find the vertical height of the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of ice cream inside the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the volume of the hemisphere of ice cream, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The ice cream has density $0.55\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Find the total mass of ice cream, in grams, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) The outside of the cone is covered with a paper wrapper (the curved surface only). Find the area of the wrapper, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Use the vertical height in the volume formula and the slant height in the curved surface area. Keep full calculator values until the final line of each part.

subtopic: Frustum bucket: volume by similar cones, filling time and metal
statement: A bucket is in the shape of a frustum of a cone. The circular top of the bucket has radius $14$ cm, the circular base has radius $9$ cm, and the vertical height of the bucket is $28$ cm. The frustum is formed by removing a small cone from the top of a large cone. (a) Let $H$ cm be the height of the large cone. Use similar triangles to show that $H=78.4$. [3] (b) Find the volume of the bucket, in liters, correct to three significant figures. Note that $1000\ \mathrm{cm}^3=1$ liter. [3] (c) Water flows into the empty bucket at a constant rate of $0.4$ liters per second. Find the time, in seconds, to fill the bucket, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The curved surface of the bucket, which has no lid, is made from sheet metal. Find the area of the curved surface of the bucket, correct to three significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{H-28}{H}=\dfrac{9}{14}$ [M1][A1] $14H-392=9H\Rightarrow5H=392$, so $H=78.4$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Large cone $=\dfrac13\pi(14)^2(78.4)$ and small cone $=\dfrac13\pi(9)^2(50.4)$ [M1][A1] $V=11800\ \mathrm{cm}^3=11.8$ liters [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{11.8}{0.4}$ [M1] $=29.5$ s [A1] [2 marks] (d) Slant height of bucket $=\sqrt{28^2+(14-9)^2}=28.4$ [M1][A1] Curved area $=\pi(14)(79.6)-\pi(9)(51.2)$ using slant heights $79.6$ and $51.2$ of the large and small cones [M1] $=2060\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Always sketch the full cone and mark the removed cone; similar triangles then link the two heights. Alternatively, the curved area of a frustum equals $\pi(R+r)\times$ slant height of the frustum.

subtopic: Cone made from a sector of paper: radius, height, volume
statement: A sector of a circle of radius $18$ cm and angle $240^\circ$ is cut from a sheet of paper. The straight edges of the sector are joined together, without overlap, to form a hollow cone. (a) Find the arc length of the sector, in terms of $\pi$. [2] (b) Find the base radius of the cone. [2] (c) Find the vertical height of the cone, correct to three significant figures, and hence its volume, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the angle between a slant edge and the axis of the cone, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [2]
tips: The radius of the sector becomes the slant height of the cone, and the arc length of the sector becomes the circumference of the base. Do not confuse the sector radius with the base radius.

subtopic: Minimizing the surface area of a closed 500 mL can
statement: A closed cylindrical can has base radius $r$ cm, height $h$ cm and volume $500\ \mathrm{cm}^3$. (a) Show that $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$. [1] (b) Hence show that the total surface area $A\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ of the can is given by $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [2] (c) Find $\dfrac{dA}{dr}$, and hence find the value of $r$ that minimizes $A$. Give your answer correct to three significant figures. [4] (d) Find the minimum surface area, and the corresponding height of the can, each correct to three significant figures. Write down the ratio $h:r$. [3] (e) The metal costs \$0.012 per $\mathrm{cm}^2$. Find the minimum cost of the metal for one can, to the nearest cent. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\pi r^2h=500$, so $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ [M1] $=2\pi r^2+2\pi r\cdot\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{1000}{r^2}$ [M1][A1] Setting $=0$: $r^3=\dfrac{250}{\pi}$ [M1] $r=4.30$ cm [A1] [4 marks] (d) $A_{\min}=349\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] $h=8.60$ cm [A1] $h:r=2:1$ (the height equals the diameter) [A1] [3 marks] (e) $349\times0.012=\$4.18$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Eliminate $h$ first so that $A$ is a function of one variable. You can also confirm the minimum by sketching $A(r)$ on your GDC.

subtopic: Submerging steel balls in a cylindrical container of water
statement: A cylindrical glass container has internal radius $6$ cm and internal height $15$ cm. It contains water to a depth of $10$ cm. A solid steel ball of radius $4.5$ cm is lowered into the water and rests on the bottom of the container. (a) Find the volume of the ball, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the rise in the water level, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the ball is completely under water. [2] (d) A second identical ball is added. Find the volume of water that overflows, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac43\pi(4.5)^3$ [M1] $=382\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Volume displaced $=$ volume of ball [R1] $\pi(6)^2\times\text{rise}=382$ [M1] rise $=3.37$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (c) New depth $=10+3.37=13.4$ cm [M1] $13.4>9$ (the diameter of the ball), so the ball is completely covered [R1] [2 marks] (d) Total rise would be $2(3.37)=6.75$ cm, giving depth $16.8$ cm [M1] This exceeds $15$ cm by $1.75$ cm [A1] Overflow $=\pi(6)^2(1.75)=198\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: An object that is completely submerged displaces its own volume of water. Treat the rise in level as a thin cylinder with the same base as the container.

subtopic: Right pyramid on a rectangular base: edges and face angles
statement: $VABCD$ is a right pyramid with a horizontal rectangular base $ABCD$, where $AB=12$ cm and $BC=9$ cm. The apex $V$ is vertically above the centre $O$ of the base, and $VO=10$ cm. (a) Show that $AC=15$ cm and find the length of $VA$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the angle between the edge $VA$ and the base, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [2] (c) Find the angle between the face $VAB$ and the base, and the angle between the face $VBC$ and the base, each correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [4] (d) Find the angle $\angle AVC$, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{12^2+9^2}=15$ [AG] $AO=7.5$ [A1] $VA=\sqrt{10^2+7.5^2}=12.5$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{10}{7.5}$ [M1] $\theta=53.1^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance from $O$ to $AB$ is $4.5$ and from $O$ to $BC$ is $6$ [M1][A1] Face $VAB$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{10}{4.5}=65.8^\circ$ [A1] Face $VBC$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{10}{6}=59.0^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\cos\angle AVC=\dfrac{12.5^2+12.5^2-15^2}{2(12.5)(12.5)}$ [M1][A1] $\angle AVC=73.7^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The perpendicular distance from the centre to each base edge differs for the two pairs of faces, so the two face angles are not equal. For $\angle AVC$ use the cosine rule in triangle $AVC$.

subtopic: Packing six cylindrical cans in a cuboid box: wasted space
statement: Six identical cylindrical cans of radius $3.3$ cm and height $12.2$ cm are packed upright in a cuboid box in two rows of three. Each can touches its neighbors and the sides of the box, and the box has no spare height. (a) Write down the length and width of the base of the box. [2] (b) Find the volume of the box, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the total volume of the six cans, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the percentage of the volume of the box that is empty, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: The diameter of a can sets the spacing in each row. Use unrounded volumes in the final percentage.

subtopic: Filling an inverted conical container at a steady rate
statement: A container is in the shape of an inverted cone (apex at the bottom) with vertical height $30$ cm and a circular top of radius $12$ cm. It is initially empty and water is poured in at a constant rate of $20\ \mathrm{cm}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. (a) Find the capacity of the container, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Show that, when the depth of water is $h$ cm, the radius of the water surface is $0.4h$ cm, and hence that the volume of water is $V=\dfrac{0.16\pi}{3}h^3$. [3] (c) Find the time taken for the water to reach a depth of $15$ cm, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the depth of water, in cm, after $60$ seconds, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Use similar triangles to write the radius of the water surface in terms of its depth. Halving the depth does not halve the volume: it gives one eighth of the capacity.

subtopic: Hollow steel pipe: volume of metal, mass and cost
statement: A steel pipe is a hollow cylinder of length $2$ m. Its outer radius is $5$ cm and its inner radius is $4.2$ cm. The steel has a density of $7.8\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. (a) Find the area of the circular cross-section of the steel, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of steel in the pipe, in $\mathrm{cm}^3$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the mass of the pipe, in kilograms, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Steel costs \$4.20 per kilogram. Find the cost of the steel in one pipe, to the nearest cent. [1]
tips: Convert the length to centimeters so that all measurements use the same unit. The volume of a hollow cylinder is the cross-sectional area of the metal times the length.

subtopic: Tetrahedron cut from the corner of a cube
statement: A solid wooden cube has edge length $10$ cm. A corner $O$ of the cube is sliced off by a plane that meets the three edges from $O$ at points $A$, $B$ and $C$, each at distance $6$ cm from $O$. The piece removed is the tetrahedron $OABC$, in which the angles $\angle AOB$, $\angle BOC$ and $\angle COA$ are all right angles. (a) Find the volume of the tetrahedron $OABC$. [2] (b) Find the exact length of $AB$, and explain why triangle $ABC$ is equilateral. [2] (c) Find the area of triangle $ABC$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Use the volume of the tetrahedron to find the perpendicular distance from $O$ to the plane $ABC$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) The face $OAB$ is the orthogonal projection of triangle $ABC$ onto the plane $OAB$. Find the angle between the plane $ABC$ and the plane $OAB$, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Base $OAB$ has area $\dfrac12(6)(6)=18$ [M1] $V=\dfrac13(18)(6)=36\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $AB=\sqrt{6^2+6^2}=6\sqrt2$ cm [A1] By symmetry $BC=CA=6\sqrt2$ as well [R1] [2 marks] (c) Equilateral triangle of side $6\sqrt2=8.49$ [M1] Area $=\dfrac12(6\sqrt2)^2\sin60^\circ$ [M1] $=31.2\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac13\times31.2\times d=36$ [M1] $d=3.46$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{area }OAB}{\text{area }ABC}=\dfrac{18}{31.2}$ [M1] $\theta=54.7^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Volume gives a neat way to find a perpendicular distance when the geometry is awkward: write the volume as $\frac13\times$ base $\times$ height in two different ways. The area of a projection is the original area times the cosine of the angle between the planes.

subtopic: Cylindrical grain store with a conical roof
statement: A grain store consists of a vertical cylinder of radius $2.5$ m and height $6$ m, topped by a cone-shaped roof of the same radius and vertical height $1.5$ m. (a) Find the volume of the cylindrical part, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of the conical roof, and hence the total volume of the store, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Wheat of density $780\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ fills the cylindrical part exactly. Find the mass of the wheat, in tonnes, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the slant height of the roof, and hence the area of the curved roof surface, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Split a composite solid into standard solids and add their volumes. Use the slant height for the curved area of the cone and the vertical height for its volume.

subtopic: Largest cylinder and cone inside a sphere: 3D optimization
statement: This question investigates the largest solid cylinder, and the largest solid cone, that can be cut from a solid sphere of radius $10$ cm. All lengths are in centimeters. A cylinder is cut so that its axis passes through the centre $O$ of the sphere and both of its circular ends lie on the surface of the sphere. Let the cylinder have half-height $y$ (so its height is $2y$) and base radius $x$, where $0<y<10$. (a) Show that $x^2=100-y^2$, and hence that the volume of the cylinder is $V=2\pi y\left(100-y^2\right)$. [3] (b) Calculate $V$, correct to three significant figures, for $y=2,\ 4,\ 6$ and $8$. Hence comment on how $V$ changes as $y$ increases from $2$ to $8$. [3] (c) Use your GDC to sketch the graph of $V$ against $y$ for $0<y<10$. Write down the maximum value of $V$ and the value of $y$ at which it occurs, each correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Differentiate $V$ with respect to $y$. Hence show that the maximum volume occurs when $y=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt3}$, and show that this is a maximum. [4] (e) Find the maximum volume of the cylinder as a percentage of the volume of the sphere, correct to three significant figures. Show that for a sphere of any radius $R$ this percentage is the same, and state its exact value. [3] (f) Now a cone is cut from the same sphere. Its apex is at the top of the sphere, its axis is vertical through $O$, and its circular base lies in a horizontal plane at distance $y$ below $O$, with its rim on the sphere, where $0\leq y<10$. Show that the volume of the cone is $V_c=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\left(100-y^2\right)(10+y)$. [3] (g) Find the value of $y$ for which the volume of the cone is a maximum, and find that maximum volume correct to three significant figures. Hence find which of the two solids, the largest cylinder or the largest cone, wastes less of the sphere, and state the percentage of the sphere wasted in each case. [5]
markscheme: (a) A rim point of the cylinder is on the sphere, so $x^2+y^2=10^2$ [M1][A1] $V=\pi x^2(2y)=2\pi y(100-y^2)$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $y=2$: $1210$; $y=4$: $2110$; $y=6$: $2410$; $y=8$: $1810$ (in $\mathrm{cm}^3$) [A2] $V$ increases to a maximum near $y=6$ and then decreases [A1] [3 marks] (c) Correct shape of graph with a single maximum [A1] $y=5.77$ [A1] $V_{\max}=2420\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dV}{dy}=2\pi\left(100-3y^2\right)$ [M1][A1] Set $\dfrac{dV}{dy}=0$: $y^2=\dfrac{100}{3}$, so $y=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt3}$ [M1] $\dfrac{d^2V}{dy^2}=-12\pi y<0$ for $y>0$, so a maximum [R1] [4 marks] (e) Sphere volume $=\dfrac43\pi(10)^3=4190$; percentage $=\dfrac{2420}{4190}\times100=57.7\%$ [M1][A1] For radius $R$: $V_{\max}=2\pi\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}\cdot\dfrac{2R^2}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi R^3}{3\sqrt3}$, so the ratio to $\dfrac43\pi R^3$ is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ ($\approx57.7\%$) [A1] [3 marks] (f) Height of cone $=10+y$ [A1] Base radius squared $=100-y^2$ [A1] $V_c=\dfrac13\pi\left(100-y^2\right)(10+y)$ [AG] [3 marks] (g) $\dfrac{dV_c}{dy}=\dfrac\pi3\left(100-20y-3y^2\right)$ [M1][A1] Setting $=0$: $(10-3y)(10+y)=0$, so $y=\dfrac{10}{3}$ (as $y\ge0$) [A1] $V_{c,\max}=1240\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] Waste: cylinder $42.3\%$, cone $70.4\%$, so the cylinder wastes less [A1] [5 marks]
tips: In Paper 3 questions, each part builds on the last: reuse the results you have shown. Sketch the graph on your GDC to check your calculus answer for the maximum, and quote exact values before rounding.

subtopic: Perpendicular bisector of two sites and the nearer site
statement: Two bicycle-repair stations are located at $A(2,1)$ and $B(8,5)$ on a coordinate grid, where each unit represents $1$ km. Every cyclist goes to the nearer station, so the plane is split into two Voronoi cells by the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. (a) Find the midpoint of $AB$. [1] (b) Find the gradient of $AB$ and the gradient of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [2] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, giving your answer in the form $ax+by=c$ where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers. [2] (d) A cyclist stands at $P(4,4)$. By finding the squared distances $AP^2$ and $BP^2$, show that the cyclist is closer to $A$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(5,3)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Gradient of $AB=\dfrac{5-1}{8-2}=\dfrac23$ [A1] Gradient of bisector $=-\dfrac32$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y-3=-\dfrac32(x-5)$ [M1] $3x+2y=21$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $AP^2=2^2+3^2=13$ and $BP^2=4^2+1^2=17$ [M1] $13<17$, so $P$ is closer to $A$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint and has gradient equal to the negative reciprocal of the gradient of the line joining the two sites. Comparing squared distances avoids square roots.

subtopic: Voronoi vertex of three sites forming a right-angled triangle
statement: Three wells are located at $A(0,0)$, $B(6,0)$ and $C(0,8)$ on a coordinate grid. The Voronoi diagram for these three sites has exactly one vertex, $V$. (a) Find the equations of the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and of $AC$. [2] (b) Write down the coordinates of $V$. [1] (c) Show that $V$ is equidistant from $A$, $B$ and $C$, and state this distance. [2] (d) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ and verify that it passes through $V$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Bisector of $AB$: $x=3$ [A1] Bisector of $AC$: $y=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=(3,4)$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $VA=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$, $VB=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$, $VC=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ [M1] Distance is $5$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Gradient of $BC=-\dfrac43$, so bisector has gradient $\dfrac34$; midpoint of $BC$ is $(3,4)$ [M1] Midpoint is $V$, so the bisector $y-4=\dfrac34(x-3)$ passes through $V$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A Voronoi vertex is equidistant from three sites, so it is the intersection of any two of the perpendicular bisectors. Check your answer using the third bisector or by computing distances.

subtopic: Voronoi vertex of an isosceles triangle with exact fractions
statement: Three sensors are placed at $A(-4,0)$, $B(4,0)$ and $C(0,6)$. Their Voronoi cells meet at a single vertex $V$. (a) Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Hence find the coordinates of $V$. [2] (d) Find the exact distance from $V$ to each of the three sensors. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=0$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Midpoint of $AC=(-2,3)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac{6}{4}=\dfrac32$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $y-3=-\dfrac23(x+2)$, i.e. $y=-\dfrac23x+\dfrac53$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Substitute $x=0$ [M1] $V=\left(0,\dfrac53\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $VA=\sqrt{16+\dfrac{25}{9}}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{\dfrac{169}{9}}=\dfrac{13}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Because $A$ and $B$ are symmetric about the $y$-axis, the vertex lies on the $y$-axis, so only one more bisector is needed. Keep fractions exact.

subtopic: Voronoi edges and vertex from three sites with a horizontal bisector
statement: Three schools are located at $A(3,2)$, $B(3,10)$ and $C(9,6)$ on a map with $1$ unit representing $1$ km. (a) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex where these two bisectors meet. [2] (d) Show that this vertex also lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AB$ is vertical, so the bisector is horizontal [M1] through $(3,6)$: $y=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Midpoint $=(6,4)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac{4}{6}=\dfrac23$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac32$ [A1] $y-4=-\dfrac32(x-6)$, so $y=-\dfrac32x+13$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $-\dfrac32x+13=6$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{14}{3}$, vertex $\left(\dfrac{14}{3},6\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Midpoint of $BC=(6,8)$, gradient of $BC=-\dfrac23$, so bisector gradient is $\dfrac32$ and $y=\dfrac32x-1$ [M1] At $x=\dfrac{14}{3}$: $y=7-1=6$, so the vertex lies on it [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle's sides meet at a single point. Use the third bisector as a check on your vertex.

subtopic: Nearest neighbor interpolation of temperature from three stations
statement: Three weather stations are located at $S_1(1,2)$, $S_2(5,6)$ and $S_3(7,1)$, where each unit is $1$ km. They record temperatures of $14^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $18^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $11^\circ\mathrm{C}$ respectively. The temperature at any other location is estimated by using the temperature at the nearest station. (a) Find the squared distance from the point $P(3,3)$ to each of the three stations. [3] (b) Hence write down the estimated temperature at $P$. [1] (c) Estimate the temperature at $Q(6,4)$, showing your working. [2] (d) A point lies exactly on the boundary between the cells of $S_1$ and $S_2$. State what is true about its distances from $S_1$ and $S_2$. [1]
tips: In nearest neighbor interpolation each point takes the value of the closest site. Compare squared distances; the smallest one gives the nearest station.

subtopic: Area of a Voronoi cell inside a square plot
statement: Two sprinklers are placed in a square lawn with corners $(0,0)$, $(10,0)$, $(10,10)$ and $(0,10)$ (units in meters). The sprinklers are at $A(2,2)$ and $B(6,6)$. Each point of the lawn is watered by the nearer sprinkler. (a) Write down the midpoint of $AB$. [1] (b) Show that the equation of the boundary between the two watering regions is $x+y=8$. [2] (c) Write down the coordinates of the points where this boundary meets the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis. [1] (d) Find the area of the part of the lawn watered by $A$. [2] (e) Find the percentage of the lawn watered by $B$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(4,4)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Gradient of $AB=1$, so the boundary has gradient $-1$ [M1] $y-4=-(x-4)$, so $x+y=8$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $(8,0)$ and $(0,8)$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Region is a right triangle with legs $8$ and $8$ [M1] Area $=\dfrac12(8)(8)=32\ \mathrm{m}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Area of $B$'s region $=100-32=68$ [M1] $68\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch the square and draw the bisector first. The region on one side of the bisector inside the square is often a triangle or trapezoid whose area you can find exactly.

subtopic: Adding a third site: new bisectors and a shortened edge
statement: Two fire lookouts are at $A(0,0)$ and $B(12,0)$, so the boundary between their cells is the line $x=6$. A third lookout is now built at $C(6,9)$. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ has equation $4x+6y=39$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, in the form $4x-6y=k$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex of $A$, $B$ and $C$. [2] (d) Describe how the boundary $x=6$ between the cells of $A$ and $B$ changes when $C$ is added. Consider only points with $y\geq0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AC=(3,4.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac32$, so gradient of bisector $=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $y-4.5=-\dfrac23(x-3)\Rightarrow4x+6y=39$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Midpoint of $BC=(9,4.5)$ and gradient of $BC=-\dfrac32$, so bisector gradient $=\dfrac23$ [M1] $4x-6y=9$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Adding the equations: $8x=48$, so $x=6$ [M1] $y=\dfrac{39-24}{6}=2.5$, vertex $(6,2.5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Only the part of $x=6$ with $0\leq y\leq2.5$ remains a boundary between $A$ and $B$ [A1] Above $y=2.5$ the cell of $C$ separates the cells of $A$ and $B$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When a new site is added, draw its bisectors with each neighboring site; the new cell is bounded by them. Old edges are shortened where they enter the new cell.

subtopic: Finding an unknown site from a given Voronoi vertex
statement: Three sites are $A(0,0)$, $B(8,0)$ and $C(c,7)$, where $c>4$. The Voronoi cells of the three sites meet at the vertex $V(4,3)$. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is $x=4$, and write down the distance $VA$. [2] (b) Find the value of $c$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ and show that it passes through $V$. [3] (d) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AB=(4,0)$ and $AB$ is horizontal, so the bisector is $x=4$ [A1] $VA=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $VC=VA=5$ [M1] $(c-4)^2+(7-3)^2=25$ [A1] $(c-4)^2=9$ and $c>4$, so $c=7$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $C=(7,7)$, midpoint $(3.5,3.5)$, gradient of $AC=1$ [M1] Bisector $y-3.5=-(x-3.5)$, so $y=7-x$ [A1] At $x=4$: $y=3$, so it passes through $V$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) Midpoint of $BC=(7.5,3.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $BC=\dfrac{7-0}{7-8}=-7$, so bisector gradient $=\dfrac17$ [A1] $y-3.5=\dfrac17(x-7.5)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the fact that $V$ is equidistant from the three sites to form an equation. The condition $c>4$ rules out the second solution of the quadratic.

subtopic: Toxic waste location inside an acute triangle of villages
statement: Three villages are at $A(2,0)$, $B(6,0)$ and $C(4,4)$, where each unit represents $1$ km. A waste-treatment plant is to be built at a point in the triangular region $ABC$ (including its boundary) that is as far as possible from its nearest village. It is known that the best point is the Voronoi vertex of the three villages. (a) Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AC$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the plant. [2] (d) Find the distance from the plant to the nearest village. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x=4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Midpoint of $AC=(3,2)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=2$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac12$ [A1] $y-2=-\dfrac12(x-3)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) At $x=4$: $y=2-\dfrac12=\dfrac32$ [M1] $(4,1.5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\sqrt{2^2+1.5^2}=2.5$ km [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The best location for a facility that must be far from all sites is a Voronoi vertex (the centre of a largest empty circle). Check that the vertex is inside the allowed region.

subtopic: Rainfall estimation by nearest rain gauge (Voronoi cells)
statement: Four rain gauges are located at $G_1(2,3)$, $G_2(8,1)$, $G_3(6,7)$ and $G_4(1,8)$, where each unit represents $1$ km. In a storm they record $14$ mm, $22$ mm, $18$ mm and $9$ mm respectively. The rainfall at any other point is estimated by the reading of the nearest gauge (nearest neighbor interpolation). (a) Find the distance from the farm $F_1(7,3)$ to each of the four gauges, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Estimate the rainfall at each of the farms $F_1(7,3)$, $F_2(3,6)$ and $F_3(5,5.5)$. [3] (c) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $G_1$ and $G_3$ has equation $y=9-x$. [3] (d) State one weakness of nearest neighbor interpolation for rainfall. [1]
markscheme: (a) $F_1G_1=5.00$, $F_1G_2=2.24$, $F_1G_3=4.12$, $F_1G_4=7.81$ km [A2] [2 marks] (b) $F_1$: nearest is $G_2$, so $22$ mm [A1] $F_2$: distances $3.16$, $7.07$, $3.16$, $2.83$, nearest is $G_4$, so $9$ mm [A1] $F_3$: nearest is $G_3$ (distance $1.80$), so $18$ mm [A1] [3 marks] (c) Midpoint of $G_1G_3=(4,5)$ [A1] Gradient of $G_1G_3=\dfrac{7-3}{6-2}=1$, so bisector gradient $=-1$ [A1] $y-5=-(x-4)\Rightarrow y=9-x$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) The estimate jumps abruptly across cell boundaries, even though rainfall changes gradually (it also ignores trends between gauges) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Compute all the distances and pick the smallest; keep unrounded values on your calculator. A good comment mentions the sudden jumps in the estimate at the edges of the cells.

subtopic: Ambulance zones: bisector, nearest hospital and Voronoi vertex
statement: Three hospitals are located at $H_1(3.2,5.4)$, $H_2(9.6,2.1)$ and $H_3(7.5,9.3)$ on a map where each unit represents $1$ km. An ambulance is always sent from the nearest hospital. (a) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $H_1$ and $H_2$. Give your answer in the form $y=mx+c$ with $m$ and $c$ correct to three significant figures. [4] (b) An accident occurs at $X(6,6)$. Find the distance from $X$ to each hospital, and state which hospital is nearest. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex where the three cells meet, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the distance from this vertex to each hospital, correct to three significant figures, and state what this distance represents. [2]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint $=(6.4,3.75)$ [A1] Gradient of $H_1H_2=\dfrac{2.1-5.4}{9.6-3.2}=-0.515625$ [A1] Bisector gradient $=1.94$ [A1] $y=1.94x-8.66$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $XH_1=2.86$, $XH_2=5.31$, $XH_3=3.62$ km [A2] Nearest is $H_1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve two perpendicular bisector equations simultaneously on the GDC [M1] $(7.20,\,5.31)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $4.00$ km [A1] The radius of the largest empty circle centered at the vertex, the greatest distance to the nearest hospital at that point [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the bisector in the form $y=mx+c$ using the midpoint and the negative reciprocal gradient. At a Voronoi vertex all three distances are equal, which is a good check on your solution.

subtopic: Toxic waste dump in a rectangular region with five villages
statement: Five villages are at $A(3,7)$, $B(6,0)$, $C(10,8)$, $D(11,2)$ and $E(0,3)$ in a rectangular region $0\leq x\leq12$, $0\leq y\leq10$, where each unit is $1$ km. A toxic waste dump is to be placed at the point of the region that is as far as possible from the nearest village. The Voronoi diagram has interior vertices at $P(3.864,3.227)$, $Q(6.923,4.538)$ and $R(7.125,4.438)$. Its edges meet the boundary of the region at $(2.25,0)$, $(8.9,0)$, $(12,5.25)$, $(6.143,10)$ and $(0,6.125)$ (coordinates to four significant figures). (a) Explain why the best location for the dump must be a Voronoi vertex, a point where an edge meets the boundary of the region, or a corner of the region. [1] (b) Show that $Q$ is, to three significant figures, equidistant from $A$, $B$ and $C$, and state this distance. [3] (c) Find the distance from each of the following points to its nearest village: $R$, $P$, $(6.143,10)$ and $(0,10)$. [4] (d) The distances from the other four boundary points and the other three corners to their nearest villages are all at most $3.75$ km. Hence write down the best location for the dump and the distance from the nearest village. [2] (e) A second dump must be placed at least $4.5$ km from every village. Using your answers, state which of the points considered in part (c) and part (d) satisfy this condition. [2]
markscheme: (a) Moving away from a site increases its distance, so the maximum of the distance to the nearest site occurs only at these extreme points of the cells [R1] [1 mark] (b) $QA=\sqrt{(6.923-3)^2+(4.538-7)^2}=4.63$ [M1] $QB=\sqrt{(6.923-6)^2+4.538^2}=4.63$ and $QC=\sqrt{(10-6.923)^2+(8-4.538)^2}=4.63$ [A1] All equal $4.63$ km (to 3 s.f.), the distance from $Q$ to the three villages [A1] [3 marks] (c) $R$: $4.58$ [A1] $P$: $3.87$ [A1] $(6.143,10)$: $4.34$ [A1] $(0,10)$: $4.24$ (in km) [A1] [4 marks] (d) The greatest distance is at $Q$ [R1] Location $Q(6.92,4.54)$, distance $4.63$ km [A1] [2 marks] (e) $Q$ ($4.63$) [A1] and $R$ ($4.58$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a toxic waste problem, list every candidate point (Voronoi vertices, boundary intersections, corners) and compute its distance to the nearest site; the largest value wins. Do not forget the boundary and the corners.

subtopic: Area of a Voronoi cell by splitting it into triangles
statement: Three observation towers are located at $A(2,2)$, $B(10,3)$ and $C(5,9)$ in a rectangular reserve $0\leq x\leq12$, $0\leq y\leq10$ (units in km). Each point of the reserve is assigned to the nearest tower. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ has equation $y=50.5-8x$. [3] (b) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ has equation $y=7-\dfrac37x$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex $V$ where these two bisectors meet, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The cell of $A$ is the quadrilateral with vertices $O(0,0)$, $P(6.3125,0)$, $V$ and $Q(0,7)$, where $P$ and $Q$ are the points where the bisectors meet the axes. Find the area of the cell of $A$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AB=(6,2.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $AB=\dfrac18$, so bisector gradient $=-8$ [A1] $y-2.5=-8(x-6)\Rightarrow y=50.5-8x$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Midpoint of $AC=(3.5,5.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac73$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac37$ [A1] $y-5.5=-\dfrac37(x-3.5)\Rightarrow y=7-\dfrac37x$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) Solve $50.5-8x=7-\dfrac37x$ [M1] $V=(5.75,\,4.54)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Split into triangles $OPV$ and $OVQ$ [M1] Areas: $\dfrac12(6.3125)(4.54)=14.3$ and $\dfrac12(7)(5.75)=20.1$ [A1] Total $=34.4\ \mathrm{km}^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split an irregular polygon into triangles with a common vertex, or use the shoelace formula on your GDC. Use unrounded coordinates of the vertex for the area.

subtopic: Adding a new fire station: new cell as a trapezoid and its area
statement: Three fire stations are located at $A(2,3)$, $B(10,2)$ and $C(6,9)$ in a rectangular county $0\leq x\leq12$, $0\leq y\leq10$ (units in km). A new station $D$ is built at $(6,4)$. The cell of $D$ in the new Voronoi diagram is bounded by the perpendicular bisectors of $D$ with each of $A$, $B$ and $C$ and by the line $y=0$. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $C$ and $D$ is the line $y=6.5$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $D$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $B$ and $D$. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the four vertices of the cell of $D$. [3] (e) Find the area of the cell of $D$, and express it as a percentage of the area of the county, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $C$ and $D$ have the same $x$-coordinate, midpoint $(6,6.5)$, so the bisector is $y=6.5$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) Midpoint of $AD=(4,3.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $AD=\dfrac14$, so bisector gradient $=-4$ [A1] $y-3.5=-4(x-4)\Rightarrow y=19.5-4x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Midpoint of $BD=(8,3)$ and gradient of $BD=-\dfrac12$, so bisector gradient $=2$ [A1] $y=2x-13$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Where $y=19.5-4x$ meets $y=0$: $(4.875,0)$ and where $y=2x-13$ meets $y=0$: $(6.5,0)$ [A1] Where $y=19.5-4x$ meets $y=6.5$: $(3.25,6.5)$ [A1] Where $y=2x-13$ meets $y=6.5$: $(9.75,6.5)$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Trapezoid with parallel sides $1.625$ and $6.5$ and height $6.5$ [A1] Area $=\dfrac12(1.625+6.5)(6.5)=26.4\ \mathrm{km}^2$ [A1] Percentage $=\dfrac{26.4}{120}\times100=22.0\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The cell of a new site is bounded by its bisectors with all of its neighbors. Find each vertex by intersecting adjacent bisectors, then use the trapezoid or shoelace formula.

subtopic: Wi-Fi hubs: bisector equations solved with matrices
statement: Three Wi-Fi hubs are located at $A(1.5,2.5)$, $B(9.5,4)$ and $C(5,11)$ on a map where each unit is $1$ km. A point is served by its nearest hub. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B$ can be written as $16x+3y=97.75$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $B$ and $C$ in the form $ax+by=c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are real numbers. [3] (c) Use your GDC to solve the two equations simultaneously, and hence find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex $V$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the distance from $V$ to hub $A$, correct to three significant figures, and verify that $V$ is also at this distance from $C$. [2] (e) Each hub has a range of $5$ km. The triangle $ABC$ is acute, and it is known that $V$ is the point of triangle $ABC$ (including its boundary) that is farthest from its nearest hub. State, with a reason, whether every point of triangle $ABC$ is within range of at least one hub. [2]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AB=(5.5,3.25)$ [A1] Gradient of $AB=\dfrac{1.5}{8}=\dfrac{3}{16}$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac{16}{3}$ [A1] $y-3.25=-\dfrac{16}{3}(x-5.5)\Rightarrow16x+3y=97.75$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Midpoint of $BC=(7.25,7.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $BC=\dfrac{7}{-4.5}$, so bisector gradient $=\dfrac{4.5}{7}$ [A1] $-9x+14y=39.75$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $\begin{pmatrix} 16 & 3 \\ -9 & 14 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 97.75 \\ 39.75 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $V=(4.98,\,6.04)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $VA=\sqrt{(4.98-1.5)^2+(6.04-2.5)^2}=4.96$ km [A1] $VC=\sqrt{(5-4.98)^2+(11-6.04)^2}=4.96$ km [A1] [2 marks] (e) Yes [A1] The largest nearest-hub distance in the triangle is at $V$, which is $4.96$ km, and $4.96<5$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write each bisector as $ax+by=c$ so the system can be solved with the matrix or solver functions on your GDC. The distances from a vertex to its three sites must be equal.

subtopic: Cyclist on a straight road: where the nearest station changes
statement: Two charging stations are at $A(2,6)$ and $B(10,2)$, where each unit represents $1$ km. A straight road follows the line $y=0.4x+2$, for $0\leq x\leq12$. A cyclist rides along the road from the point with $x=0$ to the point with $x=12$ and always uses the nearer station. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B$ has equation $y=2x-8$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the point $P$ where the road crosses the perpendicular bisector. [2] (c) Find the distance $PA$, correct to three significant figures, and state the distance $PB$. [2] (d) State which station the cyclist uses at the start of the road and which station at the end, giving a reason for each. [3]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AB=(6,4)$ [A1] Gradient of $AB=-\dfrac12$, so bisector gradient $=2$ [A1] $y-4=2(x-6)\Rightarrow y=2x-8$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $0.4x+2=2x-8$ [M1] $1.6x=10$, so $P=(6.25,4.5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $PA=\sqrt{(6.25-2)^2+(4.5-6)^2}=4.51$ km [A1] $PB=PA=4.51$ km because $P$ is on the bisector [A1] [2 marks] (d) At $(0,2)$: distance to $A=\sqrt{4+16}=4.47$ and to $B=\sqrt{100+0}=10$, so station $A$ [A1] At $(12,6.8)$: distance to $A=\sqrt{100+0.64}=10.0$ and to $B=\sqrt{4+23.04}=5.20$, so station $B$ [A1] The nearest station changes at $P$, where the road crosses the cell boundary [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The place where a path crosses a Voronoi boundary is where the nearest site changes. Solve the equation of the path together with the equation of the bisector.

subtopic: Population served by each clinic from Voronoi cell areas
statement: Three clinics are located at $A(3,2)$, $B(9,2)$ and $C(6,8)$ in a rectangular district $0\leq x\leq12$, $0\leq y\leq10$ (units in km). The population density is uniform at $240$ people per $\mathrm{km}^2$, and each resident uses the nearest clinic. (a) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $C$. [3] (b) The perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B$ is $x=6$. Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex of the three clinics. [2] (c) The cell of $A$ is bounded by $x=0$, $y=0$, $x=6$ and the bisector of $A$ and $C$. Find the area of the cell of $A$. [2] (d) By symmetry, the cell of $B$ has the same area. Find the area of the cell of $C$, and the population served by each clinic. [3]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AC=(4.5,5)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=2$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac12$ [A1] $y-5=-\dfrac12(x-4.5)$, so $y=7.25-0.5x$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Substitute $x=6$: $y=7.25-3=4.25$ [M1] $(6,4.25)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Trapezoid with parallel sides $4.25$ (at $x=6$) and $7.25$ (at $x=0$), width $6$ [M1] Area $=\dfrac12(4.25+7.25)(6)=34.5\ \mathrm{km}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Area of $C=120-2(34.5)=51\ \mathrm{km}^2$ [A1] Population of $A$ and $B$: $34.5\times240=8280$ each [A1] Population of $C$: $51\times240=12240$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When density is uniform, population is proportional to area. Use symmetry in the diagram to avoid repeating work, and check that the three areas add up to the area of the district.

subtopic: Drone flight path crossing a Voronoi boundary (vector line)
statement: Two depots are at $A(2,8)$ and $B(10,4)$, where each unit is $1$ km. A drone leaves the origin $O$ and flies with position at time $t$ hours given by $\mathbf{r}=t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ for $t\geq0$. It is controlled by the depot nearer to its current position. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B$ is $y=2x-6$. [3] (b) Find the value of $t$ at which the drone crosses the perpendicular bisector, and the coordinates of the crossing point. [3] (c) Find the speed of the drone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Which depot controls the drone at $t=0$, and which at $t=2$? Justify your answers using distances. [3]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AB=(6,6)$ [A1] Gradient of $AB=-\dfrac12$, so bisector gradient $=2$ [A1] $y-6=2(x-6)\Rightarrow y=2x-6$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $x=3t$, $y=t$, so $t=2(3t)-6$ [M1] $5t=6$ gives $t=1.2$ [A1] Point $(3.6,1.2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\left|\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\right|=\sqrt{10}$ [M1] $=3.16$ km/h [A1] [2 marks] (d) $t=0$: $O$ to $A=\sqrt{68}=8.25$ and to $B=\sqrt{116}=10.8$, so $A$ [A1] $t=2$: point $(6,2)$, distance to $A=\sqrt{16+36}=7.21$, to $B=\sqrt{16+4}=4.47$, so $B$ [A1] Consistent with the crossing at $t=1.2$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the points on the path as a function of $t$ and substitute into the equation of the bisector. The speed is the magnitude of the direction vector when $t$ is in hours and distances in km.

subtopic: Cell tower coverage: vertex and farthest point in a cell
statement: Three towers are at $A(2,2)$, $B(8,2)$ and $C(5,7)$ in a rectangular region $0\leq x\leq10$, $0\leq y\leq8$ (units in km). A phone connects to the nearest tower.
