(a) Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $C$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex $V$ and the distance from $V$ to tower $A$. [3] (d) The cell of $A$ has vertices $(0,0)$, $(5,0)$, $V$ and $(0,6.6)$. Find the farthest distance from tower $A$ to a point in its cell, correct to three significant figures. [3] (e) Each tower has a range of $5$ km. Is the whole cell of $A$ within range of tower $A$? Justify. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Midpoint of $AC=(3.5,4.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac53$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac35$ [A1] $y-4.5=-\dfrac35(x-3.5)$, so $y=6.6-0.6x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) At $x=5$: $y=6.6-3=3.6$, so $V=(5,3.6)$ [A1] $VA=\sqrt{3^2+1.6^2}$ [M1] $=3.4$ km [A1] [3 marks] (d) Distances from $A$: to $(0,0)$ $=2.83$, to $(5,0)$ $=3.61$, to $V$ $=3.4$, to $(0,6.6)$ $=\sqrt{4+21.16}$ [M1] $=5.02$ km [A1] The farthest point of a convex cell from its site is a vertex of the cell, so the greatest distance is $5.02$ km [R1] [3 marks] (e) No, the point $(0,6.6)$ is $5.02>5$ km from $A$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The farthest point of a cell from its own site is always one of the cell's vertices (or a corner of the region), so you only have to check a few distances.

subtopic: Delivery warehouses: area by shoelace and expected orders
statement: Four warehouses $W_1(2,2)$, $W_2(11,3)$, $W_3(5,8)$ and $W_4(12,10)$ serve a rectangular region $0\leq x\leq15$, $0\leq y\leq12$ (units in km). Each customer is served by the nearest warehouse. The cell of $W_2$ is the pentagon with vertices $(6.78,0)$, $(15,0)$, $(15,6)$, $(9.12,6.84)$ and $(6.38,3.56)$ (to three significant figures). The areas of the cells of $W_1$, $W_3$ and $W_4$ are $33.6\ \mathrm{km}^2$, $58.5\ \mathrm{km}^2$ and $36.6\ \mathrm{km}^2$ respectively. (a) Use the shoelace formula or your GDC to find the area of the cell of $W_2$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Verify that the four areas add up to the area of the region, to three significant figures. [2] (c) A customer's location is chosen at random, with all locations in the region equally likely. Find the probability that the customer is served by $W_2$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) There are $1200$ orders in a day, spread uniformly over the region. Find the expected number of orders handled by each warehouse, to the nearest whole number. [3]
markscheme: (a) Use of the shoelace formula with the five vertices in order [M1][A1] Area $=51.3\ \mathrm{km}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Area of region $=15\times12=180$ [A1] $33.6+51.3+58.5+36.6=180\approx180$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{51.3}{180}$ [M1] $=0.285$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Expected orders $=1200\times\dfrac{\text{area}}{180}$ [M1] $W_1$: $224$, $W_2$: $342$, $W_3$: $390$, $W_4$: $244$ [A2] [3 marks]
tips: For a uniform random location, probability equals area divided by total area. Enter the vertices in order around the polygon when using the shoelace formula.

subtopic: Moving one site: displacement of a Voronoi vertex
statement: Three sensors are at $A(2,2)$, $B(8,2)$ and $C(5,8)$, where each unit represents $1$ km. The Voronoi cells of the three sensors meet at a vertex $V_1$. Sensor $B$ is then moved to a new position $B'(8,4)$, giving a new vertex $V_2$ where the cells of $A$, $B'$ and $C$ meet. (a) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $C$, and the coordinates of $V_1$. [4] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B'$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of $V_2$. [2] (d) Find the distance between $V_1$ and $V_2$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) Verify that $V_2$ is equidistant from $A$, $B'$ and $C$, and state this distance correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: A Voronoi vertex moves when a site moves because its bisectors change. Recompute only the bisectors that involve the moved site; the bisector of the two unmoved sites stays the same.

subtopic: Fire station response: farthest point in a cell and travel time
statement: Four fire stations are at $A(3,3)$, $B(11,2)$, $C(7,9)$ and $D(14,10)$ in a rectangular county $0\leq x\leq16$, $0\leq y\leq12$ (units in km). A fire is served by the nearest station. The cell of $C$ has vertices $(0,12)$, $(10.14,12)$, $(10.92,6.59)$, $(7.25,4.50)$ and $(0,9.33)$ (to two decimal places). (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $C$ is $y=\dfrac{28}{3}-\dfrac23x$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $C$ and $D$, and verify that it passes through the vertex $(10.14,12)$ to two decimal places. [3] (c) Find the greatest distance from station $C$ to any point in its cell, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) A fire engine travels at an average speed of $60$ km h$^{-1}$ in a straight line. Find the longest possible response time from station $C$ to a fire in its cell, in minutes, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AC=(5,6)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac32$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $y-6=-\dfrac23(x-5)\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{28}{3}-\dfrac23x$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Midpoint of $CD=(10.5,9.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $CD=\dfrac17$, so bisector gradient $=-7$, giving $y=83-7x$ [A1] At $y=12$: $x=\dfrac{71}{7}=10.14$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Distances to the five vertices: $7.62$, $4.34$, $4.60$, $4.51$, $7.01$ [M1][A1] Greatest $=7.62$ km at $(0,12)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $60$ km h$^{-1}$ $=1$ km per minute [M1] Time $=7.62$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The farthest point in a convex cell is one of its vertices, so compute the distance to each vertex and choose the largest. Convert the speed to km per minute before dividing.

subtopic: Three collinear sites and a fourth site: unbounded strip cell
statement: Four sites are at $A(2,3)$, $B(6,3)$, $C(10,3)$ and $D(6,9)$ in a rectangular region $0\leq x\leq12$, $0\leq y\leq10$ (units in km). (a) Write down the equations of the perpendicular bisectors of $A$ and $B$, and of $B$ and $C$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $B$ and $D$. [1] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $D$, and verify that it passes through the point $(4,6)$. [3] (d) The cell of $B$ is the rectangle with $4\leq x\leq8$ and $0\leq y\leq6$. Find its area. [2] (e) Find the greatest distance from $B$ to a point in its cell, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=4$ [A1] and $x=8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=6$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Midpoint of $AD=(4,6)$ [A1] Gradient of $AD=\dfrac{6}{4}=\dfrac32$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $y-6=-\dfrac23(x-4)$, which passes through $(4,6)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $4\times6$ [M1] $=24\ \mathrm{km}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Corners of the cell: $(4,0)$, $(8,0)$, $(4,6)$, $(8,6)$, each at distance $\sqrt{2^2+3^2}$ from $B$ [M1] $=3.61$ km [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When sites are collinear, the bisectors of neighboring sites are parallel lines, so those cells are strips. Use the symmetry of the layout to get the second vertex from the first.

subtopic: Length of a Voronoi edge: a boundary fence between three districts
statement: Three depots are located at $A(1,2)$, $B(7,1)$ and $C(4,6)$ in a rectangular region $0\leq x\leq12$, $0\leq y\leq10$ (units in km). A fence is to be built along the boundary between the cells of $A$ and $B$. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B$ is $y=6x-22.5$, and find where it meets the $x$-axis. [4] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $C$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex of the three depots, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The boundary between the cells of $A$ and $B$ runs from $(3.75,0)$ to $V$. Find its length, correct to three significant figures, and the cost of the fence at \$85 per meter, correct to three significant figures. Note that $1$ unit is $1$ km. [3]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AB=(4,1.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $AB=-\dfrac16$, so bisector gradient $=6$ [A1] $y-1.5=6(x-4)\Rightarrow y=6x-22.5$ [AG] At $y=0$: $x=3.75$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Midpoint of $AC=(2.5,4)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac43$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac34$ [A1] $y=5.875-0.75x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $6x-22.5=5.875-0.75x$ [M1] $V=(4.20,\,2.72)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Length $=\sqrt{(4.20-3.75)^2+2.72^2}=2.76$ km [M1][A1] Cost $=2.76\times1000\times85=\$235000$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The length of a Voronoi edge is the distance between its two end points, one of which is a vertex and the other is where the edge meets the boundary. Convert kilometers to meters before costing.

subtopic: Toxic waste siting, adding a site and nearest neighbor estimates
statement: This question investigates where to place a toxic waste facility in a rectangular region. The region is $0\leq x\leq12$, $0\leq y\leq10$ (units in km). Five villages are at $P(9,10)$, $Q(12,1)$, $R(2,6)$, $S(12,8)$ and $T(2,1)$. Each point of the region belongs to the cell of the nearest village. The nitrate levels (mg per liter) in the wells of $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ and $T$ are $12$, $8$, $15$, $9$ and $11$ respectively. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $T$ and $R$ is $y=3.5$, and that the perpendicular bisector of $T$ and $Q$ is $x=7$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $R$ and $Q$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $P$ and $Q$. [3] (d) Hence show that the cells of $P$, $Q$ and $R$ meet at the point $V(7.5,4.5)$, and find the distance from $V$ to each of these three villages, correct to three significant figures. [3] (e) The only other interior vertex of the Voronoi partition is $(7,3.5)$, where the cells of $T$, $R$ and $Q$ meet. The remaining points where edges meet the boundary or corners of the region are all within $5.1$ km of their nearest village. Find the distance from $(7,3.5)$ to its nearest village, and hence state the location in the region that is farthest from the nearest village, with that distance. [4] (f) A new village $W$ is founded at $V(7.5,4.5)$. Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $W$ and $T$, and find the coordinates of the point where it meets the line $y=3.5$, correct to three significant figures. [4] (g) With $W$ present, the interior vertex $V$ no longer exists. Use the fact that the point $(4.357,10)$, where the bisector of $P$ and $R$ meets the top boundary, is $4.64$ km from $R$, and that the point $(6.5,0)$ is $4.61$ km from its nearest village, to explain why the best location for the toxic waste facility moves to the boundary. State the new location and the new greatest distance, and comment on the change. [4] (h) Use nearest neighbor interpolation to estimate the nitrate level at the point $X(7.4,4.6)$ and at the point $Y(7.6,4.4)$ (before village $W$ was added). Comment on the result. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T$ and $R$ have the same $x$-coordinate and midpoint $(2,3.5)$, so the bisector is $y=3.5$ [A1] $T(2,1)$ and $Q(12,1)$ have the same $y$-coordinate and midpoint $(7,1)$ [M1] so the bisector is $x=7$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Midpoint of $RQ=(7,3.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $RQ=\dfrac{1-6}{12-2}=-\dfrac12$, so bisector gradient $=2$ [A1] $y-3.5=2(x-7)$, so $y=2x-10.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Midpoint of $PQ=(10.5,5.5)$ [A1] Gradient of $PQ=\dfrac{1-10}{12-9}=-3$, so bisector gradient $=\dfrac13$ [A1] $y-5.5=\dfrac13(x-10.5)$, so $y=\dfrac x3+2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $2x-10.5=\dfrac x3+2$ [M1] $x=7.5$, $y=4.5$ [AG] $VP=\sqrt{1.5^2+5.5^2}=\sqrt{32.5}=5.70$ km, and $VQ=VR=5.70$ km [A1] [3 marks] (e) $(7,3.5)$ to $T$: $\sqrt{5^2+2.5^2}=5.59$ km [M1][A1] This is less than $5.70$ [R1] The toxic waste facility should be at $V(7.5,4.5)$, with distance $5.70$ km from the nearest village [A1] [4 marks] (f) Midpoint of $WT=(4.75,2.75)$ [A1] Gradient of $WT=\dfrac{3.5}{5.5}=\dfrac{7}{11}$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac{11}{7}$ [A1] $y-2.75=-\dfrac{11}{7}(x-4.75)$ [A1] Setting $y=3.5$: $x=4.27$, so the point is $(4.27,\,3.5)$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) The old best point $V$ is now $0$ km from village $W$, so it is no longer a good location [R1] Candidate distances: $(4.357,10)$ gives $4.64$ and $(6.5,0)$ gives $4.61$ [M1] Largest is at $(4.357,10)$ [A1] New distance $4.64$ km, smaller than the earlier $5.70$ km: adding a village always reduces (or keeps) the greatest distance from the nearest village [A1] [4 marks] (h) $XR=\sqrt{5.4^2+1.4^2}=5.58$, $XP=5.63$, $XQ=5.84$, so $X$ is nearest to $R$: $15$ mg per liter [A1] $YQ=5.56$, $YR=5.82$, $YP=5.77$, so $Y$ is nearest to $Q$: $8$ mg per liter [A1] Nearby points $0.28$ km apart receive very different estimates, a weakness of the method (the estimate is discontinuous at cell boundaries) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: In an extended question, set out your bisector equations clearly and re-use them in later parts. For toxic waste problems, check every Voronoi vertex, boundary point and corner, and say why you can ignore the others.

subtopic: Reflection in the y-axis: matrix, image and area
statement: A triangle has vertices $A(1,\,2)$, $B(4,\,2)$ and $C(4,\,5)$. (a) Write down the $2\times2$ matrix $\mathbf{R}$ that represents a reflection in the $y$-axis. [1] (b) Use $\mathbf{R}$ to find the coordinates of the images $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$. [2] (c) The area of triangle $ABC$ is $4.5$ square units. Find $\det\mathbf{R}$ and explain why the area of triangle $A'B'C'$ is also $4.5$ square units. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf{R}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ so $A'(-1,\,2)$ [M1] $B'(-4,\,2)$ and $C'(-4,\,5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{R}=(-1)(1)-0=-1$ [A1] The area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf{R}|=1$, so the area is unchanged (a reflection preserves lengths and areas) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The columns of a transformation matrix are the images of $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. A negative determinant means orientation is reversed, but the area factor is the absolute value $|\det|$.

subtopic: Quarter-turn rotation and its inverse
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ represents a rotation about the origin. (a) State the angle and direction of this rotation. [1] (b) Find the image of the point $P(3,\,-2)$ under $\mathbf{R}$. [2] (c) Find $\mathbf{R}^{-1}$ and hence find the point whose image under $\mathbf{R}$ is $(5,\,-1)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) A rotation of $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the origin [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf{R}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0(3)+(-1)(-2) \\ 1(3)+0(-2) \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ so the image is $(2,\,3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{R}=0-(-1)(1)=1$, so $\mathbf{R}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{R}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -5 \end{pmatrix}$ so the point is $(-1,\,-5)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The inverse of a rotation is a rotation through the same angle in the opposite direction, so you can write $\mathbf{R}^{-1}$ down or use the $2\times2$ inverse formula. Check by applying $\mathbf{R}$ to your answer.

subtopic: Horizontal and vertical stretch with area factor
statement: A transformation $\mathbf{T}$ stretches the plane by scale factor $3$ parallel to the $x$-axis and by scale factor $\dfrac12$ parallel to the $y$-axis. (a) Write down the matrix $\mathbf{T}$. [1] Triangle $OPQ$ has vertices $O(0,\,0)$, $P(4,\,0)$ and $Q(0,\,6)$. (b) Find the images of $P$ and $Q$ under $\mathbf{T}$. [2] (c) Find the area of triangle $OPQ$, and use $\det\mathbf{T}$ to find the area of its image. Verify your answer using the coordinates from part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $P'=(12,\,0)$ [A1] $Q'=(0,\,3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Area of $OPQ=\dfrac12(4)(6)=12$ [A1] $\det\mathbf{T}=3\times\dfrac12=\dfrac32$, so image area $=\dfrac32\times12=18$ [A1] Using the images: $\dfrac12(12)(3)=18$, which agrees [R1] [3 marks]
tips: For a stretch, the determinant is the product of the two scale factors. Check an area scale factor against a direct calculation when the coordinates are easy.

subtopic: Enlargement with a negative scale factor
statement: An enlargement about the origin with scale factor $-2$ is represented by the matrix $\mathbf{E}$. (a) Write down $\mathbf{E}$. [1] (b) Find the image of the point $(3,\,-1)$. [1] (c) Find $\det\mathbf{E}$. [1] (d) The image of a region under $\mathbf{E}$ has area $36$ square units. Find the area of the original region. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{E}=\begin{pmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(-6,\,2)$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\det\mathbf{E}=(-2)(-2)-0=4$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Image area $=4\times$ original area [M1] original area $=\dfrac{36}{4}=9$ square units [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A negative scale factor enlarges and also sends each point through the origin to the opposite side. Areas scale by the square of the scale factor, which here is $(-2)^2=4$.

subtopic: Shear transformation of the unit square
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ represents a shear. (a) Find the images of the vertices $(0,\,0)$, $(1,\,0)$, $(1,\,1)$ and $(0,\,1)$ of the unit square. [3] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{S}$ and hence write down the area of the image of the unit square. [2] (c) Find all the invariant points of $\mathbf{S}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{S}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} x+2y \\ y \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $(0,0)\to(0,0)$ and $(1,0)\to(1,0)$ [A1] $(1,1)\to(3,1)$ and $(0,1)\to(2,1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{S}=1\times1-2\times0=1$ [A1] The area of the image is $1$ square unit [A1] [2 marks] (c) Invariant: $x+2y=x$ and $y=y$ [M1] which gives $y=0$, so every point on the $x$-axis is invariant [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A shear keeps one line (here the $x$-axis) fixed pointwise and has determinant $1$, so it preserves area. To find invariant points, set the image equal to the original point.

subtopic: Order of composition: reflection then stretch
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}$ be the matrix of a reflection in the line $y=x$ and let $\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ be a stretch. (a) Write down $\mathbf{A}$. [1] (b) Find the matrix $\mathbf{BA}$. [2] (c) Find the image of $P(1,\,4)$ when $\mathbf{A}$ is applied first and then $\mathbf{B}$. [2] (d) Find $\mathbf{AB}$ and state whether $\mathbf{AB}=\mathbf{BA}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf{BA}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{BA}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ so the image is $(8,\,3)$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Since $\mathbf{AB}\neq\mathbf{BA}$, the order of the transformations matters [R1] [2 marks]
tips: When $\mathbf{A}$ is applied first, the combined matrix is $\mathbf{BA}$ (the matrix applied first is written on the right). Check your product with the point in part (c).

subtopic: Eigenvalues and invariant lines of an upper triangular matrix
statement: A transformation is represented by $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}$. [2] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Hence write down the equations of the two invariant lines of the transformation that pass through the origin. [1] (d) Find the image of the point $(2,\,-2)$ and describe what happens to it. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{M}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(3-\lambda)(2-\lambda)=0$ [M1] $\lambda=3$ and $\lambda=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) For $\lambda=3$: $y=0$, so an eigenvector is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=2$: $(3-2)x+y=0$, so $y=-x$ [M1] an eigenvector is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $y=0$ and $y=-x$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] the point lies on the invariant line $y=-x$ and is moved to $(4,\,-4)$, twice as far from the origin along the same line [A1] [2 marks]
tips: An eigenvector gives the direction of an invariant line through the origin, and the eigenvalue is the scale factor along that line. For a triangular matrix the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.

subtopic: Finding a parameter from an area scale factor
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} k & 2 \\ 3 & k+1 \end{pmatrix}$ represents a transformation of the plane, where $k$ is a real constant. (a) Show that $\det\mathbf{M}=k^2+k-6$. [2] A triangle of area $5$ square units is mapped by $\mathbf{M}$ to a triangle of area $30$ square units. (b) Find all possible values of $k$. [4] (c) For $k=3$, state whether the orientation of the triangle is preserved, giving a reason. [1] (d) Find the values of $k$ for which $\mathbf{M}$ has no inverse. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=k(k+1)-2\times3$ [M1] $=k^2+k-6$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $|\det\mathbf{M}|=\dfrac{30}{5}=6$ [M1] $k^2+k-6=6$ gives $(k+4)(k-3)=0$, so $k=-4$ or $k=3$ [A1] $k^2+k-6=-6$ gives $k(k+1)=0$ [M1] so $k=0$ or $k=-1$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{M}=9+3-6=6>0$, so orientation is preserved [A1] [1 mark] (d) $k^2+k-6=0$ [M1] $(k+3)(k-2)=0$, so $k=-3$ or $k=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf{M}|$, so the equation $|\det\mathbf{M}|=6$ gives two cases, positive and negative. Do not forget the negative case.

subtopic: Identifying a composite of a reflection and a rotation
statement: Let $\mathbf{X}$ be the matrix of a reflection in the $x$-axis and let $\mathbf{R}$ be the matrix of a rotation of $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the origin. (a) Write down $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{R}$. [2] (b) Find the matrix $\mathbf{RX}$ that represents reflection followed by rotation. [2] (c) Identify the single transformation represented by $\mathbf{RX}$. [2] (d) Find $\mathbf{XR}$ and describe the single transformation it represents. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{RX}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{RX}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} y \\ x \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] a reflection in the line $y=x$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{XR}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] a reflection in the line $y=-x$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A product of a reflection and a rotation is always a reflection (determinant $-1$). Find the mirror line by seeing where $(x,y)$ is sent, or by solving $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}$.

subtopic: Rotating a robot arm through repeated 35 degree turns
statement: A robot arm pivots about the origin $O$ in a horizontal plane. The tip of the arm is at $P(24.0,\,7.0)$, with distances in centimeters. The arm rotates $35^\circ$ anticlockwise about $O$. (a) Write down the rotation matrix, giving each entry correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the tip after the rotation, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Show that the distance of the tip from $O$ is unchanged by the rotation. [2] (d) The arm makes repeated rotations of $35^\circ$. Find the least number of rotations for the tip to return to its starting position. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} \cos35^\circ & -\sin35^\circ \\ \sin35^\circ & \cos35^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.819 & -0.574 \\ 0.574 & 0.819 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 24\cos35^\circ-7\sin35^\circ \\ 24\sin35^\circ+7\cos35^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $(15.6,\,19.5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $OP=\sqrt{24^2+7^2}=25$ [A1] New distance: $\sqrt{15.645^2+19.500^2}=25.0$ [A1] (or: rotations preserve lengths) [2 marks] (d) The total angle $35n$ must be a multiple of $360$ [M1] $n=72$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use degree mode for $\cos35^\circ$ and $\sin35^\circ$. For part (d), solve $35n=360k$ for the smallest positive integer $n$.

subtopic: Enlargement followed by a clockwise rotation of a logo
statement: A designer's logo is a triangle with vertices $A(2,\,1)$, $B(6,\,1)$ and $C(2,\,4)$ on a coordinate grid with units in centimeters. The logo is enlarged about the origin by scale factor $1.5$ and then rotated $20^\circ$ clockwise about the origin. (a) Write down the matrix of the rotation, with entries correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the single matrix that represents the enlargement followed by the rotation. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the image of $B$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the area of the image of the logo, and explain why the rotation does not affect the area. [3]
markscheme: (a) Clockwise rotation: $\begin{pmatrix} \cos20^\circ & \sin20^\circ \\ -\sin20^\circ & \cos20^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.940 & 0.342 \\ -0.342 & 0.940 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Matrix $=1.5\times\begin{pmatrix} 0.940 & 0.342 \\ -0.342 & 0.940 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1.41 & 0.513 \\ -0.513 & 1.41 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} 1.41\times6+0.513\times1 \\ -0.513\times6+1.41\times1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $B'=(8.97,\,-1.67)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Area of $ABC=\dfrac12(4)(3)=6$ [A1] $\det=1.5^2\times1=2.25$, so the image area is $2.25\times6=13.5\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] A rotation has determinant $1$ (it preserves lengths and angles), so only the enlargement changes the area [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The matrix for a clockwise rotation through $\theta$ is $\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}$. The matrix of the transformation applied first is written closest to the point.

subtopic: Reflection in a mirror line at 28 degrees to the x-axis
statement: A laser beam is reflected by a flat mirror. Using coordinates in centimeters, the mirror lies along the line through the origin that makes an angle of $28^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis. A reflection in a line through the origin at angle $\theta$ to the positive $x$-axis has matrix $\begin{pmatrix} \cos2\theta & \sin2\theta \\ \sin2\theta & -\cos2\theta \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write down the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ of the reflection in the mirror line, with entries correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) A small lamp is placed at the point $(5,\,2)$. Find the position of its mirror image, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Show that, for any angle $\theta$, the matrix has determinant $-1$ and that applying the reflection twice returns every point to its original position. [3] (d) Use your GDC to verify, correct to 3 significant figures, that the point $(\cos28^\circ,\,\sin28^\circ)$ is invariant under the reflection. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} \cos56^\circ & \sin56^\circ \\ \sin56^\circ & -\cos56^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.559 & 0.829 \\ 0.829 & -0.559 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4.45 \\ 3.03 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] image $(4.45,\,3.03)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det=-\cos^22\theta-\sin^22\theta=-1$ [A1] $\mathbf{M}^2=\begin{pmatrix} \cos^22\theta+\sin^22\theta & \cos2\theta\sin2\theta-\sin2\theta\cos2\theta \\ \sin2\theta\cos2\theta-\cos2\theta\sin2\theta & \sin^22\theta+\cos^22\theta \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{I}$ so applying it twice changes nothing [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} \cos28^\circ \\ \sin28^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ evaluated with unrounded values [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.883 \\ 0.469 \end{pmatrix}$ which equals $(\cos28^\circ,\,\sin28^\circ)=(0.883,\,0.469)$, so the point lies on the mirror line and is invariant [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The matrix is given, so in part (c) the work is just squaring it and using $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$. For part (d), keep full calculator precision, since rounding early can make the last digit differ.

subtopic: Shear used to slant a rectangle of text
statement: A graphic designer slants a rectangular text box with the shear $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.4 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The box has vertices $O(0,\,0)$, $A(5,\,0)$, $B(5,\,2)$ and $C(0,\,2)$, with units in centimeters. (a) Find the coordinates of the vertices of the image of the box. [3] (b) Use $\det\mathbf{S}$ to write down the area of the image, and state the area of the original box. [2] (c) Find the point that is mapped to $(7,\,2)$ by $\mathbf{S}$. [2] (d) The designer wants a shear of the form $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ that moves $B$ to the point $(7,\,2)$. Find $k$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{S}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} x+0.4y \\ y \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $O'=(0,\,0)$ and $A'=(5,\,0)$ [A1] $B'=(5.8,\,2)$ and $C'=(0.8,\,2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{S}=1$ so the image area is $10\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] The original area is $5\times2=10\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x+0.4y=7$ with $y=2$ [M1] $x=6.2$, so the point is $(6.2,\,2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $5+2k=7$ [M1] $k=1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Under a shear parallel to the $x$-axis, the $y$-coordinate never changes, so you only need to track the $x$-coordinate. Shears have determinant $1$.

subtopic: Area of the image of a circular region under a matrix
statement: A circular patch of radius $3$ cm, centered at the origin, is transformed by the matrix $\mathbf{N}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0.5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{N}$. [1] (b) Find the area of the image of the patch, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the image of the point $(3,\,0)$ on the boundary of the patch. [1] (d) The $0.5$ in matrix $\mathbf{N}$ is replaced by $k$. Find the possible values of $k$ for which the image of the patch has area $36\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{N}=2(3)-1(0.5)=5.5$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Area of the patch $=\pi\times3^2=9\pi$ [A1] Image area $=5.5\times9\pi$ [M1] $=156\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{N}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 1.5 \end{pmatrix}$ so the image is $(6,\,1.5)$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\det=6-k$ and $|6-k|\times9\pi=36\pi$ [M1] so $|6-k|=4$ [A1] $k=2$ or $k=10$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf{N}|$ whatever the shape, so the image of a circle is an ellipse whose area is $|\det\mathbf{N}|$ times the circle's area. In part (d), remember the absolute value gives two values of $k$.

subtopic: Recovering original points using an inverse matrix
statement: A photo-editing program warps an image using the matrix $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, so that a point $(x,\,y)$ moves to the point given by $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{T}$ and write down $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$. [3] (b) After warping, two marked points appear at $P'(7,\,14)$ and $Q'(-7,\,0)$. Find the coordinates of the original points $P$ and $Q$. [3] (c) A region in the warped image has area $63$ square units. Find the area of the corresponding region in the original image. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{T}=3(4)-(-1)(2)=14$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{14}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 14 \end{pmatrix}=\dfrac{1}{14}\begin{pmatrix} 4(7)+14 \\ -2(7)+3(14) \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $P=(3,\,2)$ [A1] $Q=(-2,\,1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Original area $=\dfrac{63}{14}$ [M1] $=4.5$ square units [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To undo a transformation apply the inverse matrix; the area factor of the inverse is $\dfrac{1}{|\det|}$. Check each answer by applying $\mathbf{T}$ to it.

subtopic: Finding a transformation matrix from two image points
statement: A linear transformation of the plane is represented by the matrix $\mathbf{A}$. It maps the point $(2,\,1)$ to $(5,\,-4)$ and the point $(1,\,3)$ to $(5,\,3)$. (a) By writing $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and using your GDC, find $\mathbf{A}$. [4] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{A}$ and state the area scale factor of the transformation. [2] (c) Find the image of the point $(4,\,-2)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}^{-1}$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\dfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Multiplying: $\mathbf{A}=\dfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 5 \\ -15 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{A}=2(2)-1(-3)=7$ [A1] The area scale factor is $7$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2(4)+1(-2) \\ -3(4)+2(-2) \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ -16 \end{pmatrix}$ so the image is $(6,\,-16)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the information as one matrix equation $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{Q}$ with the points as columns, then use $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ (inverse on the right). Check by applying $\mathbf{A}$ to $(2,1)$.

subtopic: Eigenvalues and invariant lines of a stretching transformation
statement: A transformation of the plane has matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}$. [3] (b) Find the equations of the two invariant lines through the origin. [3] (c) Triangle $T$ has vertices $(0,\,0)$, $(1,\,1)$ and $(1,\,-2)$. Find the area of $T$ and the area of its image under $\mathbf{M}$. [3] (d) Describe geometrically what the eigenvalues tell you about the effect of the transformation on points on the two invariant lines. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{M}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=\lambda^2-7\lambda+10$ [M1][A1] $\lambda=2$ and $\lambda=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=5$: $-x+y=0$, direction $(1,\,1)$, so the line is $y=x$ [M1][A1] For $\lambda=2$: $2x+y=0$, so the line is $y=-2x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Area of $T=\dfrac12|1(-2)-1(1)|=1.5$ [A1] $\det\mathbf{M}=12-2=10$ [A1] Image area $=15$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Points on $y=x$ are moved along that line to $5$ times their distance from the origin [A1] points on $y=-2x$ are moved along that line to $2$ times their distance from the origin [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eigenvalues come from $\det(\mathbf{M}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0$, and each eigenvector gives the direction of an invariant line. Note that $\det\mathbf{M}$ equals the product of the eigenvalues, which provides a check.

subtopic: Powers of a rotation matrix on a turntable
statement: A turntable rotates a point on its edge through $40^\circ$ anticlockwise about its center $O$ at each step. The rotation is represented by the matrix $\mathbf{R}$ in coordinates centered at $O$. (a) Use your GDC to show that $\mathbf{R}^9=\mathbf{I}$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Write down the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $\mathbf{R}^n=\mathbf{I}$. [1] (c) A point starts at $(10,\,0)$. Find its position after $4$ steps, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Write $\mathbf{R}^{-1}$ in the form $\mathbf{R}^k$ for a positive integer $k$, and give a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} \cos40^\circ & -\sin40^\circ \\ \sin40^\circ & \cos40^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{R}^9=\begin{pmatrix} 1.00 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.00 \end{pmatrix}$ (off-diagonal entries are zero to 3 significant figures) [A1] [2 marks] (b) $n=9$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\mathbf{R}^4$ is a rotation of $160^\circ$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix} 10\cos160^\circ \\ 10\sin160^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=(-9.40,\,3.42)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{R}^{-1}=\mathbf{R}^8$ [A1] because $\mathbf{R}^9=\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^8=\mathbf{I}$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A rotation through $\theta$ repeated $n$ times is a rotation through $n\theta$. The matrix returns to $\mathbf{I}$ when $n\theta$ is a multiple of $360^\circ$; $9\times40=360$.

subtopic: Three-step composite transformation for a sprite animation
statement: In a game, a character sprite is transformed in three steps, in this order: first an enlargement about the origin with scale factor $1.2$ (matrix $\mathbf{E}$), then a reflection in the $x$-axis (matrix $\mathbf{X}$), then a rotation of $30^\circ$ anticlockwise about the origin (matrix $\mathbf{R}$). (a) Write down $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{R}$, giving entries correct to 3 significant figures where necessary. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the single matrix $\mathbf{C}$ that represents all three steps. [3] (c) The sprite's hand is at $(10,\,4)$. Find its position after the three steps, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find $\det\mathbf{C}$ and state the effect of the combined transformation on areas. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{E}=\begin{pmatrix} 1.2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.866 & -0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.866 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{E}$ (the first step is on the right) [M1][A1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1.04 & 0.6 \\ 0.6 & -1.04 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{C}\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=(12.8,\,1.84)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{C}=-1.44$ [A1] Areas are multiplied by $1.44$, and the orientation is reversed [A1] [2 marks]
tips: With several steps, the matrix of the last step is written on the far left: $\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{E}$. The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants.

subtopic: Area of a transformed parallelogram using vertices
statement: A parallelogram $ABCD$ has vertices $A(1,\,1)$, $B(5,\,1)$, $C(6,\,4)$ and $D(2,\,4)$. It is transformed by $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the area of $ABCD$. [2] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$ and use it to find the area of the image. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ and $D'$. [2] (d) Use the coordinates from part (c) and the shoelace formula (or your GDC) to confirm the area found in part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) Base $AB=4$, height $=3$ [M1] area $=12$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{M}=2(3)-(-1)(1)=7$ [A1] Image area $=7\times12=84$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A'(1,\,4)$ [A1] $B'(9,\,8)$, $C'(8,\,18)$ and $D'(0,\,14)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Shoelace: $\dfrac12\left|(1\cdot8-9\cdot4)+(9\cdot18-8\cdot8)+(8\cdot14-0\cdot18)+(0\cdot4-1\cdot14)\right|$ [M1] $=\dfrac12|-28+98+112-14|$ [A1] $=\dfrac12(168)=84$, which agrees with part (b) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The area scale factor is the same for every shape. You can check a determinant calculation by using the shoelace formula on the transformed vertices, which is a good habit when the GDC is allowed.

subtopic: Repeated shear applied to a point
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ represents a shear. (a) Find $\mathbf{S}^2$. [2] (b) Hence write down an expression for $\mathbf{S}^n$ for a positive integer $n$. [1] (c) Find the image of the point $(2,\,6)$ under $\mathbf{S}^n$. [2] (d) The shear is applied repeatedly to the point $(2,\,6)$. Find the least number of applications for which the $x$-coordinate of the image exceeds $50$. [2] (e) State, with a reason, which coordinate never changes. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{S}^2=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{S}^n=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5n \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5n \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2+3n \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $2+3n>50$ [M1] $n>16$, so $n=17$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) The $y$-coordinate, because the bottom row of $\mathbf{S}^n$ is $(0,\,1)$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: For shears, the pattern $\mathbf{S}^n$ has $n$ times the shear factor. At $n=16$ the $x$-coordinate is exactly $50$, which does not exceed $50$, so be careful with the strict inequality.

subtopic: Non-commuting composites: stretch and clockwise rotation
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}$ be the matrix of a rotation of $50^\circ$ clockwise about the origin and let $\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ be a stretch of scale factor $3$ parallel to the $x$-axis. (a) Write down $\mathbf{A}$ with entries correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find $\mathbf{AB}$ and $\mathbf{BA}$, giving entries correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the image of the point $(2,\,1)$ when (i) $\mathbf{B}$ is applied first and then $\mathbf{A}$; (ii) $\mathbf{A}$ is applied first and then $\mathbf{B}$. Give coordinates correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) A region of area $8$ square units is transformed by either composite. Show that the image area is the same in both cases and find it. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} \cos50^\circ & \sin50^\circ \\ -\sin50^\circ & \cos50^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.643 & 0.766 \\ -0.766 & 0.643 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 1.93 & 0.766 \\ -2.30 & 0.643 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $\mathbf{BA}=\begin{pmatrix} 1.93 & 2.30 \\ -0.766 & 0.643 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) (i) $\mathbf{AB}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=(4.62,\,-3.95)$ [A1] (ii) $\mathbf{BA}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=(6.15,\,-0.889)$ [A1] The two images are different, so the order matters [R1] [3 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{AB}=\det\mathbf{A}\times\det\mathbf{B}=1\times3=3=\det\mathbf{BA}$ [M1] Image area $=3\times8=24$ square units in both cases [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The product of two matrices depends on the order, but the determinant of the product does not, because $\det(\mathbf{AB})=\det\mathbf{A}\det\mathbf{B}=\det(\mathbf{BA})$. In part (c), remember that "$\mathbf{B}$ first" means the matrix product $\mathbf{AB}$.

subtopic: Unknown parameter from the area of an image triangle
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} a & 2 \\ 1 & a \end{pmatrix}$ represents a transformation of the plane, where $a$ is a real constant. Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1,\,0)$, $B(4,\,0)$ and $C(1,\,3)$. (a) Find an expression for $\det\mathbf{M}$ in terms of $a$. [1] (b) Find the area of triangle $ABC$. [2] The image of triangle $ABC$ under $\mathbf{M}$ has area $22.5$ square units. (c) Find the possible values of $a$. [3] (d) Given that $a>0$, find the exact distance between $A'$ and $C'$, the images of $A$ and $C$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=a^2-2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Base $AB=3$ and height $AC=3$ [M1] area $=4.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $|a^2-2|\times4.5=22.5$, so $|a^2-2|=5$ [M1] $a^2-2=5$ gives $a^2=7$ [A1] $a^2-2=-5$ gives $a^2=-3$, which has no real solution, so $a=\sqrt7$ or $a=-\sqrt7$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\overrightarrow{A'C'}=\mathbf{M}\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} a & 2 \\ 1 & a \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 3a \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] with $a=\sqrt7$: $A'C'=\sqrt{36+9a^2}=\sqrt{36+63}$ [A1] $=\sqrt{99}=3\sqrt{11}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The area scale factor is $|\det\mathbf{M}|$, and an equation involving an absolute value can give two cases, one of which may have no solution. A linear transformation maps the displacement $\overrightarrow{AC}$ to $\mathbf{M}\overrightarrow{AC}$, which avoids finding both image points.

subtopic: Image of a straight line under a matrix and invariant points
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ represents a transformation of the plane. A line $L$ has equation $y=2x+1$. (a) Find the images of the points $(0,\,1)$ and $(1,\,3)$ on $L$. [2] (b) Hence find the equation of the image $L'$ of the line $L$, giving your answer in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Find all the invariant points of $\mathbf{T}$. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point where $L$ and $L'$ intersect, and state with a reason whether this point is invariant under $\mathbf{T}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Gradient $=\dfrac{4-1}{5-1}=\dfrac34$ [M1] $y-1=\dfrac34(x-1)$ [M1] $y=0.75x+0.25$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2x+y=x$ and $x+y=y$ [M1] the second equation gives $x=0$, the first then gives $y=0$, so the only invariant point is the origin [A1] [2 marks] (d) $2x+1=0.75x+0.25$ [M1] $x=-0.6$ and $y=-0.2$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix} -0.6 \\ -0.2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} -1.4 \\ -0.8 \end{pmatrix}\neq\begin{pmatrix} -0.6 \\ -0.2 \end{pmatrix}$, so the point is not invariant (the only invariant point is the origin) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The image of a line under a linear map is a line, so two image points are enough. A point lying on both $L$ and its image is not automatically invariant: invariance needs $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}$.

subtopic: Identifying a reflection matrix and a composite rotation
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ represents a transformation of the plane. (a) Show that $\mathbf{M}^2=\mathbf{I}$. [2] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$. [1] (c) Find the equation of the line of invariant points of $\mathbf{M}$. [3] The matrix $\mathbf{M}$ has the form $\begin{pmatrix} \cos2\theta & \sin2\theta \\ \sin2\theta & -\cos2\theta \end{pmatrix}$ for a reflection in a line through the origin at angle $\theta$ to the positive $x$-axis, where $0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$. (d) Find $\theta$, correct to 3 significant figures, and show that your value is consistent with your answer to part (c). [2] The reflection $\mathbf{M}$ is followed by a reflection $\mathbf{N}$ in the $y$-axis. (e) Show that the combined transformation is a rotation about the origin, and find its angle, correct to 1 decimal place, and direction. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}^2=\begin{pmatrix} 0.36+0.64 & 0.48-0.48 \\ 0.48-0.48 & 0.64+0.36 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{I}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{M}=(0.6)(-0.6)-(0.8)(0.8)=-1$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}$ gives $0.6x+0.8y=x$ [M1] so $-0.4x+0.8y=0$ [A1] $y=0.5x$ (the second equation $0.8x-1.6y=0$ is the same line) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\cos2\theta=0.6$ gives $2\theta=53.13^\circ$, so $\theta=26.6^\circ$ [M1] $\tan26.565^\circ=0.5$, which matches the gradient found in part (c) [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\mathbf{NM}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} -0.6 & -0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] This has the form $\begin{pmatrix} \cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi \end{pmatrix}$ with $\cos\varphi=-0.6$ and $\sin\varphi=0.8$ (and $\det=1$), so it is a rotation [R1] $\varphi=180^\circ-53.13^\circ=126.9^\circ$ anticlockwise [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} c & s \\ s & -c \end{pmatrix}$ with $c^2+s^2=1$ is always a reflection, and the product of two reflections is a rotation (determinant $+1$). For the rotation angle, use both the cosine and the sine to choose the correct quadrant.

subtopic: Stretching a circle into an ellipse
statement: A circular glass lens has boundary $x^2+y^2=9$, with units in centimeters. A design software applies a stretch of scale factor $2$ parallel to the $x$-axis and scale factor $1.5$ parallel to the $y$-axis. (a) Write down the matrix of this transformation. [1] (b) Show that the image of the boundary has equation $\dfrac{x^2}{36}+\dfrac{y^2}{20.25}=1$. [3] (c) The area of an ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is $\pi ab$. Find the area of the image, correct to 3 significant figures, and show that it agrees with the area found using the determinant. [3] (d) Find the positive $y$-coordinate of the point on the image boundary with $x=3$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) A point $(x,\,y)$ maps to $(X,\,Y)=(2x,\,1.5y)$ so $x=\dfrac{X}{2}$ and $y=\dfrac{Y}{1.5}$ [M1] Substituting into $x^2+y^2=9$: $\dfrac{X^2}{4}+\dfrac{Y^2}{2.25}=9$ [M1] Dividing by $9$: $\dfrac{X^2}{36}+\dfrac{Y^2}{20.25}=1$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $a=6$ and $b=4.5$, so area $=\pi(6)(4.5)=27\pi=84.8\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1][A1] Using the determinant: $\det=2\times1.5=3$ and the circle has area $9\pi$, so $3\times9\pi=27\pi$, which agrees [R1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{9}{36}+\dfrac{y^2}{20.25}=1$ [M1] $y^2=15.1875$, so $y=3.90$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the inverse mapping $x=X/2$, $y=Y/1.5$ and substitute it into the original equation. The area of an ellipse is $\pi ab$ and also equals $|\det|\times$ the area of the circle, which is a useful check.

subtopic: Spiral matrices, rotation-enlargements and complex numbers
statement: This question investigates matrices of the form $\mathbf{M}(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}$ and their connection with complex numbers. A point $(x,\,y)$ is identified with the complex number $x+\mathrm{i}y$. You may use the fact that $\mathbf{M}(p,q)$ multiplies the length of every vector by $\sqrt{p^2+q^2}$. (a) For $\mathbf{M}(3,4)$, find the determinant. Show that $\mathbf{M}(3,4)=5\mathbf{R}$, where $\mathbf{R}$ is a rotation matrix, and find the angle of rotation in degrees, correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Find the image of the point $(2,\,1)$ under $\mathbf{M}(3,4)$, and show that it corresponds to the product $(3+4\mathrm{i})(2+\mathrm{i})$. [3] (c) Show that $\mathbf{M}(a,b)\,\mathbf{M}(c,d)=\mathbf{M}(ac-bd,\,ad+bc)$. [3] (d) Let $\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{M}(1,1)$. Use part (c) to find $\mathbf{N}^2$, $\mathbf{N}^4$ and $\mathbf{N}^8$, and hence find the image of $(3,\,-5)$ under $\mathbf{N}^8$. [4] (e) The matrix $\mathbf{Q}=0.95\,\begin{pmatrix} \cos20^\circ & -\sin20^\circ \\ \sin20^\circ & \cos20^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ acts repeatedly on the point $P_0(1,\,0)$, giving the points $P_n=\mathbf{Q}^nP_0$. (i) Use your GDC to find the coordinates of $P_5$, correct to 3 significant figures. (ii) Show that $OP_n=0.95^n$, where $O$ is the origin. (iii) Find the smallest $n$ for which $OP_n<0.1$. [7] (f) Find the exact form of the total length of the infinite path $P_0P_1P_2\ldots$ as an infinite series, and hence find its value correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (g) Now consider the matrix $\mathbf{M}(a,b)$ acting repeatedly on a point. Find the condition on $a$ and $b$ for the points to spiral towards the origin. Determine whether the points spiral in towards the origin or spiral outwards for $\mathbf{M}(0.8,\,0.7)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det=3^2+4^2=25$ [A1] $\mathbf{M}(3,4)=5\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & -0.8 \\ 0.8 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] with $\cos\theta=0.6$ and $\sin\theta=0.8$ this is $5\mathbf{R}$ [A1] $\theta=53.1^\circ$ anticlockwise [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}(3,4)\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 3(2)-4(1) \\ 4(2)+3(1) \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 11 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $(3+4\mathrm{i})(2+\mathrm{i})=6+3\mathrm{i}+8\mathrm{i}-4=2+11\mathrm{i}$, which corresponds to $(2,\,11)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} c & -d \\ d & c \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} ac-bd & -ad-bc \\ bc+ad & -bd+ac \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\mathbf{M}(ac-bd,\,ad+bc)$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{N}^2=\mathbf{M}(1\cdot1-1\cdot1,\,1\cdot1+1\cdot1)=\mathbf{M}(0,2)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{N}^4=\mathbf{M}(0\cdot0-2\cdot2,\,0\cdot2+2\cdot0)=\mathbf{M}(-4,0)=-4\mathbf{I}$ [A1] $\mathbf{N}^8=\mathbf{M}(16,0)=16\mathbf{I}$ [A1] Image of $(3,-5)$ is $(48,\,-80)$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) (i) $\mathbf{Q}^5\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $P_5=(-0.134,\,0.762)$ [A1][A1] (ii) $\mathbf{Q}^n=0.95^n\times$(rotation through $20n^\circ$) [M1] a rotation preserves lengths, so $OP_n=0.95^n\times1=0.95^n$ [AG] (iii) $0.95^n<0.1$ gives $n>\dfrac{\ln0.1}{\ln0.95}=44.9$ [M1] $n=45$ [A1] [7 marks] (f) $\overrightarrow{P_nP_{n+1}}=(\mathbf{Q}-\mathbf{I})P_n$ and $\mathbf{Q}-\mathbf{I}=\mathbf{M}(0.95\cos20^\circ-1,\,0.95\sin20^\circ)$ [M1] so each step is $k$ times $OP_n$ where $k=\sqrt{(0.95\cos20^\circ-1)^2+(0.95\sin20^\circ)^2}=0.342$ [A1] Step $n$ has length $k(0.95)^n$, so the total length is $k\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}0.95^n$ [A1] $=\dfrac{k}{1-0.95}=6.84$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) $OP_n=\left(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right)^n$ [M1] The points spiral inward if $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}<1$, that is $a^2+b^2<1$ [A1] For $\mathbf{M}(0.8,\,0.7)$: $0.64+0.49=1.13>1$, so the points spiral outwards [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Treat $\mathbf{M}(a,b)$ as the complex number $a+b\mathrm{i}$: multiplying matrices corresponds to multiplying complex numbers, so modulus multiplies and angles add. In part (f), the step vector is $(\mathbf{Q}-\mathbf{I})P_n$ and the steps form a geometric series with ratio $0.95$.

subtopic: Integrating a power function with a negative index
statement: A curve $C$ has gradient function $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=12x^3-\dfrac{6}{x^2}+5$ for $x>0$, and passes through the point $(1,\,10)$. (a) Find $\displaystyle\int\left(12x^3-\dfrac{6}{x^2}+5\right)\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (b) Find the equation of $C$. [2] (c) Find the value of $y$ on $C$ when $x=2$. [1]
tips: Write $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ as $x^{-2}$ before integrating: the integral of $-6x^{-2}$ is $+6x^{-1}$. Do not forget the constant of integration, then use the given point to find it.

subtopic: Exact definite integrals of exponential and reciprocal functions
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln2}4\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^{\mathrm{e}^2}\left(\dfrac3x+2\right)\mathrm{d}x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int4\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\mathrm{d}x=2\mathrm{e}^{2x}$ [A1] $\left[2\mathrm{e}^{2x}\right]_0^{\ln2}=2\mathrm{e}^{2\ln2}-2$ [M1] $=2(4)-2=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac3x+2\right)\mathrm{d}x=3\ln x+2x$ [A1] $\left[3\ln x+2x\right]_1^{\mathrm{e}^2}=(6+2\mathrm{e}^2)-(0+2)$ [M1] $=4+2\mathrm{e}^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\mathrm{e}^{\ln a}=a$ and $\ln\mathrm{e}^2=2$, $\ln1=0$ to keep answers exact. The integral of $\mathrm{e}^{kx}$ is $\dfrac1k\mathrm{e}^{kx}$.

subtopic: Integrating sine and cosine of a linear argument
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}6\cos3x\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}8\sin2x\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (c) Find $\displaystyle\int10\cos\left(\dfrac x2\right)\mathrm{d}x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int6\cos3x\,\mathrm{d}x=2\sin3x$ [A1] $\left[2\sin3x\right]_0^{\pi/6}=2\sin\dfrac\pi2-2\sin0$ [M1] $=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int8\sin2x\,\mathrm{d}x=-4\cos2x$ [A1] $\left[-4\cos2x\right]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}=-4\cos\pi+4\cos\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] $=4+0=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $20\sin\left(\dfrac x2\right)$ [A1] $+\,c$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $\int\cos(kx)\,\mathrm{d}x$ divide by $k$ (and for $\int\sin(kx)\,\mathrm{d}x$ divide by $-k$). Angles must be in radians for calculus, and the constant $c$ is needed in an indefinite integral.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from a quadratic acceleration
statement: A toy train moves along a straight track. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=6t-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, for $t\ge0$. When $t=0$ the train is at the starting point $s=0$ with velocity $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the displacement from the starting point when $t=2$. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the train between $t=1$ and $t=3$. [2] (d) Show that the train never changes direction, and state what this tells you about the distance traveled in part (c). [2]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int(6t-4)\,\mathrm{d}t=3t^2-4t+c$ [M1][A1] $v(0)=3$ gives $c=3$ so $v=3t^2-4t+3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $s=\displaystyle\int v\,\mathrm{d}t=t^3-2t^2+3t$ (with $s(0)=0$) [M1] $s(2)=8-8+6=6\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $s(3)-s(1)=(27-18+9)-(1-2+3)$ [M1] $=18-2=16\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The discriminant of $3t^2-4t+3$ is $16-36=-20<0$ and the leading coefficient is positive, so $v>0$ for all $t$ [R1] The train never reverses, so the distance traveled between $t=1$ and $t=3$ equals the displacement, $16\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integrate acceleration to get velocity, using the initial velocity to find the constant, and integrate again for displacement. Distance equals displacement when the velocity never changes sign.

subtopic: Exact area enclosed between a parabola and a line
statement: A garden bed is bounded by the curve $y=x^2$ and the straight path $y=2x+3$, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the two points where the path meets the curve. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the garden bed. [4]
tips: Area between curves is $\int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,\mathrm{d}x$. Be careful with signs when substituting the lower limit $x=-1$.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule from tabulated rainfall rates
statement: The rate of rainfall, $r$ millimeters per hour, is recorded at hourly intervals. $t$ (hours): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; $r$: 0, 4, 6, 5, 2. (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ strips to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^4 r\,\mathrm{d}t$. [3] (b) State what this integral represents, including units. [1] (c) The graph of $r$ against $t$ is concave down for $0\le t\le4$. State, with a reason, whether your estimate in part (a) is an overestimate or an underestimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac12(1)\left[0+2+2(4+6+5)\right]$ [M1][A1] $=16$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The total rainfall in the $4$ hours, in millimeters [A1] [1 mark] (c) The estimate is an underestimate [A1] because on a concave-down graph the chords lie below the curve, so the trapezia have smaller area than the region under the curve [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Trapezoidal rule: $\dfrac h2\left[\text{first}+\text{last}+2(\text{sum of the others})\right]$. For a concave-down curve the trapezoidal rule underestimates, and for a concave-up curve it overestimates.

subtopic: Exact volumes of revolution about the x-axis
statement: The inside of a decorative bowl is formed by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{x+1}$, for $0\le x\le3$, through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. (a) Write down an integral for the volume $V$ of the solid formed. [2] (b) Find the exact value of $V$. [3] (c) A second solid is formed by rotating the curve $y=\dfrac2x$, for $1\le x\le4$, through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. Find the exact volume of this solid. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^3\left(\sqrt{x+1}\right)^2\mathrm{d}x$ [M1] $=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^3(x+1)\,\mathrm{d}x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\pi\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_0^3$ [M1] $=\pi\left(\dfrac92+3\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac{15\pi}{2}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\pi\displaystyle\int_1^4\dfrac{4}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=4\pi\left[-\dfrac1x\right]_1^4$ [M1] $=4\pi\left(-\dfrac14+1\right)$ [A1] $=3\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The volume formula is $V=\pi\int y^2\,\mathrm{d}x$, so square the function first (the square root disappears here). For $\int x^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}x$ use $-x^{-1}$.

subtopic: Water pumped into a tank at a sinusoidal rate
statement: Water is pumped into a storage tank at a rate $r(t)=12+8\sin(0.4t)$ cubic meters per hour, where $t$ is the time in hours and $0\le t\le10$. (a) Find the volume of water pumped in during the first $10$ hours, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) The tank initially contains $50\ \mathrm{m^3}$ of water. Find the volume in the tank after $10$ hours. [1] (c) Find the first time at which the rate of pumping is exactly $15\ \mathrm{m^3\,h^{-1}}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the mean rate of pumping over the first $10$ hours. [1]
tips: Use your GDC's numerical integration with the angle in radians (check the mode). For (c), solve the equation numerically or rearrange to $\sin(0.4t)=0.375$ and take the first solution.

subtopic: Area of a metal plate between an exponential and a parabola
statement: A metal plate is cut so that its upper edge follows the curve $y=6-x^2$ and its lower edge follows the curve $y=\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. The two edges meet at two points. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the two points where the edges meet, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the area of the plate, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) The plate is coated at a cost of \$0.35 per square centimeter. Use the unrounded area to find the cost of coating one face of the plate, to the nearest cent. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solve $6-x^2=\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}$ on the GDC [M1] $x=-2.39$ and $x=1.86$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Area $=\displaystyle\int_{-2.3868}^{1.8612}\left(6-x^2-\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}\right)\mathrm{d}x$ [M1][A1] $=14.3\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $14.3408\times0.35$ [M1] $=\$5.02$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Store the intersection points in your GDC's memory and reuse the unrounded values as the limits. Area between curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve.

subtopic: Volume of a vase from a rotated sinusoidal profile
statement: The outer surface of a vase is formed by rotating the curve $y=2+\sin(0.5x)$, for $0\le x\le8$, through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the vase. [2] (b) Find the volume of the vase, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the greatest diameter of the vase. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^8\left(2+\sin(0.5x)\right)^2\mathrm{d}x$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=153\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) The greatest radius occurs when $\sin(0.5x)=1$, which is at $x=\pi$ (within the interval) [M1] greatest radius $=3$, so the greatest diameter is $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Remember to square the whole expression $2+\sin(0.5x)$ and include the factor $\pi$. For the greatest radius, use the maximum value of the sine function, but check that it occurs inside the interval.

subtopic: Displacement and total distance with a change of direction
statement: A drone moves along a straight corridor. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v(t)=4\mathrm{e}^{-0.3t}-1.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for $0\le t\le8$. Positive velocity means moving away from the start of the corridor. (a) Find the time at which the drone is instantaneously at rest, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the drone when $t=2$. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the drone during the $8$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the drone during the $8$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) The drone starts at $s=3$ meters from the start of the corridor. Find the position of the drone when $t=8$, and the greatest value of $s$ during the $8$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4\mathrm{e}^{-0.3t}-1.5=0$ [M1] $t=3.27$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a(t)=-1.2\mathrm{e}^{-0.3t}$ [M1] $a(2)=-0.659\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^8v\,\mathrm{d}t$ [M1] $=0.124\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The velocity changes sign at $t=3.269$ [M1] Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^{3.269}v\,\mathrm{d}t+\left|\int_{3.269}^{8}v\,\mathrm{d}t\right|$ $=3.429+3.305$ [A1] $=6.73\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $s(8)=3+0.124=3.12\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] The greatest value of $s$ occurs when $v=0$, at $t=3.269$ [M1] $s=3+3.429=6.43\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The total distance requires splitting the integral where the velocity changes sign (or integrating $|v|$ on the GDC). Displacement, distance and position are different quantities: position adds the starting value $s(0)$.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule for the area of a curved lawn
statement: The curved edge of a lawn is modeled by $y=\sqrt x$ for $1\le x\le5$, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters. The lawn lies between this edge and the $x$-axis. (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ equal strips to estimate the area of the lawn, correct to 4 significant figures. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the exact area of the lawn, correct to 4 significant figures. [1] (c) Explain, using the shape of the curve, why the trapezoidal rule gives an underestimate. [2] (d) Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (a), correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (e) Using your GDC, find the least number of strips for which the trapezoidal rule has a percentage error of less than $0.1\%$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $h=1$: $\dfrac12(1)\left[\sqrt1+\sqrt5+2\left(\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt4\right)\right]$ [M1][A1] $=6.764\ \mathrm{m^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_1^5\sqrt x\,\mathrm{d}x=6.787\ \mathrm{m^2}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) The curve $y=\sqrt x$ is concave down (second derivative $-\dfrac14x^{-3/2}<0$) [R1] so each chord lies below the curve and the trapezia have less area than the region under the curve [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{6.7869-6.7643}{6.7869}\times100$ [M1] $=0.333\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Calculating the trapezoidal estimate for increasing $n$: $n=7$ gives an error of about $0.11\%$ and $n=8$ gives $0.084\%$ [M1] so the least number of strips is $8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Percentage error is $\dfrac{|\text{exact}-\text{approximate}|}{\text{exact}}\times100$. Keep full calculator accuracy in part (d) rather than the rounded values.

subtopic: Net signed area versus total area for a cubic
statement: The height of a hiking trail above a reference level is modeled by $f(x)=x^3-4x$, where $x$ is the horizontal distance in hundreds of meters, for $-2\le x\le3$. (a) Find the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=0$. [2] (b) Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$. [2] (c) Find the total area of the regions enclosed between the graph of $f$ and the $x$-axis for $-2\le x\le3$. [3] (d) Explain why your answers to parts (b) and (c) are different. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x(x-2)(x+2)=0$ [M1] $x=-2,\ 0,\ 2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}(x^3-4x)\,\mathrm{d}x=6.25$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}f\,\mathrm{d}x=4$, $\ \displaystyle\int_0^2f\,\mathrm{d}x=-4$, $\ \displaystyle\int_2^3f\,\mathrm{d}x=6.25$ [M1][A1] Total area $=4+4+6.25=14.25$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) In part (b) the regions below the $x$-axis count as negative and cancel part of the regions above, whereas in part (c) all areas are counted as positive [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A definite integral gives signed area. To find the area enclosed by a curve and the axis, split at each zero and take the absolute value of each part, or integrate $|f(x)|$ on your GDC.

subtopic: Cumulative drug dose with an unknown upper limit
statement: A drug is absorbed into the bloodstream at a rate $r(t)=20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}$ milligrams per hour, where $t$ is the time in hours after the drug is taken. (a) Find the amount of drug absorbed during the first $2$ hours, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the time $k$ at which a total of $50$ mg has been absorbed, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the total amount absorbed over all time cannot exceed $80$ mg. [2] (d) Find the time at which the rate of absorption first falls below $1$ mg per hour, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^2 20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}\,\mathrm{d}t=80\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}\right)$ [M1] $=31.5$ mg [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^k20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}\,\mathrm{d}t=80\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}\right)=50$ [M1] $\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}=0.375$ [A1] $k=3.92$ hours [A1] [3 marks] (c) The amount absorbed by time $k$ is $80\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}\right)$ [M1] and $\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}>0$, so the amount is always less than $80$ mg (it approaches $80$ as $k\to\infty$) [R1] [2 marks] (d) $20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}<1$ [M1] $t>4\ln20=12.0$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The amount absorbed up to time $k$ is the definite integral $\int_0^k r(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$. Setting it equal to a target value gives an equation in $k$ that you can solve algebraically or with your GDC solver.

subtopic: Reservoir volume from a net rate of change
statement: The volume of water $V$ in a reservoir, in millions of liters, changes at a rate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t$, where $t$ is the time in days and $0\le t\le12$. Initially $V=120$. (a) Find the value of $t$ at which $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Justify that $V$ is greatest at this value of $t$. [2] (c) Find the greatest volume of water in the reservoir, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the time at which the volume first returns to $120$ million liters after reaching its greatest value, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) A warning is issued if the volume falls below $110$ million liters. Find the volume at $t=12$ and the time at which the warning is first issued. Give your answers correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Solve $6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t=0$ on the GDC [M1] $t=5.71$ days [A1] [2 marks] (b) The rate is positive before $t=5.71$ (for example at $t=5$ it is $1.80$) and negative after (for example at $t=6$ it is $-0.777$) [R1] so $V$ increases and then decreases, giving a maximum at $t=5.71$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $V=120+\displaystyle\int_0^{5.7085}\left(6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t\right)\mathrm{d}t$ [M1][A1] $=146$ million liters [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\displaystyle\int_0^{t}\left(6+3\sin(0.5u)-1.2u\right)\mathrm{d}u=0$ with $t>5.71$ [M1][A1] $t=10.5$ days [A1] [3 marks] (e) $V(12)=120+\displaystyle\int_0^{12}\left(6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t\right)\mathrm{d}t=106$ million liters [A1] Solve $V=110$ for $t>5.71$ [M1] $t=11.6$ days [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The reservoir volume is $V(t)=V(0)+\int_0^t\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}u}\,\mathrm{d}u$. A maximum of $V$ occurs where its derivative changes sign from positive to negative, so show the sign change rather than only solving for zero.

subtopic: Temperature found by integrating a rate of change
statement: A metal rod is heated so that its temperature $T\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ changes at the rate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t}=3\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$, where $t$ is the time in minutes after heating starts. The initial temperature is $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (a) Find an expression for $T$ in terms of $t$. [3] (b) Find the temperature after $4$ minutes, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (c) Find the temperature that the rod approaches in the long run, with a reason. [2] (d) Find the time at which the temperature reaches $14\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T=\displaystyle\int3\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}\,\mathrm{d}t=-6\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}+c$ [M1][A1] $T(0)=10$ gives $c=16$, so $T=16-6\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $T(4)=16-6\mathrm{e}^{-2}=15.2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) As $t\to\infty$, $\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}\to0$ [R1] so $T\to16\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $16-6\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}=14$ [M1] $t=2\ln3=2.20$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integrating $\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$ gives $-2\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$, so the factor $3$ becomes $-6$. Use the initial condition to find the constant before answering later parts.

subtopic: Area under a concentration curve in pharmacology
statement: The concentration of a medicine in a patient's blood, in milligrams per liter, is modeled by $C(t)=8t\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}$, where $t$ is the time in hours after the dose and $t\ge0$. (a) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{12}C(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) State what this integral represents, including its units. [1] (d) The dose is considered effective if the area under the concentration curve over the first $12$ hours is at least $30$. State whether the dose is effective, with a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) Using the GDC maximum function [M1] maximum concentration $5.89$ mg/L at $t=2.00$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{12}8t\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}\,\mathrm{d}t=31.4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) The area under the concentration curve (total exposure to the medicine) over the first $12$ hours, in $\mathrm{mg\,h\,L^{-1}}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $31.4\ge30$ [R1] so the dose is effective [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The unit of an integral is the product of the units of the integrand and the variable, here $(\mathrm{mg/L})\times\mathrm{h}$. Use the GDC maximum function to answer part (a) without differentiating.

subtopic: Volume of revolution of a region between two parabolas
statement: The region $R$ is enclosed by the curves $y=x^2+1$ and $y=7-x^2$. The region is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis to form a solid, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. (a) Show that the curves intersect at $x=\pm\sqrt3$. [2] (b) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid. [3] (c) Find the volume of the solid, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Show that the exact volume is $64\sqrt3\,\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+1=7-x^2$ [M1] $2x^2=6$, so $x=\pm\sqrt3$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) The upper curve is $y=7-x^2$ and the lower curve is $y=x^2+1$ [M1] $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}\left[\left(7-x^2\right)^2-\left(x^2+1\right)^2\right]\mathrm{d}x$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $V=348\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $\left(7-x^2\right)^2-\left(x^2+1\right)^2=48-16x^2$ [M1] $V=\pi\left[48x-\dfrac{16x^3}{3}\right]_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}=2\pi\left(48\sqrt3-16\sqrt3\right)$ [M1] $=64\sqrt3\,\pi$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: For a region between two curves rotated about the $x$-axis, subtract the squares of the functions, not the square of the difference: $V=\pi\int(y_{\text{upper}}^2-y_{\text{lower}}^2)\,\mathrm{d}x$. Using symmetry, the integral from $-\sqrt3$ to $\sqrt3$ is twice the integral from $0$ to $\sqrt3$.

subtopic: Total cost from a marginal cost function
statement: A factory's marginal cost, in dollars per unit, when $x$ units have been produced is $\mathrm{MC}(x)=0.002x^2-0.6x+60$, for $0\le x\le300$. (a) Find the increase in total cost when production rises from $100$ units to $200$ units, correct to the nearest dollar. [2] (b) The fixed cost, which is the total cost when $x=0$, is \$5000. Find an expression for the total cost $C(x)$. [3] (c) Find the total cost of producing $150$ units. [1] (d) Find the production level at which the marginal cost is least, and the least marginal cost. [2]
tips: Total cost is the integral of marginal cost plus the fixed cost. In part (d), the marginal cost is itself a function, so minimize it by differentiating it (or use the GDC minimum function).

subtopic: Accuracy of the trapezoidal rule for the integral of 1/x
statement: This question investigates how accurately the trapezoidal rule approximates $I=\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac1x\,\mathrm{d}x$ and how the error behaves as the number of strips increases. Let $T_n$ be the trapezoidal rule estimate of $I$ using $n$ equal strips, and let $E_n=T_n-I$. (a) Find the exact value of $I$ and write it correct to 5 significant figures. [2] (b) Show that $T_4=0.69702$, correct to 5 significant figures, stating the function values used. [3] (c) Use your GDC to find $T_8$ correct to 5 significant figures, and find $E_4$ and $E_8$ correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (d) Find $\dfrac{E_4}{E_8}$, and hence suggest how $E_n$ depends on $n$. [2] (e) Show that the trapezoidal rule overestimates $I$ for every $n$, by considering the second derivative of $\dfrac1x$. [3] (f) Assume $E_n\approx\dfrac{c}{n^2}$ for some constant $c$. Use $E_4$ to find $c$, correct to 3 significant figures, and hence estimate the least number of strips needed for $E_n<1\times10^{-5}$. [4] (g) Consider the combination $\mathrm{R}=\dfrac{4T_8-T_4}{3}$. Find $\mathrm{R}$ correct to 5 significant figures and its error $\mathrm{R}-I$ correct to 3 significant figures, using unrounded values, and comment on its accuracy compared with $T_8$. [4] (h) The region under the curve $y=\dfrac1x$ for $1\le x\le2$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. (i) Find the exact volume $V$ of the solid formed. (ii) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ strips to estimate $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac1{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x$ and hence estimate $V$, correct to 4 significant figures. (iii) Find the percentage error in your estimate of $V$, correct to 3 significant figures. [8]
markscheme: (a) $I=\left[\ln x\right]_1^2=\ln2$ [M1] $=0.69315$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $h=0.25$ and $f(1)=1$, $f(1.25)=0.8$, $f(1.5)=0.6667$, $f(1.75)=0.5714$, $f(2)=0.5$ [M1] $T_4=\dfrac{0.25}{2}\left[1+0.5+2(0.8+0.6667+0.5714)\right]$ [A1] $=0.69702$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $T_8=\dfrac{0.125}{2}\left[f(1)+f(2)+2\left(f(1.125)+\dots+f(1.875)\right)\right]$ [M1] $=0.69412$ [A1] $E_4=0.69702-0.693147=0.00388$ [A1] $E_8=0.000975$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\dfrac{E_4}{E_8}=3.98\approx4$ [A1] Doubling $n$ divides the error by about $4$, so $E_n$ is approximately proportional to $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ [R1] [2 marks] (e) $f(x)=x^{-1}$, $f'(x)=-x^{-2}$, $f''(x)=2x^{-3}$ [A1] $f''(x)>0$ for $1\le x\le2$ so the graph is concave up [R1] each chord lies above the curve, so each trapezium has area greater than the area under the curve, giving $T_n>I$ [R1] [3 marks] (f) $c=E_4\times4^2=0.0620$ [A1] $\dfrac{c}{n^2}<10^{-5}$ [M1] $n^2>6200$ so $n>78.8$ [A1] least $n=79$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) $\mathrm{R}=\dfrac{4(0.69412)-0.69702}{3}$ [M1] $=0.69315$ [A1] $\mathrm{R}-I=7.35\times10^{-6}$ [A1] This error (about $7\times10^{-6}$) is roughly $130$ times smaller than $E_8\approx9.75\times10^{-4}$, so $\mathrm{R}$ is much more accurate than $T_8$ [R1] [4 marks] (h) (i) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\left[-\dfrac1x\right]_1^2$ [M1] $=\pi\left(-\dfrac12+1\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] (ii) For $y=x^{-2}$: $\dfrac{0.25}{2}\left[1+0.25+2(0.64+0.4444+0.3265)\right]$ [M1] $=0.50899$ [A1] $V\approx\pi\times0.50899=1.599$ [A1] (iii) $\dfrac{1.5991-1.5708}{1.5708}\times100=1.80\%$ [M1][A1] [8 marks]
tips: In the final parts, remember the volume integral uses $\pi y^2$, so the trapezoidal rule must be applied to $y^2=\dfrac1{x^2}$, not to $\dfrac1x$. The $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ pattern in part (d) is the key to part (f).

subtopic: Magnitude and unit vector of a 2D displacement
statement: A warehouse robot makes two moves. The first move is the displacement $\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ and the second is $\mathbf{q}=\begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$, both in meters. (a) Find $|\mathbf{p}|$. [1] (b) Find the single displacement $\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}$. [1] (c) Find a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{q}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|\mathbf{p}|=\sqrt{25+144}=13$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}=\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 18 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $|\mathbf{q}|=\sqrt{64+36}=10$ [M1] unit vector $=\dfrac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ $=\begin{pmatrix} -0.8 \\ 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A unit vector is the vector divided by its own magnitude. Check your answer by confirming that its magnitude is 1.

subtopic: Scalar product and perpendicular vectors in 3D
statement: The vectors $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ are given. (a) Find $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}$. [2] (b) Write down what your answer to part (a) tells you about the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. [1] (c) The vector $\mathbf{c}=\begin{pmatrix} k \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{a}$. Find the value of $k$. [2]
