markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda^2+\lambda-6=0$ [M1] $\lambda=2$ and $\lambda=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\lambda=2$: $-x+2y=0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=-3$: $4x+2y=0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf x=c_1e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+c_2e^{-3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] the eigenvalues have opposite signs, so the origin is a saddle point [A1] [2 marks] (d) $2c_1+c_2=3$ and $c_1-2c_2=4$ [M1] $c_1=2$, $c_2=-1$ [A1] $x=4e^{2t}-e^{-3t}$, $y=2e^{2t}+2e^{-3t}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) as $t\to\infty$ the $e^{2t}$ terms dominate, so $\frac yx\to\frac12$ (the solution approaches the line in the direction $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: With eigenvalues of opposite sign, only trajectories starting along the eigenvector for the negative eigenvalue approach the origin. In (d) set up two simultaneous equations from the initial condition.

subtopic: Spiral sink and period of oscillation for coupled populations
statement: The deviations $x$ and $y$ (in hundreds) of a prey population and a predator population from their equilibrium values are modeled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-0.2x+0.8y$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-0.8x-0.2y$, where $t$ is in years. (a) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of the matrix of the system. [2] (b) Classify the equilibrium at the origin and describe the phase portrait. [2] (c) Find the period of the oscillations. [2] (d) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.1$, given $x=10$ and $y=5$ at $t=0$. [2] (e) Find the factor by which the amplitude of the oscillations decreases over one period. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\lambda=-0.2\pm0.8i$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) the real part is negative and the eigenvalues are complex, so the origin is a stable spiral (spiral sink) [A1] trajectories spiral inward toward the origin [A1] [2 marks] (c) period $=\frac{2\pi}{0.8}$ [M1] $=7.85$ years [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\frac{dx}{dt}=-2+4=2$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=-8-1=-9$ [M1] $x\approx10.2$, $y\approx4.1$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) factor $=e^{-0.2\times7.854}$ [M1] $=0.208$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $\lambda=p\pm qi$ the real part $p$ controls growth or decay and the imaginary part $q$ gives the angular frequency, so the period is $2\pi/q$. Over one period the amplitude is multiplied by $e^{p\times\text{period}}$.

subtopic: Euler's method for a drug infusion model
statement: A drug is infused into a patient's bloodstream at a constant rate. The concentration $C$ in mg L$^{-1}$ at time $t$ hours satisfies $\dfrac{dC}{dt}=12-0.5C$, with $C=0$ when $t=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to complete a table of values of $t$ and $C$ from $t=0$ to $t=2$, and state the estimate of $C(2)$. [4] (b) The exact solution is $C=24\left(1-e^{-0.5t}\right)$. Find the exact value of $C(2)$ to 4 significant figures and the percentage error in the Euler estimate, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) State one way to reduce the error in the estimate. [1]
tips: On the GDC you can build the table in a spreadsheet by repeating the Euler formula. Percentage error is relative to the exact value.

subtopic: Rabbit and fox populations: equilibrium and Euler step
statement: The numbers of rabbits $x$ and foxes $y$ in a reserve at time $t$ months are modeled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.6x-0.03xy$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.01xy-0.4y$. (a) Show that $(x,y)=(40,20)$ is an equilibrium point of the system. [3] (b) Find $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ when $x=80$ and $y=10$, and interpret your answers. [3] (c) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.5$, given $x=50$ and $y=10$ at $t=0$. [3] (d) The solution curves in the $xy$-plane are closed loops. Explain what this implies for the two populations. [1]
markscheme: (a) equilibrium requires $\frac{dx}{dt}=0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}=0$ [M1] $x(0.6-0.03y)=40\left(0.6-0.6\right)=0$ [A1] $y(0.01x-0.4)=20\left(0.4-0.4\right)=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{dx}{dt}=48-24=24$ [A1] $\frac{dy}{dt}=10(0.8-0.4)=4$ [A1] both populations are increasing at that moment [R1] [3 marks] (c) at $(50,10)$: $\frac{dx}{dt}=30-15=15$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}=10(0.5-0.4)=1$ [M1] $x=50+0.5(15)=57.5$ [A1] $y=10+0.5(1)=10.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) closed loops mean both populations rise and fall periodically, with the predator cycle lagging behind the prey cycle [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Euler's method for a system updates both variables using the rates at the same starting point. At an equilibrium both derivatives are zero.

subtopic: Fish population with constant harvesting
statement: A fish population $P$ in a lake, $t$ years after monitoring began, is modeled with harvesting by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.5P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{800}\right)-40$. (a) Use your GDC to find the equilibrium values of $P$, giving your answers to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Determine the stability of each equilibrium. [3] (c) Without harvesting, the maximum growth rate is $100$ fish per year. Deduce what happens to the population if the harvesting rate is increased to $120$ fish per year. [2] (d) Find $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ when $P=50$, and interpret the result. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.5P\left(1-\frac{P}{800}\right)-40=0$ [M1] $P=90.2$ [A1] $P=710$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) test the sign of $\frac{dP}{dt}$ on each side of the equilibria [M1] for $90.2<P<710$ it is positive (for example $P=400$ gives $60$), and for $P>710$ it is negative, so $P=710$ is stable [A1] for $P<90.2$ it is negative, so $P=90.2$ is unstable [A1] [3 marks] (c) the growth term has maximum $0.5(400)(0.5)=100$ at $P=400$ [M1] since $100<120$, $\frac{dP}{dt}<0$ for every $P$ and the population collapses to zero [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.5(50)\left(1-\frac{50}{800}\right)-40=-16.6$ fish per year [A1] this is below the unstable equilibrium $90.2$, so the population keeps falling toward extinction [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A stable equilibrium attracts nearby solutions, an unstable one repels them. Check the sign of the derivative in each region between and beyond the equilibria.

subtopic: Logistic solution for the spread of a rumor
statement: A rumor spreads through a school of $1200$ students. The number $N$ of students who have heard the rumor $t$ days after it started satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0.08N\left(1-\dfrac{N}{1200}\right)$ with $N(0)=150$. The solution is $N(t)=\dfrac{1200}{1+7e^{-0.08t}}$. (a) Verify that $N(0)=150$ and find the limit of $N$ as $t\to\infty$. [2] (b) Find the time at which $600$ students have heard the rumor. [2] (c) Use the differential equation to find the maximum rate at which the rumor spreads, and state when it occurs. [2] (d) Find the time at which $1000$ students have heard the rumor. [2]
tips: Rearrange the given solution to isolate the exponential term and take logarithms. The logistic growth rate is greatest when the population is half the carrying capacity.

subtopic: Separable model for the thickness of pond ice
statement: Ice forms on a pond. Its thickness $h$ cm at time $t$ days satisfies $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{0.6}{h}$, with $h=1$ when $t=0$. (a) Show that $h^2=1.2t+1$. [4] (b) Find the time taken for the ice to reach a thickness of $4$ cm. [2] (c) Find the thickness of the ice after $30$ days. [1] (d) State one limitation of this model for large values of $t$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int h\,dh=\int0.6\,dt$ [M1] $\frac{h^2}{2}=0.6t+c$ [A1] $h(0)=1$ gives $c=\frac12$ [A1] $h^2=1.2t+1$ [AG] [4 marks] (b) $16=1.2t+1$ [M1] $t=12.5$ days [A1] [2 marks] (c) $h=\sqrt{37}=6.08$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (d) the model predicts that the thickness grows without bound, whereas in reality it is limited by air temperature and insulation by the ice [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Separate $h$ and $t$, integrate both sides, and use the initial condition to find the single constant. Comment on what the model predicts as $t\to\infty$.

subtopic: Salt concentration in a stirred tank
statement: A tank holds $200$ L of pure water. A salt solution containing $0.5$ g of salt per liter flows into the tank at $10$ L per minute, and the well-stirred mixture flows out at $10$ L per minute, so the volume stays constant. Let $Q$ grams be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=5-\dfrac{Q}{20}$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation with $Q(0)=0$ to show that $Q=100\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the time at which the tank contains $90$ g of salt. [2]
markscheme: (a) salt in: $0.5\times10=5$ g per minute [A1] salt out: $10\times\frac{Q}{200}=\frac{Q}{20}$ g per minute, so $\frac{dQ}{dt}=5-\frac{Q}{20}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\frac{dQ}{5-\frac{Q}{20}}=\int dt$ [M1] $-20\ln\left(5-\frac{Q}{20}\right)=t+c$ [A1] $5-\frac{Q}{20}=Ae^{-t/20}$ [A1] $Q(0)=0$ gives $A=5$, so $Q=100\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) $90=100\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$ so $e^{-t/20}=0.1$ [M1] $t=20\ln10=46.1$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rate of change equals rate in minus rate out, with the outflow concentration equal to $Q$ divided by the volume. The salt amount cannot exceed $100$ g here, so the bracket $5-\frac{Q}{20}$ stays positive.

subtopic: Pollutant exchange between two lakes
statement: Pollutant moves between two connected lakes. Let $x$ and $y$ be the masses in kg of the pollutant in Lake 1 and Lake 2 at time $t$ years, where $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-0.5x+0.2y$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.5x-0.5y$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf x}{dt}=A\mathbf x$, stating the matrix $A$. [1] (b) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of $A$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue, with first component $1$. [2] (d) Initially $x=100$ and $y=0$. Find the particular solution. [3] (e) Find the time at which Lake 2 contains the greatest mass of pollutant, and that mass. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} -0.5 & 0.2 \\ 0.5 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\lambda=-0.184$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.816$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\lambda=-0.184$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1.58 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.816$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1.58 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $c_1+c_2=100$ and $1.58\left(c_1-c_2\right)=0$ [M1] $c_1=c_2=50$ [A1] $x=50e^{-0.184t}+50e^{-0.816t}$, $y=79.1\left(e^{-0.184t}-e^{-0.816t}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) maximum of $y$ on the GDC (or $\frac{dy}{dt}=0$) [M1] $t=2.36$ years, $y=39.7$ kg [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eigenvectors can be scaled, so the first-component-1 form just keeps answers comparable. Both eigenvalues are negative, so the pollutant decays to zero in both lakes.

subtopic: Terminal velocity of a parachutist from a separable equation
statement: The velocity $v$ m s$^{-1}$ of a parachutist falling after opening the parachute satisfies $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=9.8-0.2v$, where $t$ is in seconds and $v(0)=0$. (a) Find the terminal velocity. [1] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $v=49\left(1-e^{-0.2t}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the time taken to reach a velocity of $40$ m s$^{-1}$. [2] (d) Find the distance fallen in the first $10$ seconds. [2]
tips: Terminal velocity is an equilibrium solution, found by setting the derivative to zero. Integrate $\frac{1}{a-bv}$ with a factor $-\frac1b$.

subtopic: Step size, error and stability of Euler's method for logistic growth
statement: This question investigates how the step size affects the accuracy and stability of Euler's method. The population $P$ (in thousands) of algae in a pond satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.5P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{50}\right)$, where $t$ is in days and $P(0)=5$. (a) Find the equilibrium values of $P$, and state, with a reason, whether $P$ is increasing or decreasing when $0<P<50$. [3] (b) Use Euler's method with step size $h=1$ to estimate $P(1)$, $P(2)$ and $P(3)$. [4] (c) The exact solution is $P(t)=\dfrac{50}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$. Show that it satisfies the initial condition, find $P(3)$ to 4 significant figures, and find the error in your estimate of $P(3)$ from part (b). [4] (d) Use a GDC spreadsheet with step sizes $h=0.5$, $0.25$ and $0.125$ to estimate $P(3)$ to 4 significant figures, and describe how the error changes as $h$ is halved. [4] (e) Now take $h=3$. Find the estimates $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ at $t=3,6,9,12$, and show that Euler's method produces a value greater than the carrying capacity $50$. [4] (f) For general $h$, Euler's method gives $P_{n+1}=g(P_n)$, where $g(P)=P+0.5hP\left(1-\dfrac P{50}\right)$. (i) Show that $g(50)=50$. (ii) Find $g'(50)$ in terms of $h$. (iii) Given that the iteration settles to $P=50$ only if $|g'(50)|<1$, find the range of values of $h$ for which this happens. [5] (g) Take $h=4.2$. Find $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ to 4 significant figures, describe what happens, and refer to your answer to part (f). [3]
tips: In (f) the derivative of the update function at a fixed point controls whether small errors shrink or grow. In (d) and (g) keep unrounded values in your spreadsheet and round only for the final answer.

subtopic: Predator-prey model: linearization, Euler's method and a conserved quantity
statement: This question investigates a predator-prey model. The numbers of rabbits $x$ and foxes $y$ (in hundreds) in a region at time $t$ months satisfy $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.8x-0.04xy$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.02xy-0.6y$. (a) Find the two equilibrium points of the system. [3] (b) Starting from $x=40$, $y=15$ at $t=0$, use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.2$. [4] (c) Near the equilibrium point with $x,y>0$, let $x=30+u$ and $y=20+w$, where $u$ and $w$ are small. Show that, ignoring the term in $uw$, $\dfrac{du}{dt}=-1.2w$ and $\dfrac{dw}{dt}=0.4u$. [4] (d) Write the linearized system in matrix form, find its eigenvalues, and hence find the period of small oscillations about the equilibrium, to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) Interpret the eigenvalues found in (d) in the context of the populations. [2] (f) Continue Euler's method with $h=0.1$ using a GDC spreadsheet to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=5$, to 3 significant figures. [2] (g) Show that $V(x,y)=0.02x-0.6\ln x+0.04y-0.8\ln y$ satisfies $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$ along any solution of the system. [4] (h) Find $V$ at $t=0$ and, using the Euler estimates, at $t=10$ ($100$ steps, where $x=48.7$ and $y=17.2$). Hence comment on the accuracy of Euler's method for this system. [3]
markscheme: (a) set $x(0.8-0.04y)=0$ and $y(0.02x-0.6)=0$ [M1] $(0,0)$ [A1] $(30,20)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x_{n+1}=x_n+0.1x_n(0.8-0.04y_n)$, $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1y_n(0.02x_n-0.6)$ [M1] step 1: $x_1=40+0.1(8)=40.8$, $y_1=15+0.1(3)=15.3$ [A1] step 2: $\frac{dx}{dt}=40.8(0.8-0.612)=7.6704$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}=15.3(0.816-0.6)=3.3048$ so $x(0.2)\approx41.6$ [A1] $y(0.2)\approx15.6$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\frac{du}{dt}=\frac{dx}{dt}=(30+u)\left(0.8-0.04(20+w)\right)$ [M1] $=(30+u)(-0.04w)$ [A1] $=-1.2w-0.04uw\approx-1.2w$ [A1] $\frac{dw}{dt}=(20+w)\left(0.02(30+u)-0.6\right)=(20+w)(0.02u)=0.4u+0.02uw\approx0.4u$ [AG] [4 marks] (d) $\begin{pmatrix} u' \\ w' \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1.2 \\ 0.4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} u \\ w \end{pmatrix}$, so $\lambda^2+0.48=0$ [M1] $\lambda=\pm0.693i$ [A1] period $=\frac{2\pi}{0.693}=9.07$ months [A1] [3 marks] (e) the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, so the equilibrium is a centre and the populations oscillate periodically [A1] with a period of about $9.07$ months, and with small oscillations that neither grow nor decay [A1] [2 marks] (f) $x(5)\approx17.5$ [A1] $y(5)\approx21.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (g) $\frac{dV}{dt}=\left(0.02-\frac{0.6}{x}\right)\frac{dx}{dt}+\left(0.04-\frac{0.8}{y}\right)\frac{dy}{dt}$ [M1] first term $=\left(0.02x-0.6\right)(0.8-0.04y)$ [A1] second term $=\left(0.04y-0.8\right)\left(0.02x-0.6\right)$ [A1] sum $=\left(0.02x-0.6\right)\left[(0.8-0.04y)+(0.04y-0.8)\right]=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (h) $V(40,15)=-2.98$ [A1] $V(48.7,17.2)=-2.94$ [A1] $V$ should stay constant, but the Euler estimate has drifted upward, so Euler's method is accumulating error (the numerical solution spirals outward) and is unreliable over long times with this step size [R1] [3 marks]
tips: In (c) factor the right-hand sides around the equilibrium so that one factor is the small quantity $u$ or $w$. In (g) apply the chain rule and look for cancellation between the two terms.

subtopic: Binomial test: exact Type I and Type II errors
statement: A driving instructor believes that more than half of learner drivers pass the practical test at their first attempt. She records the outcomes for a random sample of $6$ learners from a large driving school. Let $X$ be the number who pass first time and let $p$ be the probability that a randomly chosen learner passes first time. She tests $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.5$ against $\mathrm{H}_1:p>0.5$ and decides to reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ if $X\ge5$. (a) Describe a Type I error in this context and find its probability, giving your answer as an exact fraction. [4] (b) In fact $p=\dfrac{2}{3}$. Find, as an exact fraction, the probability of a Type II error. [4]
markscheme: (a) A Type I error is concluding that more than half of learners pass first time when in fact $p=0.5$ [A1] Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(6,0.5)$ so $P(X\ge5)=\dfrac{\binom{6}{5}+\binom{6}{6}}{2^6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6+1}{64}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{7}{64}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $P(X=6)=\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^6=\dfrac{64}{729}$ [A1] $P(X=5)=6\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^5\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=\dfrac{192}{729}$ [A1] Type II error means $X\le4$, so probability $=1-P(X\ge5)$ [M1] $=1-\dfrac{256}{729}=\dfrac{473}{729}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis; a Type II error is failing to reject a false one. For the Type II error, use the complement of the critical region rather than adding five separate probabilities.

subtopic: One-tailed z-test: critical region and Type II error
statement: The masses of pots of honey filled by a machine are normally distributed with standard deviation $4$ g. The machine is set so that the mean mass is $50$ g. An inspector suspects that the machine is underfilling. She takes a random sample of $16$ pots and carries out a one-tailed test at the $5\%$ significance level. Let $\bar X$ denote the sample mean. You may use the fact that $P(Z<-1.645)=0.05$ where $Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Show that, under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}(50,1)$, and hence find the critical region for $\bar x$. [3] (c) The sample mean is $48.6$ g. State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [2] (d) The mean mass is in fact $47$ g. The probability of a Type II error can be written as $P(Z>k)$. Find the exact value of $k$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=50$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu<50$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=\dfrac{4^2}{16}=1$ [M1] $\dfrac{\bar x-50}{1}<-1.645$ [M1] Critical region: $\bar x<48.355$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $48.6>48.355$, so $48.6$ is not in the critical region [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the machine underfills [A1] [2 marks] (d) A Type II error occurs when $\bar X\ge48.355$ [M1] When $\mu=47$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}(47,1)$ [A1] $k=\dfrac{48.355-47}{1}=1.355$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The critical region for the sample mean comes from standardizing: set the z-value equal to the critical z and solve for the sample mean. For a Type II error, switch to the distribution of the sample mean under the true mean.

subtopic: Chi-squared goodness of fit: equal preference
statement: A cafe owner suspects that customers are not equally likely to choose each of four pastries. Over one morning, $120$ customers each choose one pastry: croissant $36$, muffin $24$, scone $32$, danish $28$. A chi-squared goodness of fit test is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level to test whether the four pastries are equally popular. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Write down the expected frequency for each pastry and the number of degrees of freedom. [2] (c) Calculate the value of $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$. [2] (d) The critical value at the $5\%$ level is $7.815$. State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the four pastries are equally popular (choices follow a uniform distribution); $\mathrm{H}_1$: they are not equally popular [A1] [1 mark] (b) Expected frequency $=\dfrac{120}{4}=30$ for each pastry [A1] Degrees of freedom $=4-1=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\chi^2=\dfrac{6^2+(-6)^2+2^2+(-2)^2}{30}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{80}{30}=\dfrac{8}{3}\approx2.67$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $2.67<7.815$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is insufficient evidence that the pastries are not equally popular [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Under a uniform null hypothesis every expected frequency is the total divided by the number of categories. Compare the calculated statistic with the critical value, and word the conclusion in terms of the original claim.

subtopic: Chi-squared test of independence with a 2 by 3 table
statement: A school survey asks $200$ students how they usually travel to school (walk, cycle or bus) and records whether each student is male or female. The results are: male: walk $36$, cycle $24$, bus $40$; female: walk $24$, cycle $36$, bus $40$. A chi-squared test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Show that the expected number of male students who cycle is $30$ under the null hypothesis. [2] (c) State the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Given that the other expected frequencies are $30,\ 40,\ 30,\ 30,\ 40$ for male walk, male bus, female walk, female cycle and female bus respectively, show that $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=4.8$. [3] (e) The critical value is $5.991$. State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the method of travel is independent of gender [A1] [1 mark] (b) Cyclists: $24+36=60$; males: $36+24+40=100$ [M1] Expected $=\dfrac{100\times60}{200}=30$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(2-1)(3-1)=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Differences between observed and expected are $\pm6$ for walk and cycle, and $0$ for bus [M1] $\chi^2=\dfrac{36}{30}\times4+0$ [M1] $=4.8$ [AG] [3 marks] (e) $4.8<5.991$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the method of travel depends on gender [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expected frequency is (row total times column total) divided by the grand total, and the degrees of freedom are (rows minus 1)(columns minus 1). Cells whose observed and expected values agree contribute nothing to the statistic.

subtopic: Paired t-test with hand calculation of the statistic
statement: Nine athletes complete a reaction-time test before and after a training programme. The reduction in reaction time (before minus after), in milliseconds, for each athlete is: $7,\ 7,\ 7,\ 7,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 4$. The reductions may be assumed to come from a normal distribution. A coach tests whether the programme reduces mean reaction time, using a one-tailed $t$-test at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) Find the mean reduction. [1] (b) Show that the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation of the reductions is $3$ ms. [3] (c) State suitable hypotheses for the test. [1] (d) Find the value of the test statistic. [2] (e) The critical value of $t$ for this test is $1.860$. State the conclusion in context. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar d=\dfrac{36}{9}=4$ ms [A1] [1 mark] (b) Deviations from the mean: $3,3,3,3,-3,-3,-3,-3,0$ [M1] Sum of squares $=8\times9=72$ [A1] $s^2=\dfrac{72}{8}=9$, so $s=3$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu_d=0$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu_d>0$ where $\mu_d$ is the mean reduction [A1] [1 mark] (d) $t=\dfrac{4-0}{3/\sqrt9}$ [M1] $=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $4>1.860$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence that the training programme reduces mean reaction time [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In a paired test, work with the differences as a single sample and use $n-1$ degrees of freedom, here $8$. Check that the sum of squared deviations is divided by $n-1$, not $n$.

subtopic: One-sample t-test with confidence interval, nitrate level
statement: A regulator states that the mean nitrate concentration in a river should be $12.0$ mg per litre. An environmental scientist takes eight independent water samples and measures the nitrate concentration, in mg per litre: $12.4,\ 11.8,\ 13.1,\ 12.9,\ 11.5,\ 12.2,\ 13.4,\ 12.7$. Assume that concentrations are normally distributed. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (b) State suitable hypotheses to test whether the mean concentration differs from $12.0$ mg per litre. [1] (c) Find the $p$-value for a $t$-test. [2] (d) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (e) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean concentration and explain how it is consistent with your answer to part (d). [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=12.5$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=0.650$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=12.0$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu\ne12.0$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Two-tailed one-sample $t$-test with $7$ degrees of freedom, $t=2.17$ [M1] $p=0.0661$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0661>0.05$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the mean nitrate concentration differs from $12.0$ mg per litre [A1] [2 marks] (e) $(11.96,\ 13.04)$ [A1] The interval contains $12.0$, consistent with not rejecting $\mathrm{H}_0$ at the $5\%$ level [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A two-sided $5\%$ test and a $95\%$ confidence interval always agree about whether the hypothesized mean is plausible. Use the $t$ option on your GDC because the population standard deviation is estimated from the sample.

subtopic: Two-sample pooled t-test, one-tailed with a 10% follow-up
statement: A researcher investigates whether caffeine shortens reaction time. One independent random sample of $14$ volunteers drinks a caffeinated beverage and a second independent random sample of $16$ volunteers drinks a placebo. Each volunteer then completes a reaction test. Reaction times in milliseconds are assumed to be normally distributed with equal population variances. The summary statistics, where $s$ is the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation, are: caffeine group $n=14$, mean $248$, $s=21$; placebo group $n=16$, mean $262$, $s=24$. (a) State suitable hypotheses for the researcher's test. [2] (b) Find the pooled estimate of the common variance. [2] (c) Find the value of the test statistic and the $p$-value. [3] (d) State the conclusion of the test at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (e) State the conclusion at the $10\%$ significance level and explain why the two conclusions differ. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu_C=\mu_P$ [A1] $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu_C<\mu_P$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s_p^2=\dfrac{13\times21^2+15\times24^2}{28}$ [M1] $=513$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Pooled two-sample $t$-test, $28$ degrees of freedom [M1] $t=-1.69$ [A1] $p=0.0512$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $0.0512>0.05$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level that caffeine shortens mean reaction time [A1] [2 marks] (e) $0.0512<0.10$, so reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ at the $10\%$ level: there is evidence that caffeine shortens reaction time [A1] The $p$-value lies between the two significance levels, so the decision depends on how much risk of a Type I error is accepted [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The alternative hypothesis is one-tailed because the researcher expects caffeine to shorten the time. A $p$-value just above the significance level means the data are borderline, not that the effect is absent.

subtopic: Paired t-test, resting heart rate after a fitness course
statement: Ten adults take part in an eight-week fitness course. Their resting heart rates, in beats per minute, are recorded before and after the course. Before: $78,\ 85,\ 92,\ 70,\ 88,\ 81,\ 76,\ 95,\ 83,\ 89$. After: $74,\ 80,\ 93,\ 66,\ 82,\ 79,\ 70,\ 90,\ 81,\ 83$ (the values are in the same order for the same ten adults). The differences (before minus after) may be assumed to be normally distributed. (a) Find the mean and the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation of the differences. [2] (b) Explain why a paired test is more appropriate than a two-sample test. [1] (c) State hypotheses for a test of whether the course lowers the mean resting heart rate. [1] (d) Find the value of the test statistic and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion at the $1\%$ significance level, and state one assumption required for the test. [2]
markscheme: (a) Differences: $4,\ 5,\ -1,\ 4,\ 6,\ 2,\ 6,\ 5,\ 2,\ 6$; mean $=3.9$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=2.28$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The two sets of measurements are taken on the same individuals, so they are not independent [R1] [1 mark] (c) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu_d=0$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu_d>0$, where $\mu_d$ is the mean (before minus after) difference [A1] [1 mark] (d) One-sample $t$-test on the differences, $9$ degrees of freedom [M1] $t=5.40$ [A1] $p=0.000216$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.000216<0.01$, so reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence that the course lowers mean resting heart rate [A1] The differences are normally distributed (or the adults are a random sample) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: With before and after measurements on the same people, take differences first and then run a one-sample $t$-test. Define the sign of the difference clearly so that the alternative hypothesis points the right way.

subtopic: Binomial test: p-value, critical region and Type II error
statement: A bakery's loyalty app has historically been used by $20\%$ of its customers. After a redesign, the manager believes that the proportion $p$ of customers who use the app has increased. She asks a random sample of $25$ customers and $9$ of them use the app. (a) State suitable hypotheses for a binomial test. [1] (b) Find the $p$-value of the test. [3] (c) State the conclusion of the test at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (d) State the conclusion at the $1\%$ significance level. [1] (e) Find the critical region for a test at the $5\%$ significance level using a sample of $25$ customers, and state the actual significance level of this test. [3] (f) Find the probability of a Type II error if the true value of $p$ is $0.35$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.2$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p>0.2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(25,0.2)$ [M1] $p$-value $=P(X\ge9)=1-P(X\le8)$ [M1] $=0.0468$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.0468<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence that the proportion using the app has increased [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0468>0.01$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ at the $1\%$ level [A1] [1 mark] (e) $P(X\ge8)=0.109>0.05$ and $P(X\ge9)=0.0468\le0.05$ [M1] Critical region: $X\ge9$ [A1] Actual significance level $=0.0468$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) Type II error: $X\le8$ when $X\sim\mathrm{B}(25,0.35)$ [M1] $P(X\le8)=0.467$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Because the binomial distribution is discrete, the actual significance level of a critical region is usually below the nominal level. Remember that $P(X\ge9)=1-P(X\le8)$ when using the cumulative function on your GDC.

subtopic: Poisson test with critical region and Type II error, rescue calls
statement: A coastal rescue station has historically received call-outs at a mean rate of $4$ per day, modelled as a Poisson process. After a new ferry route opens, the coordinator believes the rate has increased. She records the total number of call-outs over a period of $2$ consecutive days. Let $X$ be this total and let $\lambda$ be the mean number of call-outs in a $2$-day period. (a) State the distribution of $X$ under the null hypothesis and write down suitable hypotheses. [2] (b) In the $2$-day period there are $14$ call-outs. Find the $p$-value of the test. [3] (c) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (d) Find the critical region for the test at the $5\%$ significance level, and the probability of a Type I error. [3] (e) After the ferry route opens, the true mean rate is $6$ call-outs per day. Find the probability of a Type II error. [3] (f) State one assumption required for the Poisson model to be valid. [1]
markscheme: (a) $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(8)$ under $\mathrm{H}_0$ [A1] $\mathrm{H}_0:\lambda=8$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\lambda>8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $p$-value $=P(X\ge14)=1-P(X\le13)$ [M1] using $\mathrm{Po}(8)$ [M1] $=0.0342$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.0342<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: sufficient evidence that the rate of call-outs has increased [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X\ge13)=0.0638>0.05$ and $P(X\ge14)=0.0342\le0.05$ [M1] Critical region: $X\ge14$ [A1] Probability of Type I error $=0.0342$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) True $\lambda=12$ over $2$ days, so $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(12)$ [M1] Type II error: $X\le13$ [M1] $P(X\le13)=0.682$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) Call-outs occur independently and at a constant average rate (singly) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Rescale the Poisson mean to match the time period of the sample before testing: $4$ per day becomes $8$ per two days. For the critical region, find the smallest $k$ with $P(X\ge k)\le0.05$.

subtopic: Goodness of fit to a binomial model with cell pooling
statement: A manufacturer packs components in boxes of $4$. The quality manager claims that each component is defective independently with probability $0.3$. She inspects $150$ boxes and records the number of defective components in each: $0$ defective in $31$ boxes, $1$ in $62$, $2$ in $38$, $3$ in $17$ and $4$ in $2$. Let $X$ be the number of defective components in a box. A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test is used to test whether $X\sim\mathrm{B}(4,0.3)$ at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) Show that the expected number of boxes with exactly $2$ defective components is $39.69$. [2] (b) The expected frequencies for $3$ and $4$ defective components are $11.34$ and $1.215$. Explain why the last two categories are combined. [1] (c) State the hypotheses. [1] (d) State the degrees of freedom. [1] (e) Find the value of $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and the $p$-value. [3] (f) State the conclusion of the test. [2] (g) State which category contributes most to $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(X=2)=\binom{4}{2}(0.3)^2(0.7)^2=0.2646$ [M1] Expected $=150\times0.2646=39.69$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) The expected frequency for $4$ defectives ($1.215$) is less than $5$, so categories $3$ and $4$ are combined (expected $12.555$) [R1] [1 mark] (c) $\mathrm{H}_0$: $X\sim\mathrm{B}(4,0.3)$; $\mathrm{H}_1$: $X$ does not follow $\mathrm{B}(4,0.3)$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $4$ categories after combining and no parameter estimated, so $\nu=4-1=3$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) Observed: $31,62,38,19$; expected: $36.015,\ 61.74,\ 39.69,\ 12.555$ [M1] $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=4.08$ [A1] $p=0.253$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $0.253>0.05$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: the data are consistent with each component being defective with probability $0.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (g) The combined category ($3$ or $4$ defective), contributing about $3.31$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Combine categories until every expected frequency is at least $5$, then count the remaining categories when finding the degrees of freedom. Because $p=0.3$ was given rather than estimated from the data, no extra degree of freedom is lost.

subtopic: Chi-squared independence, age group and transport mode
statement: A city survey asks $300$ residents about their age group and their main mode of transport. The observed frequencies are: young (under $30$): bus $42$, bicycle $31$, car $17$; middle-aged: bus $38$, bicycle $44$, car $28$; older (over $60$): bus $20$, bicycle $35$, car $45$. A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Show that the expected frequency of older residents who travel mainly by car is $30$. [2] (c) State the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Find the value of $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [2] (f) Identify the cell that contributes most to $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and describe what this suggests. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: age group and transport mode are independent; $\mathrm{H}_1$: they are not independent (associated) [A1] [1 mark] (b) Older residents: $20+35+45=100$; car users: $17+28+45=90$ [M1] Expected $=\dfrac{100\times90}{300}=30$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(3-1)(3-1)=4$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Matrix $\chi^2$ test [M1] $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=22.7$ [A1] $p=0.000147$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.000147<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence that transport mode depends on age group [A1] [2 marks] (f) Older residents who use a car: contribution $\dfrac{(45-30)^2}{30}=7.5$ [A1] Many more older residents travel mainly by car than expected if mode were independent of age [A1] [2 marks]
tips: On the GDC, enter the observed values as a matrix and the calculator returns both the statistic and the expected matrix. When commenting on a large contribution, compare observed with expected to say which direction the association goes.

subtopic: Z-test power: critical region, Type II error and sample size
statement: A cereal factory fills boxes whose masses are normally distributed with standard deviation $12$ g. The boxes are supposed to have mean mass $500$ g. An inspector suspects that the machine underfills, and takes a random sample of $16$ boxes. She tests $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=500$ against $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu<500$ at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) Find the critical region for the sample mean $\bar x$, giving the boundary to two decimal places. [3] (b) State the probability of a Type I error. [1] (c) The true mean mass is $494$ g. Find the power of the test. [3] (d) The inspector instead uses a $1\%$ significance level with the same sample size. Find the new critical region boundary and the new power when $\mu=494$. [3] (e) Return to the $5\%$ level. Find the smallest sample size $n$ for which the power is at least $0.95$ when $\mu=494$. [4] (f) State one disadvantage of reducing the significance level from $5\%$ to $1\%$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}\left(500,\left(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{16}}\right)^2\right)=\mathrm{N}(500,3^2)$ [M1] Boundary $c$ with $P(\bar X<c)=0.05$: $c=500-1.645\times3$ [M1] Critical region: $\bar x<495.07$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $0.05$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) When $\mu=494$, $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}(494,3^2)$ [M1] Power $=P(\bar X<495.07)$ [M1] $=0.639$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Critical boundary $=500-2.326\times3=493.02$ [A1] Power $=P(\bar X<493.02)$ with $\bar X\sim\mathrm{N}(494,3^2)$ [M1] $=0.372$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Standard error $\dfrac{12}{\sqrt n}$ and boundary $500-1.645\dfrac{12}{\sqrt n}$ [M1] Power $=P\left(\bar X<500-1.645\dfrac{12}{\sqrt n}\right)$ with mean $494$ [M1] $n=43$ gives $0.949$ (not enough) [A1] $n=44$ gives $0.953$, so smallest $n=44$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) The probability of a Type II error increases (the power falls) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Always rebuild the sampling distribution of the mean when the sample size or the true mean changes: the standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n$. Power is $1-P(\text{Type II error})$, calculated using the true mean, not the hypothesized one.

subtopic: Two-tailed binomial test: critical regions and power, website clicks
statement: The probability that a visitor to a website clicks on an advertisement has been $0.4$. After the page layout is changed, the web manager wants to test, at the $5\%$ significance level, whether the probability $p$ has changed in either direction. She will observe $30$ independent visitors and let $X$ be the number who click. Each tail of the critical region should have probability as close as possible to, but not more than, $2.5\%$. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the lower and upper parts of the critical region, showing the probabilities that justify your choice. [6] (c) State the critical region and the actual significance level of the test. [2] (d) In the sample, $17$ visitors click. State the conclusion of the test. [2] (e) Find the power of the test if the true value of $p$ is $0.6$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.4$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p\ne0.4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(30,0.4)$ [M1] Lower tail: $P(X\le6)=0.0172\le0.025$ [A1] and $P(X\le7)=0.0435>0.025$ [A1] Upper tail: $P(X\ge18)=0.0212\le0.025$ [A1] and $P(X\ge17)=0.0481>0.025$ [A1] Lower part: $X\le6$; upper part: $X\ge18$ [A1] [6 marks] (c) Critical region: $X\le6$ or $X\ge18$ [A1] Actual significance level $=0.0172+0.0212=0.0384$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $17$ is not in the critical region [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the click probability has changed [A1] [2 marks] (e) Power $=P(X\le6)+P(X\ge18)$ with $X\sim\mathrm{B}(30,0.6)$ [M1] $=0.0000092+0.5785$ [M1] $=0.578$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a two-tailed test with a discrete distribution, find each tail separately and take the largest tail not exceeding half the significance level. The actual significance level is the sum of the two tail probabilities, which is less than $5\%$.

subtopic: One-sample t-test: p-value and critical sample mean, tablet battery
statement: A manufacturer states that the battery of its tablet lasts $60$ hours on average. A reviewer believes the true mean is higher. She tests $15$ tablets chosen at random. The battery lives are assumed normally distributed, with sample mean $62.9$ hours and unbiased standard deviation estimate $s=5.2$ hours. (a) Find the estimated standard error of the sample mean. [1] (b) State hypotheses for the reviewer's test. [1] (c) Find the value of the test statistic and the $p$-value. [3] (d) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (e) Find the least value of the sample mean, correct to $2$ decimal places, that would lead to the rejection of $\mathrm{H}_0$ at the $5\%$ level, assuming the sample standard deviation is again $5.2$ hours. [3] (f) A colleague suggests treating $5.2$ as the known population standard deviation and using a $z$-test. State the corresponding critical sample mean and explain why it is smaller than your answer to part (e). [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5.2}{\sqrt{15}}=1.34$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=60$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu>60$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $t=\dfrac{62.9-60}{1.3426}=2.16$ [M1] [A1] $p=0.0243$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $0.0243<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: sufficient evidence that the mean battery life exceeds $60$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (e) Critical $t$ with $14$ degrees of freedom and upper tail $0.05$: $1.761$ [M1] $\bar x=60+1.761\times1.3426$ [M1] $\bar x\ge62.36$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $60+1.645\times1.3426=62.21$ [A1] The $t$-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution (to allow for estimating $\sigma$), so the $t$ critical value is larger and a bigger sample mean is needed [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the inverse $t$ function on your GDC with $n-1$ degrees of freedom to find a critical value, then convert it back to a sample mean using the standard error. With small samples, the $t$ critical value is noticeably larger than the $z$ critical value.

subtopic: Chi-squared independence test for a 2 by 2 table, gym classes
statement: A gym surveys $180$ members. Of the $80$ members on a monthly contract, $48$ regularly attend group classes and $32$ do not. Of the $100$ members on an annual contract, $36$ regularly attend group classes and $64$ do not. A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $1\%$ significance level. Do not apply a continuity correction. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the expected number of monthly-contract members who regularly attend classes. [2] (c) Write down the degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Find the value of $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [2] (f) Give a brief description of the association found, using the data. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: attending classes is independent of contract type; $\mathrm{H}_1$: attending classes depends on contract type [A1] [1 mark] (b) Total attending $=48+36=84$ [M1] Expected $=\dfrac{80\times84}{180}=37.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(2-1)(2-1)=1$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=10.3$ [M1][A1] $p=0.00134$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.00134<0.01$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: sufficient evidence of an association between contract type and class attendance [A1] [2 marks] (f) $\dfrac{48}{80}=60\%$ of monthly members attend classes compared with $\dfrac{36}{100}=36\%$ of annual members, so monthly members are more likely to attend [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A $2\times2$ table has one degree of freedom. After rejecting independence, compare row percentages to describe the direction of the association rather than just saying a link exists.

subtopic: Poisson model investigation: dispersion, goodness of fit and rate test
statement: This question investigates whether the number of arrivals at a mountain hut check-in desk can be modelled by a Poisson distribution, and then uses the model to test a claim about the arrival rate. The number of hikers arriving in each of $200$ consecutive five-minute intervals was recorded. Number of arrivals: $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6,\ 7$; number of intervals: $20,\ 46,\ 47,\ 38,\ 25,\ 13,\ 7,\ 4$. (a) Show that the sample mean is $2.445$, and find the unbiased estimate of the population variance. [4] (b) Comment on whether the relationship between your two answers is consistent with a Poisson model. [1] (c) Assuming that the number of arrivals in a five-minute interval is $\mathrm{Po}(2.445)$, find the expected number of intervals with $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5$ and at least $6$ arrivals. [3] (d) A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test of the Poisson model is carried out at the $5\%$ level. State the hypotheses, and explain why the categories for $6$ and $7$ arrivals are combined, and find the degrees of freedom. [3] (e) Find $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and the $p$-value, and state your conclusion. [5] (f) Let $Y$ be the total number of arrivals in all $200$ intervals. If arrivals in each interval are independent with $\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$, show that $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(200\lambda)$. [2] (g) A manager claims that the mean number of arrivals per five-minute interval is $2.2$, but a ranger believes it is higher. Using $Y$ and the data above, carry out a test at the $5\%$ level: state the hypotheses, find the $p$-value and state the conclusion. [5] (h) Use a normal approximation with continuity correction to estimate the $p$-value in part (g), and comment on the accuracy of the approximation. [4]
markscheme: (a) Total arrivals $=0(20)+1(46)+2(47)+3(38)+4(25)+5(13)+6(7)+7(4)=489$ [M1] $\bar x=\dfrac{489}{200}=2.445$ [AG] Unbiased variance estimate $s_{n-1}^2=2.78$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) For a Poisson distribution the mean equals the variance; $2.78$ is close to $2.445$, so the data are broadly consistent with a Poisson model [R1] [1 mark] (c) $200\times P(X=k)$ with $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(2.445)$ [M1] Expected: $17.3,\ 42.4,\ 51.8,\ 42.3,\ 25.8,\ 12.6$ [A1] at least $6$: $7.69$ (the remainder) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the number of arrivals follows a Poisson distribution; $\mathrm{H}_1$: it does not [A1] The expected frequency for $7$ arrivals alone is below $5$ so $6$ and $7$ are combined into a single category [R1] There are $7$ categories and $1$ parameter ($\lambda$) was estimated from the data, so $\nu=7-1-1=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Observed: $20,46,47,38,25,13,11$ against expected values above [M1] $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=3.05$ [A1] $p=0.692$ [A1] $0.692>0.05$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: the Poisson model is a reasonable fit [A1] [5 marks] (f) The sum of independent Poisson random variables is Poisson [M1] with mean equal to the sum of the means, $200\lambda$ [AG] [2 marks] (g) $\mathrm{H}_0:\lambda=2.2$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\lambda>2.2$ [A1] Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(440)$ [A1] $p$-value $=P(Y\ge489)=1-P(Y\le488)$ [M1] $=0.0113$ [A1] $0.0113<0.05$: reject $\mathrm{H}_0$, sufficient evidence that the mean number of arrivals per interval exceeds $2.2$ [A1] [5 marks] (h) $Y\approx\mathrm{N}(440,440)$ [M1] $P(Y\ge489)\approx P(Y>488.5)$ [M1] $z=\dfrac{488.5-440}{\sqrt{440}}=2.31$, $p\approx0.0104$ [A1] Close to the exact value $0.0113$, so the approximation is reasonably accurate (slightly underestimates the tail) [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Expected frequencies must be at least $5$ for a valid $\chi^2$ test, so merge sparse categories and subtract one extra degree of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data. In part (g), do not forget to scale the Poisson mean to the whole recording period.

subtopic: Power function of a binomial test and discreteness, onboarding rate
statement: This question investigates how the power of a binomial test depends on the true proportion and on the sample size. A mobile app has historically had an onboarding completion rate of $0.3$. A designer introduces a new onboarding flow and wants to test whether the completion probability $p$ has increased. She tests $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.3$ against $\mathrm{H}_1:p>0.3$ using a random sample of $20$ new users and a significance level of at most $5\%$. Let $X$ be the number of users in the sample who complete onboarding. (a) State the hypotheses, and find the critical region by calculating the relevant probabilities. [4] (b) State the actual significance level. Find the probability of a Type II error when $p=0.5$, and hence the power of the test at $p=0.5$. [4] (c) The power of the test is a function of the true value $p$. Find the power when $p=0.4$, $p=0.6$ and $p=0.7$. [3] (d) Use your GDC to find the value of $p$ for which the power equals $0.5$, and interpret this value in context. [3] (e) Write down the value of the power when $p=0.3$, and explain what this value represents. [2] (f) The designer increases the sample size to $21$ users. Find the new critical region (with significance level at most $5\%$), the actual significance level, and the power when $p=0.5$. Comment on the result compared with part (b). [4] (g) For each sample size $n$, the critical region is chosen as the largest set of the form $X\ge c$ with significance level at most $5\%$. Find the smallest $n$ for which the power at $p=0.5$ is at least $0.9$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.3$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p>0.3$ [A1] Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,0.3)$; $P(X\ge9)=0.113>0.05$ [A1] $P(X\ge10)=0.0480\le0.05$ [A1] Critical region: $X\ge10$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Actual significance level $=0.0480$ [A1] When $p=0.5$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,0.5)$ and Type II error is $P(X\le9)$ [M1] $=0.412$ [A1] Power $=1-0.412=0.588$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Power $=P(X\ge10)$ for $\mathrm{B}(20,p)$ [M1] $p=0.4$: $0.245$ [A1] $p=0.6$: $0.872$, $p=0.7$: $0.983$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $P(X\ge10)=0.5$ for $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,p)$ [M1] $p=0.475$ [A1] If the true completion rate is $0.475$ the test detects the increase only half the time [R1] [3 marks] (e) Power $=P(X\ge10)$ at $p=0.3$ $=0.0480$ [A1] This is the probability of rejecting $\mathrm{H}_0$ when it is true, that is, the probability of a Type I error [R1] [2 marks] (f) $P(X\ge10)=0.0676>0.05$ and $P(X\ge11)=0.0264$ for $\mathrm{B}(21,0.3)$, so critical region is $X\ge11$ with actual level $0.0264$ [A1][A1] At $p=0.5$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(21,0.5)$ is symmetric so $P(X\ge11)=0.5$ [A1] The power is lower than $0.588$ despite the larger sample, because the critical value jumps up and the significance level falls (discreteness) [R1] [4 marks] (g) For each $n$ find the smallest $c$ with $P(X\ge c)\le0.05$ under $\mathrm{B}(n,0.3)$, then evaluate $P(X\ge c)$ under $\mathrm{B}(n,0.5)$ [M1] $n=50$: $c=21$, power $0.899<0.9$ [A1] $n=52$: $c=22$, power $0.894<0.9$ [A1] $n=53$: $c=22$, level $0.0495$, power $0.916\ge0.9$ [A1] Table shows no smaller $n$ reaches $0.9$ (the power is not monotonic in $n$, so every smaller value must be checked), so $n=53$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Part (f) shows that power does not rise steadily with sample size for a discrete test: the critical region jumps at certain values of $n$, so you must check each $n$ with your GDC table rather than assume monotonic behavior. In part (d), define the power as a function of $p$ and use the solver or graph intersection.
